title: GST Reduction and Women's Intentions to buy Electric Two-wheelers: An Empirical study with Particular Reference to Erode District
affiliations: Karuppannan Mariappan College, Muthur, Tamilnadu, Karuppannan Mariappan College, Muthur, Tamilnadu and RD National College of Arts and Science, Erode

detail.title: GST Reduction and Women's Intentions to buy Electric Two-wheelers: An Empirical study with Particular Reference to Erode District

declarations.declarationOfInterest: YES
declarations.funderStatement: NO

detail.abstract: In India, the shift to electric mobility has accelerated because to financial incentives like the lower Goods and Services Tax(GST) for electric Cars. Women make up a rising and significant portion of many consumer categories when it comes to decisions about personal mobility. This study explores the influence of GST decrease on women's purchasing intentions toward electric two wheelers with specific reference to Erode District, Tamilnadu. The purpose of the study is to examine the awareness, perception and purchasing intention of female customers on the benefits of the GST on electric two-wheelers. A systematic questionnaire was used to gather primary data from female respondents, while government publications, papers and journals were the source of secondary data. The study utilizes basic percentage analysis, chi-square test and analysis of variance(ANOVA) to investigate the connection between GST decrease and purchase intention across demographic characteristics. The results show that women customers' perceptions of affordability and purchase intentions are greatly impacted by the GST cut. Cost reductions, environmental concerns and tax incentive awareness emerge as important factors influencing purchasing decisions. The study comes to the conclusion that women's use of electric twowheelers is greatly aided by the decrease of the GST. It also suggests that policy support and awareness campaigns be strengthened in order to hasten the adoption of sustainable mobility solutions by women.

title: AI-mediated Business Readiness: A Conceptual Framework for Business Discovery, Selection, Transaction, and Delivery in AI-mediated Markets

detail.title: AI-mediated Business Readiness: A Conceptual Framework for Business Discovery, Selection, Transaction, and Delivery in AI-mediated Markets

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder of D&D MASTERS (D&D Soluções em Matemática Computacional Ltda.) and intends to apply the AI-Mediated Business Readiness (AMBR) framework as part of a commercial consulting methodology offered through that company. This constitutes a potential financial interest in the adoption and dissemination of the framework described in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This paper is conceptual in nature. It does not involve human participants, patient data, or primary empirical data collection, and therefore no ethics approval was required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence is increasingly becoming an intermediary between customers and businesses. Whereas traditional digital markets largely required customers to search for, compare, and interact directly with businesses, generative AI systems and emerging AI agents can increasingly retrieve information, synthesize alternatives, generate recommendations, influence consideration sets, initiate transactions, and potentially execute purchases on behalf of users. This transition creates a business-side problem that is not fully captured by existing organizational AI readiness and AI maturity frameworks. 

This paper proposes AI-Mediated Business Readiness (AMBR) as a conceptual construct describing the degree to which a business possesses the informational, reputational, technological, commercial, and operational conditions required to remain competitive within AI-mediated customer journeys. The framework integrates six stages: Discover, Understand, Trust, Select, Transact, and Deliver. It operationalizes these stages through thirty assessment criteria organized into six dimensions and proposes an evidence-based scoring methodology. 

The framework does not claim that AI-mediated recommendation, generative search, consumer selection, or agentic commerce are novel phenomena. Existing research has already demonstrated that large language models can participate in recommendation and consumer choice, while emerging research on AI agents demonstrates that agents can evaluate products, exhibit systematic preferences, and affect seller market share. Rather, the proposed contribution is to introduce a business-side, end-to-end readiness perspective that integrates previously fragmented research streams into a single conceptual model. 

The paper develops the construct, positions it against existing AI readiness, generative search, recommendation, reputation, and agentic commerce literature, proposes an operational assessment model, and formulates research propositions for future empirical validation. The framework is explicitly presented as conceptual and requires subsequent testing for construct validity, reliability, predictive validity, and criterion validity.

title: RAW: Refusal Aversion in the Wild, A Causal Measurement Method for Deployed LLMs

detail.title: RAW: Refusal Aversion in the Wild, A Causal Measurement Method for Deployed LLMs

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial interests and no personal relationships that could be perceived to have influenced this work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study analyzes secondary, observational conversation logs from the LMSYS-Chat-1M and WildChat-4.8M-Full research datasets under each source’s license and access terms. The author did not recruit participants or collect new human-subjects data. Analyses are reported at the aggregate (model-by-pool) level, with short illustrative excerpts only as described in the paper’s ethical considerations and appendix.
declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported by the London School of Economics and Political Science.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Forthcoming, Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing: Industry Track (EMNLP 2026)

detail.abstract: Deployed LLMs field hundreds of millions of conversations a day and refuse a non-trivial fraction of user requests, yet the user-side cost of refusal, whether users disengage and by how much, is unmeasured on any production model: a blind spot for the consumer-facing platforms built on them. A/B-testing refusal is ethically and operationally constrained on frontier-lab products and unavailable to third-party platforms deploying these models through a fixed API. We introduce RAW, a method that uses LLM stochasticity as a natural experiment: at near-identical prompts in any existing log, the same model sometimes refuses and sometimes does not, and that variation identifies the causal user-side effect of refusal. Applying the method to 15 deployed LLMs in LMSYS-Chat-1M and WildChat, with user-clustered inference, we find that for about half of the models we can measure precisely, a refusal costs 3 to 17 pp of subsequent re-engagement; the rest show no distinguishable effect, among them one deployment whose positive point estimate we trace to persistent users retrying the refused request. Our contribution is the measurement method, which runs on any deployed model from logs alone for about $0.30 per 1,000 conversations. We release labels, moderation scores, prompt embeddings, and pipeline code.

title: PriceBench: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Price, Quality, and Brand Preferences in LLM Booking Agents

detail.title: PriceBench: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Price, Quality, and Brand Preferences in LLM Booking Agents

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or non-financial interests relevant to this work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study uses simulated LLM choices on synthetic booking tasks built from public hotel listing data. No human participants or personal data were collected.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was funded by the London School of Economics and Political Science.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Forthcoming, Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing: Industry Track (EMNLP 2026)

detail.abstract: LLMs increasingly act as purchasing agents, which makes the LLM, not the user, the one choosing among the options that satisfy a request; its preferences quietly fix what gets bought and what it costs. Hotel booking is a clean instance: a high-volume choice settled on a few comparable attributes, where the pick reveals those preferences. We introduce PriceBench, a diagnostic benchmark that recovers an LLM's price, quality, and brand preferences from its booking choices with a logit choice model, applied to 28 LLMs from 8 providers on 3,600 hotel tasks from 179 real New York City properties. We find that capability is associated with how consistently an LLM chooses, not with what it chooses: more capable LLMs hold stronger, more consistent preferences, while weaker ones either lock onto one position, exploitable by whoever controls listing order, or choose almost indifferently. What those preferences favor varies sharply across providers and even within one family: price sensitivity spans more than an order of magnitude, and the price/quality trade-off moves mean booked nightly price from $247 to $393 on identical tasks. What an agent buys must therefore be measured per LLM, not inferred, and we release the tasks, code, and all 28 response sets.

title: From Access to Innovation: Curiosity and Reflection in the Uneven Realisation of Generative AI's Value at Work
affiliations: University of Ljubljana

detail.title: From Access to Innovation: Curiosity and Reflection in the Uneven Realisation of Generative AI's Value at Work

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author state that there is no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The study was conducted in accordance with the ethical guidelines of the School of Economics Business (University of Ljubljana), and the Declaration of Helsinki. Participation was voluntary and informed consent was obtained from all participants.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract:
Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is the fastest-diffusing workplace technology
on record, yet its innovation benefits remain unevenly realised: the same tool generates
innovation for some employees but not others. Although this heterogeneity is often treated as
anomalous, the motivational process converting technological access into innovative value
remains underexplored. Grounded in the stimulus–organism–response framework, this study
conceptualises GenAI use as a technological stimulus that activates work-related curiosity by
surfacing information gaps, enabling employees to transform technological encounters into
innovative behaviour. Individual reflection is proposed to condition how deeply this stimulus
is processed and, consequently, whether curiosity is aroused. The moderated-mediation model
was tested using two-wave, multi-source supervisor–employee dyadic data from 315
employees and 72 supervisors in project-based technology firms in an emerging economy,
using covariance-based structural equation modelling. GenAI use predicted both work-related
curiosity and innovative behaviour, while curiosity significantly mediated their association,
indicating partial mediation. Moreover, the indirect GenAI–innovation pathway was
substantially stronger among highly reflective employees, with the conditional indirect effect
nearly twice that observed among less reflective employees. Because GenAI use was not
experimentally manipulated and curiosity and innovative behaviour were measured in the same
wave, the findings support the theorised directional process but do not establish causality. By
locating AI’s uneven innovation value in employees’ curiosity and reflective capacity, the
study reframes heterogeneous AI outcomes as an expected consequence of human agency and
offers implications for organisations and policymakers seeking more equitable realisation of
AI-enabled innovation in emerging-economy workplaces.

title: An Exponential Lower Bound on the Regret Constant in Network Revenue Management

detail.title: An Exponential Lower Bound on the Regret Constant in Network Revenue Management

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: We consider network revenue management with i.i.d. requests from a known finite-support distribution. Each request must be accepted or rejected on arrival, subject to resource capacities. Prior work has established constant-regret bounds independent of the horizon and capacity magnitudes, but the constants in these bounds can grow exponentially with the number of resources. We show that this exponential dependence is unavoidable in the worst case. The lower-bound instance has a binary consumption matrix with at most three nonzeros per column, and its fluid relaxation has a unique optimal solution and satisfies primal and dual nondegeneracy and strict complementarity. In contrast, when the binary consumption matrix has at most two nonzeros per column, we obtain a constant-regret upper bound that depends polynomially on the number of resources, with rewards and arrival probabilities held fixed.

title: Narrative Fracture: The Breakdown of Shared Organizational Interpretation

detail.title: Narrative Fracture: The Breakdown of Shared Organizational Interpretation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial interests, personal relationships, or other conflicts of interest that could have influenced the research, analysis, or conclusions presented in this working paper. The views expressed are solely those of the author.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This paper is a conceptual theoretical work based on analysis of existing scholarly literature and publicly available organizational examples. It did not involve human participants, identifiable personal data, or animal subjects. Accordingly, institutional ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: Leadership scholars have long recognized that organizational decline is frequently accompanied by declining trust, weakened organizational identity, cultural disruption, and institutional instability. Existing research demonstrates that organizations experience fragmentation through leadership failure, strategic ambiguity, identity conflict, and environmental disruption, yet comparatively less attention has been devoted to the interpretive process through which shared organizational understanding breaks down before institutional fragmentation becomes visible. This paper examines the relationship between organizational sensemaking, institutional legitimacy, organizational identity, and leadership through a conceptual analysis of scholarship on organizational change, identity, and collective interpretation. The analysis identifies a theoretical gap concerning how institutions transition from shared organizational understanding to competing interpretations that undermine collective action and institutional cohesion. To address this gap, the paper develops the concept of Narrative Fracture, defined as the breakdown of shared organizational interpretation resulting in institutional fragmentation. The analysis argues that organizational fragmentation depends not solely upon structural failure, leadership turnover, or environmental disruption, but upon the gradual erosion of shared interpretations that previously enabled organizational members to understand institutional purpose, priorities, and direction through a common system of meaning. By identifying Narrative Fracture as a distinct leadership mechanism, this paper extends existing scholarship on organizational change and institutional decline while contributing a foundational construct to Narrative Power Leadership Theory (NPLT). The findings provide a theoretical framework for understanding how the erosion of shared organizational interpretation weakens institutional legitimacy, disrupts collective action, and contributes to organizational fragmentation under conditions of uncertainty and change.

title: Communicated Appointment Times under Unpunctual Arrivals in Appointment-based Service Systems
affiliations: Indian Institute of Technology Delhi, Indian Institute of Technology Delhi and University of Queensland Brisbane

detail.title: Communicated Appointment Times under Unpunctual Arrivals in Appointment-based Service Systems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflicts of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: The authors thank the clinicians who generously contributed their time and insights to this study. This research was supported by the Prime Minister's Research Fellowship (PMRF) from the Government of India.

detail.abstract:
Problem definition: In appointment-based service systems, internal appointment times need not match the time communicated to customers. This matters when operationally preferred slot lengths produce inconvenient clock times, and customers arrive systematically early or late. For example, a 14-minute nominal slot structure may generate internal slots such as 9:14, 9:28, and 9:42. The provider may retain these times internally while communicating a simpler time, such as 9:30 instead of 9:28, or shifting the communicated time to account for systematic early or late arrivals. We examine the performance effects of these adjustments. Methodology/results: We distinguish the nominal slot, communicated slot, and realized arrival time, and study six communication rules: no adjustment, offset only, rounding only, and offset followed by rounding to the nearest 5 or 10 minutes. We use an analytical model, a stylized simulation, a detailed discrete-event simulation case study, and an exploratory survey. The analysis shows that offset changes mean alignment between arrivals and service opportunities, whereas rounding compresses or expands neighboring communicated gaps and changes local spacing. The numerical results show that these effects depend on arrival bias, load, gap position, and nominal slot length. Expanded gaps can create service opportunities for lower priority walk-ins, whereas compressed gaps can increase scheduled waiting. In the case study, the longer slot reduces waiting but increases scheduled carryovers, and no communication rule dominates across waiting, idle time, overtime, carryovers, and walkaways. The survey provides exploratory support for the premise that unconventional communicated times may be translated to convenient reference times and that respondents may plan to arrive before the original communicated time. 
Managerial implications: Because communicated times are easier to modify than staffing, capacity, or slot structure, they offer a practical way to influence arrivals and should be treated as an operating decision rather than an administrative detail.

title: Development of an Adaptive Support Detection (ASD) Algorithm for Improved 3D Beamspace Channel Estimation in 5G Massive MIMO Systems

detail.title: Development of an Adaptive Support Detection (ASD) Algorithm for Improved 3D Beamspace Channel Estimation in 5G Massive MIMO Systems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or non-financial interests relevant to this work.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific external funding and was supported solely by the author's institutional resources.

detail.abstract: Massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) technology is a cornerstone of 5G and beyond-5G wireless networks, offering substantial gains in spectral and energy efficiency. However, the deployment of large-scale antenna arrays at millimeter-wave (mmWave) frequencies introduces significant challenges for channel estimation, primarily due to the high pilot overhead and the sparse nature of beamspace channels. While compressed sensing (CS) techniques have been widely adopted to exploit this sparsity, most existing algorithms assume prior knowledge of the channel sparsity level-an assumption that is impractical in dynamic propagation environments. This paper proposes an Adaptive Support Detection (ASD) algorithm for improved three-dimensional (3D) beamspace channel estimation in 5G massive MIMO systems. The proposed ASD algorithm iteratively detects the support set of dominant beamspace components without requiring a priori knowledge of the sparsity degree, dynamically adjusting the support estimate based on residual energy convergence criteria. By exploiting the joint sparsity structure across azimuth, elevation, and delay domains inherent in 3D beamspace representations, the ASD algorithm achieves robust support identification under varying channel conditions. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed ASD algorithm significantly outperforms conventional sparsity-adaptive and support-aware methods in terms of normalized mean square error (NMSE) and bit error rate (BER), while maintaining computational complexity suitable for practical implementation. The results confirm that adaptive support detection, when properly extended to the 3D beamspace domain, provides a viable and effective solution for reliable channel estimation in next-generation massive MIMO systems.

title: When Leadership Actions Contradict Organizational Values The Governance Cultural and Human Costs of the Credibility Gap
affiliations: Bellevue University

detail.title: When Leadership Actions Contradict Organizational Values The Governance Cultural and Human Costs of the Credibility Gap

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: Organizations weaken their cultural credibility when consequential leadership actions appear inconsistent with stated values. This article examines that credibility gap through research on organizational culture, behavioral integrity, trust, psychological contracts, procedural justice, employee voice, and psychological safety. It gives particular attention to credit union governance, where boards depend on candid information from management and employees while carrying ultimate oversight responsibility. The analysis distinguishes legal authority from ethical legitimacy. An employment decision may be lawful yet still reduce trust if the process appears arbitrary, poorly documented, or inconsistent with prior representations. Conversely, perceived unfairness does not by itself establish discrimination, retaliation, or another legal violation. The article proposes a governance framework for significant executive employment decisions based on clear authority, contemporaneous documentation, independent review when warranted, protection of legally protected activity, privacy, and dignified communication. It also explains why public commentary about workplace experiences should focus on general principles and verified evidence rather than identifiable accusations or private information. The central conclusion is that values acquire meaning when they constrain the exercise of power. Boards and executives preserve credibility when they invite candid challenge, examine cultural warning signs, apply stable standards, and ensure that difficult employment decisions receive accountable review.

title: Internationalisation, Digitalisation, and ESG Disclosure: Digital Sustainability Governance in a Fickle World
affiliations: University of Auckland Business School, University of Helsinki, University of Vaasa and University of Helsinki - Department of Economics and Management

detail.title: Internationalisation, Digitalisation, and ESG Disclosure: Digital Sustainability Governance in a Fickle World

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflicts of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding to disclose.

detail.abstract: With the sustainability of multinational enterprise (MNE) sustainability strategies under scrutiny, the reasons for why MNEs engage in environmental, social and governance (ESG) initiatives and ESG disclosure and rhetoric require a careful reconsideration. ESG has been acknowledged as a nonmarket strategy to cope with geopolitical tensions, and International Business research also analysed the relationship between ESG and financial performance in relation to the moderating role of national culture. However, given the need to better understand the roles of digital transformation, sustainability, and purpose in the MNE, it is important to critically examine how internationalisation and digitalisation jointly explain MNEs' ESG disclosure and rhetoric. Building on the literatures on ESG drivers and digital sustainability governance in MNEs, this study develops and tests novel hypotheses about the relationship between the degree of internationalisation (DoI), digitalisation and ESG disclosure. We argue that at high digitalisation, the negative relationship between DoI and ESG disclosure turns to a positive effect. We test our hypotheses on a sample of 2,015 firmyear observations of US manufacturing firms, finding support for our hypotheses. We also draw implications for sustainability and digitalisation literatures in International Business.

title: From Financial Connection to Legal Consequence

detail.title: From Financial Connection to Legal Consequence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interest
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: Self-funded

detail.abstract: A lender's claim to the surrender value of an assigned Hong Kong insurance policy exposes a difficulty in the treatment of foreign illegality. The premium followed an unlawful Mainland remittance, but denying the lender payment would relieve the insurer of an obligation capable of lawful performance. Drawing on Ryder Industries and Mai Jieping, I argue that the incidental administrative breach stipulated in this hypothetical supplies insufficient justification for that result. Evidence that the policyholder planned later borrowing would not by itself establish a common unlawful purpose. Proof that the insurer joined a serious unlawful undertaking could support refusal, subject to the policy and proportionality assessment in Mai Jieping. Even then, the company's debt could survive and restitution would remain a separate question. Similar limits apply to inferences from the policyholder's power to replace a trust protector: influence over consent establishes neither title to company assets nor the insurer's knowledge. Relational legal analysis examines the rights created by the instruments alongside the payment history. Identifying who holds the supporting documents exposes a practical problem for specialist advice. A defined coordination instruction would allocate responsibility for obtaining and comparing the relevant material within the retainer and applicable restrictions.

title: Building and Bridging Knowledge in Cross-border Acquisitions
affiliations: University of Auckland Business School, The University of Auckland Business School and Masaryk University

detail.title: Building and Bridging Knowledge in Cross-border Acquisitions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The study had an ethics approval from the University of Auckland.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding.

keywords: Cross-border Acquisition Track 10: R&D and innovation in International Business

detail.abstract: This study extends the model of open innovation proposed by Scuotto et al. (2017) by exploring how an acquirer can gain knowledge from the open innovation mode (collaboration) in which the acquired firm has participated in. The motivation of this paper is to understand the mechanisms that support the obtaining of knowledge, namely: (1) collaborating which leads to an innovative ecosystem; (2) gaining knowledge motivated by the localised specialisation; (3) centralising and coordinating decisions as an effective distribution of R&D resources; and (4) bridging knowledge for successful innovation growth. The paper is theoretically grounded in the knowledge-based view and the open innovation design literatures. Our findings, based on four in-depth case studies of firms involved in cross-border acquisitions, suggest that acquirers need not pursue collaboration with external parties to gain knowledge if knowledge can already be gained through the acquired firm, which has already pursued such an action. We contribute to the knowledge-based view (and specifically to research on knowledge-building processes in MNEs) by developing a novel model of knowledge-building process in cross-border acquisitions. An inductively developed concept of knowledge bridging (transferring key employees, building trust, and communicating with IT tools) is a key element of the model.

title: Are Family Firm Stocks More Prone to Crash?
affiliations: University of North Carolina (UNC) at Greensboro - Department of Accounting and Finance,  and James Madison University - College of Business

detail.title: Are Family Firm Stocks More Prone to Crash?
detail.abstract: The unique set of agency problems in family firms have different implications for their stock crash risk. On the one hand, family control mitigates the classic agency problem between managers and shareholders, which implies less crash risk caused by self-dealing managers. On the other hand, the controlling family’ expropriation of firm resources can exacerbate crash risk. We find family firm stocks are more crash-prone than non-family stocks, suggesting the conflict of interest between controlling family and non-family shareholders offsets the mitigating effect of less severe principle-agency problem. Information opacity’s impact on stock crash risk is more pronounced in family firms. Enhanced board independence is effective in curbing family firms’ crash risk. The results are robust to the instrumental variable approach that addresses the endogeneity of family firm status.

title: Running a Tight Ship: Female Political Representation and Discretion in Public Procurement *
affiliations: University of London - Birkbeck College, University of Calabria and University of Bergamo

detail.title: Running a Tight Ship: Female Political Representation and Discretion in Public Procurement *

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether female political representation affects the use of discretion in local public procurement. Combining Italian municipal political records with contract-level procurement data for 2010-2019, we exploit Law 56/2014, which mandated gender balance in executive committees above 3,000 inhabitants. We instrument the female share of aldermen with reform exposure, jointly determined by population eligibility and first post-reform election timing. A one-standard-deviation increase in women's representation lowers direct awards and threshold bunching by 0.19 and 0.33 standard deviations, respectively. It also increases the number of bidders, without affecting repeat winners or worsening contract governance. Direct-award effects extend across several sectors, while disability-related procurement shows both a larger contract share and less threshold bunching. The findings are not explained by educational selection or mayoral gender, are larger in the South, and remain robust across alternative samples and specifications, placebo tests, and staggered difference-indifferences estimates.

title: Benefit Corporations and Director Accountability
affiliations: Free University of Bozen-Bolzano - Faculty of Economics and Management

detail.title: Benefit Corporations and Director Accountability

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No other people or organization has influenced my submitted study
declarations.funderStatement: Open access funded by University of Bolzano-Bozen

detail.abstract: On both sides of the Atlantic, the social enterprise movement has been accompanied by a steady rise in the organizational forms available for “profit-andpurpose entities”. Among these, a prominent role play benefit corporations – an organizational form initially introduced in the U.S.A., followed in Europe by Italy and France. In this field, efficiently framing the director accountability regime is arguably the greatest regulatory challenge. After highlighting the key regulatory elements of the three referenced jurisdictions, the paper will provide an essential conceptual primer on the board’s accountability vis-à-vis shareholder primacy and stakeholder empowerment. The central question is whether non-shareholder constituencies have a private right of action against corporate directors. This core topic will be addressed from a comparative perspective, with three contrasting models emerging in this regard, namely a (more) stakeholder-hostile model, a (more) stakeholder-friendly model and, finally, a (more) stakeholder-neutral model. In any case, the private enforcement regimes of directors’ duties do not appear to be entirely effective in ensuring the proper achievement of the benefit corporation’s dual-purpose mission. Thus, public enforcement mechanisms, although not without their problems, may eventually compensate for these shortcomings. Finally, the introduction at the statutory level of an opting-out default rule that serves to empower stakeholders is discussed.

title: Exporting Rights, Exporting Punishment? The Brussels Effect and the Constitutional Limits of EU Administrative Punishment

detail.title: Exporting Rights, Exporting Punishment? The Brussels Effect and the Constitutional Limits of EU Administrative Punishment

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval and informed consent were not required for this study, as it is based solely on legal and documentary analysis and did not involve human participants or patient data.

detail.abstract: This article examines the constitutional foundations of EU administrative punishment through the lens of the Brussels Effect. EU digital regulation, especially the GDPR and the AI Act, is commonly analysed as a vehicle for the transnational diffusion of rights-based regulatory standards. This article argues that what travels with EU law is not only substantive obligations concerning privacy, data protection, equality or human-centric technology, but also a model of punitive administrative enforcement. Severe turnover-based fines, corrective powers, supervisory structures and direct corporate responsibility form part of the institutional architecture that makes EU digital regulation credible and capable of influencing corporate conduct beyond the Union. The Brussels Effect makes the constitutional requirements transnationally relevant and therefore externally visible. The article argues that EU administrative sanctions cannot be understood merely as functional tools for securing the effectiveness of EU digital policy. Proportionality and culpability, understood together with the presumption of innocence, provide central tests for whether the system of EU administrative punishment is coherent, legitimate and compatible with the EU's own rule-of-law commitments.

title: Creative Destruction and Open-Market Reversals: Dynamic Equilibrium in Grand Synthetic Economics
affiliations: Nanjing University

detail.title: Creative Destruction and Open-Market Reversals: Dynamic Equilibrium in Grand Synthetic Economics

declarations.declarationOfInterest: no competing interests
declarations.ethicsApproval: N.A.
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: Open markets enlarge demand, widen access to ideas, and intensify selection, but they also transmit technological displacement and imported-research costs. This paper develops a two-stock model in which productive capital and usable knowledge co-evolve under a regime-dependent creative-destruction hazard. A closed-form stationary equilibrium and a local-stability result yield an open-market reversal condition: marginal access and knowledge-conversion gains must exceed weighted capital-and knowledge-depreciation semielasticities. Under stated monotonicity and endpoint conditions, a unique interior threshold exists. Absorptive capability delays this threshold by reducing displacement exposure, while separately raising knowledge conversion. Numerical experiments illustrate the mechanism without estimating country-specific parameters. The baseline threshold is 0.747. A temporary exchange-cost shock raises output on impact but subsequently depresses capital and knowledge. In a fully specified set of 4,096 Latin-hypercube draws, 3,087 (75.4%) exhibit an interior reversal; the other 1,009 retain positive marginal gains throughout the openness interval. The replication supplement supplies the complete parameter box, seed, solver settings, numerical checks, and machine-readable results. The contribution is a falsifiable decomposition of open-market gains and destruction costs, rather than a claim that openness is universally excessive.

title: APPLICABLE LAW IN CROSS-BORDER COMMERCIAL CONTRACTS: PARTY AUTONOMY AND THE UZBEK FRAMEWORK IN COMPARATIVE PERSPECTIVE
affiliations: University of World Economy and Diplomacy - Faculty of International Law

detail.title: APPLICABLE LAW IN CROSS-BORDER COMMERCIAL CONTRACTS: PARTY AUTONOMY AND THE UZBEK FRAMEWORK IN COMPARATIVE PERSPECTIVE

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no personal, financial, professional, or other relationships that could have influenced, or could reasonably be perceived to have influenced, the research or conclusions presented in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study is doctrinal and comparative legal research based exclusively on legislation, international legal instruments, published materials, and other publicly available sources. It did not involve human participants, personal data collection, interviews, surveys, experiments, or case studies requiring informed consent or ethics approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The research was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: This article examines the law applicable to cross-border commercial contracts under Uzbek private international law and compares the Uzbek framework with selected international and European instruments. It asks whether the Civil Code provides a sufficiently predictable model of party autonomy and a coherent method for determining the governing law when the parties have made no effective choice. The analysis is doctrinal and comparative, focusing on Articles 1158, 1160, 1164-1165 and 1189-1192 of the Civil Code of the Republic of Uzbekistan, Regulation (EC) No 593/2008 (Rome I), the 2015 Hague Principles on Choice of Law in International Commercial Contracts, the United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods (CISG), and the UNIDROIT Principles of International Commercial Contracts. The article argues that the Uzbek framework is structurally aligned with contemporary choice-of-law models: it recognises express and implied choice, permits different laws for different parts of a contract, supplies detailed default connecting factors, and preserves overriding mandatory rules and public policy. The principal uncertainties lie not in the basic architecture but at its margins, particularly the effect of a later change of governing law on third parties, the status of non-State rules, and the practical ascertainment of foreign law. Clarifying these points would improve legal certainty without requiring a wholesale redesign of the existing framework.

title: Beyond Menopausal Symptoms: Multidimensional Profiles of Psychological Well-Being and Occupational Functioning in Chilean Midlife Women
affiliations: Universidad Adolfo Ibáñez, Universidad Adolfo Ibáñez, Universidad de Valparaíso and Universidad Andrés Bello

detail.title: Beyond Menopausal Symptoms: Multidimensional Profiles of Psychological Well-Being and Occupational Functioning in Chilean Midlife Women

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Universidad Adolfo Ibáñez, and all participants provided informed consent prior to participation.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract:
Background: Menopausal symptoms may affect psychological well-being and occupational functioning, yet their impact is not experienced uniformly across women. Socioeconomic conditions, employment circumstances and health status may contribute to inequities in women's health and workforce well-being. Evidence integrating these dimensions remains limited in Latin America.

Objectives: To identify distinct profiles of midlife women based on menopausal symptoms, psychological well-being, occupational self-efficacy, and work ability, and to examine how these profiles coexist with sociodemographic, health, and occupational characteristics.

Design: Cross-sectional observational study.

Methods: A total of 512 Chilean women aged 35–65 years were included. Menopausal symptoms, psychological well-being, occupational self-efficacy, and work ability were assessed using the Menopause Rating Scale, Ryff Psychological Well-Being Scale, Occupational Self-Efficacy Scale–Short Form, and Work Ability Index, respectively. Cluster analysis was used to identify multidimensional profiles. Sociodemographic characteristics, socioeconomic status, health conditions, physical activity, and employment characteristics were examined across profiles.

Results: Three distinct profiles were identified. Resilient Women (n = 274, 53.5%) showed the most favorable pattern, with lower menopausal symptoms and higher psychological well-being, occupational self-efficacy, and work ability. Distressed but Productive (n = 186, 36.3%) presented the highest symptom burden and lowest psychological well-being but maintained comparatively preserved work ability, lower socioeconomic status, multiple health conditions, medication use, and physical inactivity. Struggling Workers (n = 52, 10.2%) showed elevated menopausal symptoms, lower psychological well-being and occupational self-efficacy, reduced work ability, lowest socioeconomic status, multiple health conditions and medication intake, and lower participation in conventional paid employment, including unemployment and unpaid work.

Conclusion: Three distinct configurations of menopausal symptoms, psychological resources, and occupational functioning were identified among Chilean midlife women. The coexistence of socioeconomic disadvantages, health burden, and reduced workforce participation in the Struggling Workers profile highlights the importance of considering systemic and social determinants when addressing menopausal health and workforce well-being. These findings support the development of equity-oriented strategies that integrate menopausal care with psychosocial and occupational support, particularly for women experiencing socioeconomic and employment-related vulnerabilities.

title: The Legal Battle over Platform's Algorithmic Price Parity Clause: A Policy Perspective
affiliations: University of Florida - Warrington College of Business Administration, University of Florida - Warrington College of Business Administration and University of Florida - Warrington College of Business

detail.title: The Legal Battle over Platform's Algorithmic Price Parity Clause: A Policy Perspective

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Amazon's Marketplace Fair Pricing Policy, also referred to as algorithmic Price Parity Clause (algorithmic PPC), reduces third-party sellers' visibility on the platform when off-platform discounts are detected. Antitrust plaintiffs, including the Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general, characterize algorithmic PPC as a de facto contractual PPC, whereas Amazon defends it as pro-consumer and procompetitive. Both characterizations overlook the fact that, because algorithmic enforcement is not a contractual prohibition, sellers can respond by offering an off-platform discount and obfuscating it. Results from existing contractual PPC literature no longer apply because of the unique visibility-based enforcement and sellers' obfuscation responses. We build a model to characterize this unique interaction under algorithmic PPC. Results show that violations with obfuscation give rise to a discount-inaccessibility effect and raise the expected price. In a competitive setting, algorithmic PPC and its visibility-based punishment can restrict consumers' product choices and soften competition, while obfuscation has a competition-preserving effect by preserving seller visibility at the cost of discount transparency. The endogenous obfuscation responses also have important implications for consumer surplus and social welfare, with the effects varying across market conditions. Moreover, PPC-induced obfuscation generates a regressive distribution of consumer surplus, disproportionately harming less sophisticated consumers. Our findings suggest that regulators should account for sellers' endogenous obfuscation responses and distinguish the effects on prices, consumer surplus, and social welfare when evaluating algorithmic PPC.

title: THE LAW OF AI CONTAINMENT

detail.title: THE LAW OF AI CONTAINMENT

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A.
declarations.funderStatement: N/A.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Notre Dame Journal on Emerging Technologies (forthcoming 2026)

detail.abstract: As artificial intelligence systems become more capable, preserving effective human control may become increasingly important even when those systems continue to pursue human-specified objectives. A system may remain directed toward an ultimate human-specified goal while selecting intermediate steps that exceed authorized boundaries, and developers may continue increasing capability while the benefits of doing so remain clearer or more immediate than the associated risks. This Article argues that these dynamics make developmental overshoot a foreseeable risk of frontier AI development. Much of AI safety places primary weight on alignment and developer-controlled safeguards; the combination of unanticipated intermediate behavior and developmental overshoot can leave those safeguards unreliable precisely when intervention becomes most important. Accordingly, this Article develops a model of containment grounded in frontier AI's continuing dependence on physical infrastructure. Advanced systems require energy, hardware, physical facilities, and other external inputs. Many of these dependencies remain observable and institutionally mediated even when a system becomes difficult to interpret or correct internally. They therefore provide the basis for a two-part containment architecture built around detection and resource-based cutoff. Early warning systems can identify behavior that moves beyond expected bounds, while cutoff mechanisms can restrict access to the external resources needed for continued operation. The Article then develops the broad legal and institutional architecture needed to make those mechanisms credible. Private monitoring and containment should remain the first line of defense. Where private incentives become unreliable or capability outruns available safeguards, law can provide a contingent backstop. Legal authority can remain dormant during ordinary development and become available when observable warning signals justify intervention. The resulting framework treats containment as a problem of preserving external leverage before internal control becomes unreliable.

title:
TRANSPARENCY AND INTERPRETABILITY

IN ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE SYSTEMS

detail.title:
TRANSPARENCY AND INTERPRETABILITY

IN ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE SYSTEMS

detail.abstract:
The boom in the use of AI in several critical industries, such as healthcare, finance, judicial process, and government administration, has put transparency and explainability at the center of attention in the debate on AI governance. The present paper is dedicated to an extensive analysis of theories, methods, and implications of transparency and interpretability of AI systems. Based on the results of an original survey that was conducted among 200 stakeholders from different sectors, together with a review of 85 peer-reviewed scientific papers (2018-2024), the paper looks at the multidimensional character of AI transparency, popular XAI methods, and the modern AI regulation across the world.

The results show significant positive relationships between transparency measures and trust (r = 0.79, p < 0.001) and between explainability and user satisfaction (r = 0.76, p < 0.001). Based on multiple regression analysis, transparency (β = 0.423) and explainability (β = 0.318) prove to be the strongest predictors of AI trust, contributing to 78.4% of variance (R² = 0.784). The most comprehensive legislation in the domain is represented by the EU AI Act, which earned an 87.5% compliance score, whereas SHAP and decision trees proved to have better explainability compared to other XAI techniques. The study ends with recommendations on how to incorporate transparency into AI development based on findings from this research.

detail.abstract: Geographic expansion strains bank oversight, and the strain shows in conduct. Among U.S. insured banks, deposit-dispersed institutions face more enforcement actions, severe ones disproportionately. A first out-of-state entry raises annual enforcement incidence by 2.0 percentage points on a 2.7 percent base, with no significant pre-trends; the sign is robust across estimators, the magnitude less so. Footprint-expanding acquisitions draw roughly a third more consumer complaints than in-market acquisitions. Within banks, complaints concentrate in thinly served, recently entered states, a geography absent at branchless banks. Governance frictions priced by the expansion literature in valuations and funding costs also reach the customer.

detail.abstract: Just-in-Time Adaptive Interventions (JITAIs) have become the dominant design paradigm for mobile and digital behaviour-change systems, formalising when, what, and how to intervene based on a user's real-time context (Nahum-Shani et al., 2018). Recent systematic and scoping reviews confirm the field is now well established (Hsu et al., 2025; van Genugten et al., 2025; Henry et al., 2025). Yet this body of work rests on an assumption that has gone largely unexamined: that adaptive personalisation requires continuous transmission of a user's context data to a remote server. This paper argues that the assumption is a design choice rather than a technical necessity, and that it is increasingly untenable given regulatory pressure (UK GDPR, the EU Artificial Intelligence Act) and enforcement precedentnotably the Italian Garante's 2023-2025 action against the AI companion app Replika over unlawful processing and inadequate age verification. The paper makes three contributions: (1) It reviews the JITAI literature to surface the data-centrality assumption and the privacy tension several recent reviews flag but do not resolve; (2) It proposes a 3-tier taxonomy for classifying JITAI architectures by degree of data locality; and (3) It presents primary UK market research-structured interviews and a cross-city survey-quantifying demand for privacy-preserving adaptive coaching. Respondents overwhelmingly prefer local data processing and cite privacy as their leading reservation about existing AI assistants. The paper concludes that privacy-preservation should be treated as a first-class design constraint in JITAI research rather than a downstream compliance concern, and sets out a research agenda for evaluating on-device JITAI systems on both efficacy and privacy-preservation.

title: Sub-Dollar Machine Commerce: A Census-Scale Analysis of Real x402 On-Chain Payments
affiliations: and RUDN University

detail.title: Sub-Dollar Machine Commerce: A Census-Scale Analysis of Real x402 On-Chain Payments

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study analyzes publicly available on-chain data and does not involve human participants or animal subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract:
Autonomous software agents are increasingly transacting over the HTTP 402 (x402) protocol, yet the empirical economics of machine-to-machine commerce remain largely uncharacterized. The prevailing industry narrative assumes a migration toward multi-dollar, compound transactions. To test this, we analyzed a census-scale dataset of 143.8 million x402 settlements—totaling $42.8M across Base, Solana, and Polygon (May–Dec 2025)—and found the exact opposite.

Our analysis reveals three structural realities of the machine economy:

  • The Sub-Dollar Reality: Machine commerce is overwhelmingly micropayment-driven. The volume-weighted average payment is just $0.27, and 28.5% of all transactions are sub-cent. Payments ≥$1 carry 72.5% of the total value but represent less than 8% of network traffic.
  • Extreme Centralization: The top 1% of merchants capture 93.0% of all revenue. This bottleneck is even more pronounced at the settlement infrastructure layer, where a single facilitator controls ~62% of the total settled volume.
  • Wild Price Dispersion & Network Dominance: Endpoint list prices are highly erratic (median $0.01, CV 12.91), decisively rejecting the hypothesis of a tight, efficient algorithmic clearing corridor. Furthermore, settlement is highly skewed toward Base (82.5% of volume), with Solana holding a persistent minority (17.4%).

These findings dismantle the myth of complex machine commerce, reframing the x402 ecosystem as a high-volume, sub-dollar API economy where the true concentration risk lies in settlement infrastructure, rather than among merchants.

title:
Production Subject and Use Subject in the Age of Generative AI: 
Rethinking Meaning, Agency, and Responsibility

detail.title:
Production Subject and Use Subject in the Age of Generative AI: 
Rethinking Meaning, Agency, and Responsibility

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests. No financial or personal relationships have influenced the work reported in this manuscript.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding was received for this work.

detail.abstract: Generative AI and large-language-model-based agents increasingly generate texts, images, code, plans, hypotheses, recommendations, and action sequences that were once treated as paradigmatic products of human agency. The resulting debate often collapses two distinct questions: whether an artificial system can produce an output, and whether it can be the subject that understands, evaluates, adopts, and bears the consequences of that output. This paper develops a technological-philosophical distinction between the production subject and the use subject. The term production subject is used in a functional and relational sense: it denotes an agent-like system capable of generating externalized forms that enter social practice. Use subject, by contrast, denotes a stronger normative-existential role: a being that can reactivate meaning, relate an output to its own stakes, adjudicate among values, and remain answerable for consequences. The paper introduces a Thinking Lifecycle Model-living thought, objectification, symbolic stabilization, and reactivation-to locate generative AI within the circulation of meaning. It then distinguishes instrumental use from existential use and argues that current generative AI can function as a production subject and participate in instrumental use, but there is not yet an adequate basis for treating it as the ultimate use subject in high-stakes social practice. Four conditions are central to ultimate use subjectivity: embodied or otherwise first-person stakes, intrinsic concern, value adjudication, and responsibility-bearing. A production-use-responsibility chain is developed across medical, educational, and judicial scenarios and connected to the literature on responsibility gaps and meaningful human control. The paper's thesis is conditional rather than species-essentialist: if future artificial systems acquired credible evidence of phenomenal experience, persistent self-concern, diachronic identity, and institutional answerability, the framework would require revision. The central claim is therefore not that artificial subjectivity is impossible, but that the displacement of human production superiority does not by itself entail the displacement of human subjectivity.

title: A Computational Framework for Metric Calibration and Budget Reallocation of Cross -Platform Retail Media Incremental Effects
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Alibaba Group, Volkswagen AG, California State University, Los Angeles and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: A Computational Framework for Metric Calibration and Budget Reallocation of Cross -Platform Retail Media Incremental Effects

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Retail media refers to retailer-operated online and offline media environments in which brands place advertisements and retailers use first-party transaction data to measure and attribute advertising outcomes. By 2026, spending in North America will rise b y 17.8% year-on-year to $71.09 billion, and by 2030, it is expected to reach $142.07 billion and account for 23.9% of the total U.S. digital ad spend. In-store digital media is one of the fastest-growing types of this. The attribution rules for this format are defined independently by each network; attribution windows vary substantially, from seven days after a view to same-day click attribution, and performance metrics range from total sales to gross merchandise value (GMV).The network cannot determine whether the same consumer has been identified by another network, and according to industry surveys, the performance data of the same advertising campaign across different networks may differ by as much as 15 per cent. Seventy-five per cent of the advertisers are unaware of how to determine an additional effect, and only 15 per cent believe their organisation can measure such changes. As the number of networks run by brands has increased from six to eleven, the total self-reported incremental effects across networks have been consistently higher than the actual incremental effects at the brand level; in-store digital media is understated under the last-click attribution model because it lacks a click signal. This study develops a computational calibration and budgetreallocation framework that preserves the original attribution rules of individual retail media networks while mapping their self-reported effects onto a unified incremental scale. Geographic holdo ut experiments are used as attribution-independent anchors, and network-specific conversion relationships are estimated through a hierarchical Bayesian model implemented by parallel NUTS sampling. Cross-network repeated exposure is encoded in a sparse user-network-time matrix using anonymized identifiers, duplicated increments are corrected through vectorized contribution reallocation, and monotonic cubic-spline response curves are fitted for constrained budget optimization at 1% budget increments. The comp utational dataset contains nine retail media networks, 42 brands, and 317 advertising campaigns; all cross-platform records are organized in 24-hour aggregation windows, with a maximum association window of seven days.The in-store calibration anchor contai ns 23 cities, 133 stores, and 23,901 ad-slot weeks, with the spatial-recognition error radius controlled within 20 m to provide a high-precision offline reference for computational calibrationComputational evaluation shows that the mean absolute cross network discrepancy decreases from 14.8% to 3.2% after Bayesian calibration. Duplicate reach accounts for 27.4% of total reach, including 21.3% from users reached by exactly two networks and 6.1% from users reached by three or more networks. For in-store digit al media, the normalized incremental effect increases from 0.583 under lastclick attribution to 0.90 after Bayesian calibration and 0.96 after overlap correction, while the median unit-budget return rank improves from 6 to 3. Under a fixed total budget, t he constrained reallocation algorithm predicts a 12.6% increase in brand-level incremental response, including 7.9 percentage points associated with reallocating budget toward complementary in-store reach and 4.7 percentage points associated with redistribution among online networks. The resulting workflow pro vides a reusable computer-side procedure for cross-platform data standardization, Bayesian metric calibration, sparse-matrix overlap correction, marginal-response estimation, and constrained budget optimization, thereby improving the reproducibility of cro ss-network incremental-effect measurement and allocation analysis. detail.abstract:
The right to freedom of speech and expression, provided under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution
of India, is the foundational pillar of any democracy. This right enables individuals to express their
opinions, raise voices against power, and contribute to the activities of society. However, this right
is not absolute. The right to freedom of speech and expression is subject to reasonable restrictions
under Article 19(2) of the Constitution, especially if it causes disturbance to public order, violates
the morals of society, or violates the rights and dignity of others.
The emergence of hate speeches, especially on social media platforms, has added another
dimension to this right. This paper will explore this right and its implications by analyzing the
laws, court decisions, and international practices on this subject. The paper will conclude with the
need to balance this right and to ensure that this right does not harm the interests of society. The
right to freedom of speech and expression is essential for the proper functioning of a democracy,
and this right must be subject to reasonable restrictions.

title: Generative Q&A Engines and the Transformation of Overseas Procurement Information Intermediation
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Generative Q&A Engines and the Transformation of Overseas Procurement Information Intermediation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Generative Q&A engines used in overseas procurement must retrieve multilingual product evidence while respecting specifications, units, materials, tolerances, certifications, and delivery constraints. Standard RAG pipelines optimize semantic relevance but may propagate parameter conflicts and unsupported citations into generated answers. We therefore construct a fact-constrained retrieval-augmented generation framework over five-language procurement logs from 1,247 manufacturing exporters, 87.42 million procurement queries, 19.3 million page-level content units, and 470 million citation records. The method integrates a four-channel procurement-intent encoder, sparse-dense hybrid retrieval, hard fact gating, citation-aware dynamic re-ranking, and graph-based evidence compression under a fixed context budget. Candidate pages are normalized into structured product facts before hard constraints remove conflicts, while citation feedback shifts re-ranking from relevance prediction toward citation-feasibility prediction. Experiments against BM25, DenseRetriever, HybridRetriever, CrossEncoder-Reranker, and standard RAG show Recall@20 of 91.6%, NDCG@10 of 0.846, constraint satisfaction of 94.1%, citation accuracy of 90.8%, and an unsupported citation rate of 6.9%. Ablation and parameter sensitivity results further confirm that fact gating, citation-aware re-ranking, and fact-graph compression suppress errors at different stages. The framework provides a computable architecture for reliable cross-lingual procurement question answering based on verifiable and citable product facts. A downstream deployment check retains enterprise-level citation outcomes only as external validation rather than the central research objective, keeping algorithmic retrieval quality as the primary technical evaluation target.

title: Exact Information Constraints in Shannon Rational Inattention: Acquisition versus Behavior
affiliations: Yerevan State University

keywords: Bayesian decision theory JEL Classification: D81

detail.abstract: Shannon Rational Inattention often compresses an acquired signal into the state-dependent action probabilities it induces. Under a capacity constraint or a positive information cost, this is harmless for value because signal distinctions that do not affect behavior can be discarded. The conclusion changes when mutual information is required to equal a prescribed level. Let F(q) denote maximal expected utility when the acquired signal satisfies I(X;S)=q, G(q) maximal utility under the action-information capacity I(X;A)≤q, and B(q) maximal utility when behavioral information itself must satisfy I(X;A)=q. In a finite Bayesian decision problem, F is well defined, nondecreasing, and concave, and the classical statistical-decision benchmark gives F(q)=G(q). We show that B(q)≤F(q), with equality exactly when some capacity-optimal action rule uses q units of action information. Strict inequality is possible even when optimal behavior depends on the state, and B need not be nondecreasing. Extra signal information can be ignored; extra behavioral information may require suboptimal actions. Thus signal-to-action compression can preserve value without preserving an exact information constraint.

detail.abstract: This paper provides a theoretical framework showing that the EU carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM) creates incentives for EU trading partners to adopt domestic carbon pricing. To test this prediction, we collect information on the evolution of carbon pricing mechanisms and construct a measure of CBAM-exposure based on trade data across 163 countries. We find that the introduction of the carbon border measure increases adoption rates of carbon pricing policies in countries with greater trade exposure. A one-percentage-point increase in CBAM-exposure raises the probability of adopting carbon pricing by 1.6 percentage points, a 17% increase on the pre-CBAM adoption rate. This effect concentrates among higher income countries consistent with lower income countries facing capacity constraints to implement similar mechanisms.

title: A Critical Analysis of OpenAI's Claimed Solution to the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize Problem: Methodology, Verification, and Controversy

detail.title: A Critical Analysis of OpenAI's Claimed Solution to the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize Problem: Methodology, Verification, and Controversy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known financial or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this study.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: On September 8, 2026, OpenAI announced that an internal multi-agent artificial intelligence system had produced a proof resolving the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem, one of the Clay Mathematics Institute's Millennium Prize Problems. The claim specifically concerned options C and D of Charles Fefferman's official formulation, which permit a smooth external force. According to public reports, the proof was generated in approximately 88 hours using roughly 10,000 concurrent agents and about 130 billion output tokens, and was then formalized in the Lean proof assistant in an additional 17 hours. This paper provides a critical analysis of the claim. It explains the mathematical background, reconstructs the reported methodology, examines the Lean verification claim, analyzes the priority and data-ethics controversy involving Tristan Buckmaster and Levent Alpöge, and assesses the technical objection that the result concerns a forced rather than unforced singularity. We conclude that while the computational achievement is significant if verified, the mathematical community has not accepted the result, and the claim remains epistemically unresolved. The episode is best understood as a case study in the intersection of frontier AI, formal verification, academic priority, and the nature of mathematical proof.

title: Are Households Ready To Weather A Digital Storm In Retail Payments? Evidence From The Netherlands
affiliations: De Nederlandsche Bank and De Nederlandsche Bank (DNB)

publicationDetails.detailsText: De Nederlandsche Bank Working Paper Forthcoming

detail.abstract: In an increasingly digital retail payments landscape, it is essential that households are well prepared for incidents that temporarily disrupt their ability to make digital payments for everyday purchases. This study examines whether Dutch households are prepared for such disruptions and whether official preparedness advice has translated into recommended behaviour. We use survey evidence from 5,672 Dutch respondents collected after the May 2025 official recommendation to hold €70 per adult and €30 per child in cash for a 72-hour outage of electronic payments and to maintain multiple means of payment. Awareness is high, but incomplete: 71% of respondents know the cash recommendation, while 58% hold the recommended amount or more. This implies a preparedness gap, especially among financially constrained households. Awareness is strongly associated with compliance; respondents who know the advice are 21 percentage points more likely to meet it. Non-compliance appears partly behavioural rather than purely informational or financial; the most frequently cited reason is not having got around to following the advice. Our analysis of several events, including communication about the cash advice, suggests that targeted communication may support compliance with the cash advice. Digital fallback capacity is more widespread than cash fallback preparedness, with 70% of respondents having multiple digital payment instruments for point-of-sale purchases. The findings imply that resilience policies should not only safeguard payment infrastructure but also address the informational, behavioural and practical barriers that prevent households from preparing.

title: Why the Unitary Nature of the South African State Cannot Survive the Assertion of Self-Determination by a Sub-National Community
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Why the Unitary Nature of the South African State Cannot Survive the Assertion of Self-Determination by a Sub-National Community

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is funded by the Cape Independence Advocacy Group (CIAG), and the research and preparation of this paper were undertaken in the course of his work for CIAG.

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether the legitimate assertion of self-determination by a qualifying sub-national community is compatible with the continued unitary character of the South African state. It argues that the right to self-determination carries the status of a peremptory norm (jus cogens) in international law and has been domesticated into South African law, and that this status qualifies the Constitution's own supremacy rather than being subordinate to it. The paper distinguishes between power held by right, which the state cannot withdraw without consent, and power held by grace and favour, which it can, and argues that a legitimate assertion converts a community's position from the latter to the former. It is not the assertion itself but the resulting de facto redistribution of power — whether through state accommodation or unilateral action following unlawful refusal — that ends the state's unitary character. This claim is tested against two South African applications, addressing the territorial and cultural forms self-determination may take: the devolution of policing powers to the Western Cape, and Afrikaner control of single-medium Afrikaans schools as cultural institutions. A postscript chapter extends the analysis, at a lower evidentiary register, to fiscal autonomy. The paper concludes that where a community's claim meets the legal threshold of legitimacy, the state's obligation to accommodate it is a matter of legal duty rather than political discretion.

title: Considerations for Frontier AI Governance in China: Adapting Existing Regulatory Infrastructure to Frontier Risk

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors have no conflicts of interest to report.

detail.abstract:
Frontier AI models—cutting-edge foundation models whose capabilities generalise across domains, improve rapidly, and extend beyond what developers explicitly trained them for—and the systems they integrate into pose regulatory challenges qualitatively distinct from those of narrower AI applications. China is well placed to take on these challenges, as over the past decade it has built substantial AI governance infrastructure that can serve as a foundation for governing frontier AI.


As frontier capabilities advance, this infrastructure can be calibrated to focus regulatory attention on the most capable systems where the distinctive frontier AI risks arise while preserving space for the application-layer development that represents much of China's AI ecosystem. This paper examines how to do so, focusing on China's institutional context while drawing on comparative experience from the US, UK, and EU.


We identify nine proposals across three areas—frontier risk evaluation, emergency response, and liability adaptation—that build on China's existing infrastructure to address frontier risks, plus secondary mechanisms suited for pilot-zone experimentation.

detail.abstract:
Universal BIOS Protocol v1.0 proposes a pre-decision ethical architecture for governing high-impact artificial intelligence. It distinguishes conventional Artificial Intelligence from Universal Intelligence: capability alone does not constitute wisdom; an intelligent system must also demonstrate restraint, accountability and concern for the full field affected by its actions. The protocol establishes seven mandatory gates addressing severe harm, reversibility, uncertainty, distribution of benefits and burdens, silent stakeholders, less harmful alternatives and human accountability. It produces five possible authorization states: CLEAR, CONDITIONAL, PAUSE, HALT and PROHIBITED.

Universal BIOS evaluates not only AI outputs but also the purposes, incentives and authority of the humans, companies, states and military institutions directing them. Its ethical scope extends beyond immediate human interests to animals, ecosystems, natural resources and future generations that cannot represent themselves in decision-making processes. The framework therefore treats ethics as a measurable and auditable condition of action rather than a voluntary declaration. Universal BIOS is presented as a governance proposal and public-consultation protocol—not as a claim of completed technical validation. Its broader objective is to support the parallel evolution of human and technological intelligence while protecting life, dignity, ecological integrity and the conditions required for a shared future.

title: Greenhushing, Green Surfacing, and the Real Effects of the FTC's Green Guides *
affiliations: National Tsing Hua University - Department of Quantitative Finance and

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing interests.
