detail.abstract: This study was motivated to test the validity of recognition of goodwill in the consolidated financial statements of one of the listed companies on the Malawi Stock Exchange when it had lost control in a subsidiary and subsequently reclassified as an associate. Current literature does not support that theory and practice. The results of this study indicate it is indeed possible to recognise goodwill in the investee upon loss of control albeit under extreme and rare phenomenon such that transaction would be classified as extraordinary accounting transaction where the previous controlling interest would take up lower percentage of shareholding than the fair value of assets attributable to it upon the conclusion of losing the control in investee. However such a scenario did not occur in this regard and therefore the recognition of goodwill upon loss of control in the investee in this study was wrong and resulted in the material misstatement of the financial statements. Further review of the accounting policies indicated gaps in the accounting for the investments in associates and joint ventures. It is recommended that regulators should provide more oversight function on complex transactions but should also enhance training sessions on the recognition and accounting for goodwill. More importantly, the transaction should be reversed leading to restatement of the consolidated financial statements of the reporting entity with appropriate disclosures to improve quality of corporate reporting.

title: Who is Spared? How Employers Evaluate Older Workers' Productivity Signals during Downsizing

detail.title: Who is Spared? How Employers Evaluate Older Workers' Productivity Signals during Downsizing

detail.abstract:
Background and Objectives: Economic downturns force employers to make difficult downsizing decisions, potentially placing older workers at heightened likelihood of job loss. This study examines whether older workers' observable productivity signals-including recent training, attendance, performance trajectories, relational productivity, and risk-adjusted productivity-lower layoff risk. Research Design and 
Methods: We analyze data from an original multi-industry survey of 456 C-suite executives and managers with hiring authority in Singapore. In a vignette experiment, respondents evaluated profiles of older employees with various productivity signals in terms of their layoff risk during a hypothetical recession. We also examine whether employers' negative age-related stereotypes and firms' age composition moderate these effects. 
Results: All productivity signals were associated with lower perceived layoff risk, with the largest protective effects from multi-year performance improvement and peer/managerial appreciation. Moderation analyses show that employers' negative age stereotypes and firms' age-composition condition how signals are evaluated: While employers' stereotypes increase older workers' layoff risks, recent training and strong attendance provide substantial protection among employers holding negative stereotypes. Relational capacities reflected in peer/managerial appreciation remedy layoff risks in firms with larger existing shares of older employees. 
Discussion and Implications: These findings suggest that efforts to extend working lives should go beyond providing employment incentives for employers. Firm-and institutional practices that make older workers' less-visible contributions-through sustained performance, skill renewal efforts, and relational capacity-more recognizable may help promote productive aging and meaningful labor-market attachment in late working life.

title: Communities' Insularity in Hybrid and Virtual Environments. An Anticipatory Democracy Study on Meaning Co-creation Modelling Case Studies: Insularity in Romania and 8 Countries in Central-Eastern-Europe

detail.title: Communities' Insularity in Hybrid and Virtual Environments. An Anticipatory Democracy Study on Meaning Co-creation Modelling Case Studies: Insularity in Romania and 8 Countries in Central-Eastern-Europe

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The Author states that there is no personal or financial relationship with other people or organizations that may have or could be perceived to have influenced their study.

detail.abstract: Anticipatory Democracy employs Scenario Development as a methodology aimed at designing the “desirable future”. The present Insularity Study aims to provide for a relevant view of the aspirational future design in Anticipatory Democracy Research. Insularity studies emphasize the need to introduce new modelling methodologies in model-based scenario development methodology. Insularity is not just political, it is epistemic. Virtual environments require new modelling tools in order to be addressed in anticipatory research. Traditionally, Anticipatory Democracy rely on alternative planning, deliberation and vision: it starts from the assumption that a “desirable future” is reachable if appropriately planned and designed. How the meaning of “desirable future” is achieved? - This is a missing dimension Anticipatory Democracy research. This approach is suggesting that the design of “desirable future” should include a meaning-generative dimension for coping with insularity phenomena in the virtual environments with mixed communities of human and AI agents. Our Insularity Study reveals that anticipatory democracy research require a philosophy (ontology and epistemology) and a modelling theory of the multi-world virtual spaces and mixed communities in their endeavour to view, design, and reach a shared “desirable future”. VEM Model (Voinea, 2026, 2025a, 2025b) offers a way to model meaning co-creation in virtual communities which aim at a shared “desirable future”. Desirable futures depend on: shared meaning, shared values, and shared symbolic universes. Social and political Insularity disrupts all three. Insularity transforms traditional meaning-making systems into observer-dependent meaning systems. Virtual environments amplify this transformation. Therefore, anticipatory democracy must adopt meaning-generative models capable of capturing meaning co-creation in virtual multiple worlds environments.

detail.title: Understanding the Gender Wealth Gap in Germany: Asset Value vs. Asset Ownership

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the gender wealth gap among married and cohabiting couples in Germany, using data from the German Socio-Economic Panel (SOEP). It explores the gender wealth gap by investigating various components of wealth and ownership disparities among couples. On average, men possess 34% more wealth than women. This gap arises both from differences in extensive margin asset ownership and differences in wealth conditional on asset ownership. The gap in asset ownership, particularly in housing and business assets, contributes significantly to the overall gender wealth gap. Employing the Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition technique, I find that observable characteristics can account for only 65% of the observed gender wealth gap. When analyzing couples where both own a given type of asset, controlling for observable characteristics eliminates the wealth gap. However, for couples with ownership differences, observable characteristics explain only a modest portion of the wealth gap and ownership gap. My findings underscore the importance of considering gender gaps in asset ownership in understanding the gender wealth gap and highlight the limited explanatory power of observable characteristics in accounting for the gap.

title: Sticky Wage Norms and the Real Wage Cost of Unexpected Inflation
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business, University of Chicago, ADP Research and ADP Research

detail.title: Sticky Wage Norms and the Real Wage Cost of Unexpected Inflation
detail.abstract:
We use a sample of administrative payroll data covering a large and nationally representative share of U.S. workers to study how wages adjusted during the recent inflation period. Most firms apply a single modal annual nominal wage increase to the majority of their workers, and these firm-level norms changed little during the recent period of unexpected inflation. As a result, nominal wages did not keep pace with prices for a large share of workers who stayed at their firms. Forty-three percent of workers continuously employed at the same firm over the four years spanning 2021–2024 experienced a real wage decline, with a mean loss of roughly nine percent among those who fell behind. Workers could escape sticky wage norms by changing employers — job-changers’ wages rose nearly one-for-one with inflation — but switching was too infrequent to matter for most. Even accounting for job-changers, 37 percent of all workers saw real wages decline over the 4-year period. Indexing firms’ modal raises one-for-one to inflation would have closed roughly 40 percent of the resulting shortfall relative to prepandemic trend. Drawing on cross-country evidence from Belgium, whose wages are automatically indexed to inflation, we show that incomplete wage indexation, rather than inflation itself, helps explain the persistence of depressed consumer sentiment during the 2021–2024 period.

title: The Transformation of EU Waste Law in the Circular Economy: Principles, Regulatory Techniques and Emerging Legal Challenges
affiliations: NATIONAL KAPODISTRIAN UNIVERSITY OF ATHENS

detail.title: The Transformation of EU Waste Law in the Circular Economy: Principles, Regulatory Techniques and Emerging Legal Challenges
detail.abstract: EU waste law is undergoing a structural transformation. The traditional regulatory model, centred on the classification, collection, shipment, recovery and disposal of discarded materials, is being recast within a broader circular-economy architecture that regulates products, materials, information, producer responsibility and market access across the entire life cycle. This study examines that transformation as a legal, institutional and methodological shift. It analyses the continuing centrality of the Waste Framework Directive, the normative role of the waste hierarchy, the concepts of waste, by-product and end-of-waste, the polluter-pays principle and extended producer responsibility, and the increasing use of economic incentives, ecodesign requirements, digital product information, recycled-content obligations, waste-prevention targets and cross-border controls. Particular attention is paid to the 2024-2026 phase of EU circulareconomy legislation, including Regulation (EU) 2024/1781 on ecodesign for sustainable products, Regulation (EU) 2024/1157 on shipments of waste, Regulation (EU) 2025/40 on packaging and packaging waste, Directive (EU) 2025/1892 amending the Waste Framework Directive in relation to food waste and textiles, and Regulation (EU) 2025/2365 on plastic pellet losses. The study argues that EU waste law is increasingly becoming a component of a wider law of circular material flows. This evolution creates new forms of regulatory coherence, but also generates tensions concerning legal certainty, the boundary between waste and products, internal-market harmonisation, chemicals safety, data governance, responsibility allocation, enforcement and the externalisation of environmental burdens beyond the Union.

detail.abstract: Demographic ageing places the pay-as-you-go German statutory pension under sustained pressure, and the pension reform act of 2026 introduces a new state-subsidised retirement savings account with a stronger capital market orientation. Whether such offerings will be taken up depends on individual acceptance, which this paper examines empirically. Building on trust research, the life-cycle hypothesis, financial literacy research, and prospect theory, five attitudinal determinants of the acceptance of capital market-based retirement provision are derived: trust in state regulation and investor protection, scepticism towards the statutory pension, subjective financial competence, risk perception and loss aversion, and safety and guarantee preferences. The hypotheses are tested with an online survey of the German adult, non-retired population (n = 166; May to June 2025) using index construction and hierarchical OLS regression with sociodemographic controls. Of the five determinants, only risk perception and loss aversion shows a robust, independent association with acceptance (β =-0.56, p < 0.001, heteroscedasticity-consistent inference); the full model explains roughly two thirds of the variance in acceptance. Scepticism towards the statutory pension is significant only under classical standard errors, while trust, subjective financial competence, and safety preferences contribute no independent explanatory power. An exploratory item shows predominantly low openness towards digital assets in retirement portfolios. The findings suggest that broadening capital market-based retirement provision hinges less on institutional trust or appeals to pension scepticism than on lowering perceived investment risk through product design and risk-focused financial education.

detail.abstract: We use matched parent-child-employer-employee data from Canada, linked to detailed educational records, to quantify the contribution of social connections to employers to intergenerational income mobility. Sorting across employers accounts for roughly a third of the transmission of income across generations. To estimate the impact of social connections on differential representation across employers, we compare classmates -- those with the same degree from the same institution -- who have different social connections. We find social connections in the labor market explain about 15% of the firm-sorting component of the intergenerational income rank-rank relationship, about a third the explanatory power of education.

detail.abstract: Does forward-looking loss recognition alter how deteriorating loan quality maps into bank resilience? Using a 2010-2024 panel of up to 46 OECD and Asian Development Bank economies, this paper combines World Bank macro-financial data with hand-verified ECL adoption dates. NPLs show bidirectional Granger predictability with bank Z-scores and predict subsequent creditgap buildup. Single-threshold evidence is weak overall but suggestive before ECL adoption. In two-way fixed-effects models with Driscoll-Kraay inference, the NPL×post-ECL interaction is negative and significant in both main and robustness samples, and remains negative under alternative China timing and key exclusions. A Callaway-Sant'Anna event study is imprecise and fails pre-trend diagnostics, so it is treated as sensitivity evidence rather than causal confirmation. The results suggest that forward-looking provisioning changes the mapping from observed problem loans to reported soundness, with relevance for developing banking systems still transitioning to ECL regimes.

title: The Screening Model of Litigation with a Continuum of Types: An Experimental Analysis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors have no conflicts to report.
declarations.funderStatement: This was funded by an internal grant from the Culverhouse College of Business

detail.abstract: We conduct a laboratory experiment using a stylized model of civil litigation bargaining. This is a screening model with a continuum of types based on Bebchuk (1984). Most previous experimental work on the screening model has utilized two-type models. In a screening model, the recipient of the settlement offer is informed, but the party making the offer is uninformed. Among other things, this setting embeds an ultimatum game as the subjects need to divide the joint surplus which is achieved via settlement rather than trial. After the informed plaintiff learns her type, she indicates the minimum offer she is willing to accept. This allows us to measure the demand for fairness within this setting. Previous work with twotype models has shown a reduction in fairness behaviors within this embedded ultimatum game. While there is significant dispersion about the median, by this measure of the central tendency, the demand for fairness essentially disappears. We also test a prediction of the theory that the dispute rate is independent of the distribution of trial costs, depending only on their sum. In the baseline, costs are equal, but there are two treatments, where under one, the plaintiff bears most of the costs of trial, while under the second, the defendant bears most of these costs. The theory does fairly well, as we find only weak evidence that dispute rates are affected by the distribution of dispute costs.

detail.abstract: Extreme weather, ageing infrastructure and sabotage are making prolonged grid outages a tangible risk, yet most resilience research addresses response and recovery rather than preemptive sizing and operation. This paper introduces a novel two-stage stochastic linear programming framework for preemptive resilience that jointly optimises investment and operation of a building-scale integrated electricity-heat system. Resilience is enforced by a dynamic, forward-looking dual criterion: criticality guarantees critical loads throughout the outage, survivability full load over a short initial window, both imposed robustly for every outage start and duration. Two demand-side resources are exploited: the building's thermal mass as virtual heat storage allowing heat to be pre-positioned, and a widened indoor-temperature comfort band during outages. The framework is applied to a real-world building complex in Austria with heat pumps, battery storage, photovoltaics and backup generators, across eleven weather years spanning calm and volatile price regimes. Sharing assets between normal and outage operation is consistently cheaper than provisioning resilience separately, by 12% for a 48-hour design outage. Battery storage is both the principal economic flexibility and the backbone of resilience: the constraints reshape its lower state-of-charge envelope while barely altering day-today dispatch. Sector coupling reduces the storage, backup-generator and fuel capacity needed, and widening the outage temperature range delivers the same resilience at up to 45% lower additional cost. Because resilience is imposed as a hard exogenous requirement rather than weighed against avoided damages, these costs are an upper bound-yet a 48-hour outage adds only about 4% to annualised system cost.

title: Counterfactual Conduct as an Antitrust Defense?
affiliations: Cornell University - Law School

detail.title: Counterfactual Conduct as an Antitrust Defense?

detail.abstract: An antitrust defendant might try to defend its conduct by arguing that it is no worse for competition than some lawful counterfactual practice that it would otherwise have undertaken. An example of this argument has recently received attention in connection with the Google Search case. But the argument could in principle be applied quite broadly. While sometimes reasonable, such arguments can raise serious policy concerns. In some cases, it would allow a defendant to avoid liability based on possible efficiencies or other liability-relevant factors that do not apply to the challenged conduct at all. And it would sometimes allow counterfactual judicial errors to produce real ones. I also emphasize that some intuitively appealing arguments about counterfactual conduct define the but-for world incorrectly. For these reasons, courts should exercise caution before considering counterfactual conduct as an evaluative benchmark.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence regulation is increasingly shaped by a familiar political reflex: legislate against what might go wrong before establishing what has actually gone wrong. This paper tests that reflex against deployment evidence across eight sectors (education, agriculture, transportation, cybersecurity, healthcare, manufacturing, hospitality, and retail) and argues that the harms currently documented in AI deployment are narrower, more specific, and more tractable to targeted regulation than the harms most prominent in public and legislative debate. Building on regulatory theory's long-standing distinction between precautionary and evidence-based rulemaking (Sunstein, 2005; Teichmann, 2026), the paper operationalizes that distinction as a fourfactor "Real Harm Test" (documented loss, traceable causation, scalable exposure, available mitigation) and applies it sector by sector. Cross-referenced against field developments, including Waymo's commercial robotaxi launch and Zoox's steering-wheel-free vehicle testing in San Diego, and against original field observations from Cameroon and Thailand, the analysis finds that adoption consistently outpaces institutional oversight, while documented harms remain narrow and specific rather than existential, ranging from a 1,300% rise in deepfake-enabled fraud to a governance gap in which four of five universities lack a formal AI policy despite 86% institutional adoption. The paper further shows, using FY2026 federal appropriations data, that this adoptiongovernance gap tracks institutional structure: sectors with a Cabinet-level department (education, agriculture, transportation, health) can direct existing capacity toward the gap, while sectors without one (manufacturing, cybersecurity, hospitality, retail) rely on sub-agency budgets a fraction of the size, or on no dedicated federal capacity at all. Building on the author's prior published work on healthcare security governance and vulnerability lifecycles, the paper closes with differentiated policy and practice implications for regulators, executives, educators, security leaders, and frontline practitioners. As in other domains where governments have proposed directing business and technical decisions on political rather than operational grounds, the central risk here is not the technology itself; it is regulatory energy spent on hypothetical fear while documented, fixable harm goes unaddressed.

detail.abstract: A backtested Sharpe ratio summarises how large a strategy's risk-adjusted return was over a sample, not how it was distributed across the sample. We apply the Sharpe Stability Ratio (SSR) of Bajo Traver and Rodriguez Dominguez (2026), the mean of a rolling 36-month Sharpe ratio divided by a heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation consistent estimate of its long-run standard deviation, to 173 tactical and static asset allocation strategy variants published on one backtesting platform, with completed monthly histories of 18 to 106 years ending in August 2026. We report a fixed-bandwidth descriptive version of the statistic and treat it as a ranking aid. Three descriptive findings follow. First, SSR is imperfectly rank-correlated with the Sharpe ratio (0.67) and with the platform's Deflated Sharpe Ratio (0.61): of 146 variants whose Deflated Sharpe Ratio is at least 0.90, 54 have an SSR of at least 0.5 and 92 fall below it. Second, estimated SSR rankings depend strongly on the evaluation period. Aggregate rankings are stable across rolling windows and bandwidths (rank correlations of 0.94 to 0.99 with the baseline specification), but across four calendar subperiods the cross-sectional rank correlation between adjacent periods is -0.04, -0.43 and 0.08, and the S&P 500's own SSR moves from 0.15 in the 2000s to 1.63 in the 2010s. Third, the association between reported turnover and SSR is positive (rank correlation 0.31; 0.23 within tactical variants), and static allocations have the lowest median SSR. A moving block bootstrap places every percentile interval above zero and no 5th percentile above 0.5. We document the estimator, the choices behind it, and their consequences.

detail.abstract: Data centers are among the most capital-intensive investments in the modern economy, yet they employ relatively few workers directly.  Do these investments generate jobs elsewhere in the local economy?  Combining proprietary data on 1,584 U.S. data centers with synthetic difference-indifferences and local projections, we find that local non-construction employment changes little for two years after a data center opens, then begins to rise. Installed capacity is associated with 7.4 additional non-construction jobs per megawatt (MW).  Because each installed MW also predicts a further 1.7 MW of capacity over the same period, this corresponds to 2.74 jobs per effective MW. These gains are concentrated in two sectors: transportation/ warehousing, and professional/technical services. Retail, restaurants, and other local services show little employment growth. Existing capacity mostly predicts expansion by incumbent operators, and only a small share of subsequent capacity is attributable to new entrants.  Large capital investments can therefore generate local jobs even when the facilities themselves employ few workers.

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether the AI governance gaps previously identified within India-a research programme spanning three prior papers on India's national AI guidelines, welfaredelivery accountability, and sub-national state readiness-reflect a distinctly Indian problem or a broader global pattern. Drawing on five independent data sources spanning 54 countries (the Stanford HAI AI Index and Global AI Vibrancy Tool, the AGILE Index, the Oxford Insights Government AI Readiness Index, and country-by-country tracking of national AI strategies and binding legislation), this paper introduces an original empirical measure, the Strategy-to-Law Lag-the number of years between a country's first national AI strategy and its first binding AIspecific law-and classifies all 54 countries into four governance archetypes based on deployment level relative to governance strength. Only 18 of the 54 countries have enacted binding AI legislation, and 16 of these are European Union member states whose status stems from a single shared bloc-wide instrument rather than from national deployment or governance capacity. Among the 18, lag ranges from 3 years (Ireland) to 7 years (Finland, South Korea), with China recording the shortest lag among non-EU countries (4 years). Archetype classification confirms, using independently collected data, that the United States and India both fall into the "Deployment Racer" category-high AI deployment paired with comparatively weak governance capacity-with India recording the lowest governance score among all countries in that group. A weak, statistically fragile correlation between GDP per capita and Strategy-to-Law Lag (r =-0.217, n = 18) suggests that political will, rather than national wealth, better explains regulatory speed. These findings indicate that India's AI governance challenge is not an isolated domestic failing but a pronounced instance of a global pattern in which AI deployment has, almost everywhere, outpaced binding regulation.

detail.abstract: Decisions built from several sources may face a required fact that is missing, stale, disputed by equally trusted sources, or linked to the wrong entity. Our resolveadmit-decide framework keeps these states explicit and rejects any line with an unusable required fact. After admission, audit-weighted Gamma-Poisson updating learns one frequency multiplier per line; it never fills rejected facts or changes fixed pricing rules. Under stated assumptions, resolution is deterministic, the posterior is proper, and fitting is linear in the data size. A seeded simulation shows the coverage-error trade-off but does not validate real insurance prices.

title: Implied Trajectory Intensity: A Novel Market Parameter for European Derivative Pricing

detail.title: Implied Trajectory Intensity: A Novel Market Parameter for European Derivative Pricing

detail.abstract: This paper introduces the concept of implied trajectory intensity (implied 𝛼), a novel market parameter for the valuation of European derivative financial instruments within the trajectory-equilibrium pricing framework of Cadei (2026). Implied 𝛼 is defined, for each instrument, as the unique value of the path-intensity coefficient that, when applied to the trajectory-equilibrium pricing equations, reproduces a given observed market price. Crucially, implied 𝛼 is computed exclusively from observable market quantities-the derivative market price, the underlying asset price 𝑃 0 , the strike price 𝑆, the risk-free rate 𝑅 𝑓 , and the time to maturity 𝑇-without requiring any assumption about the stochastic dynamics of the underlying asset. The parameter 𝛼 may be interpreted as capturing the intensity of the admissible exponential trajectory domain of the underlying asset in continuously compounded annual terms, with the condition 𝛼 > 𝑅 𝑓 ensuring that this intensity exceeds the opportunity cost of capital represented by the risk-free rate. The paper establishes the existence and uniqueness of implied 𝛼 separately for European call options, put options, and futures contracts. For call options and futures, uniqueness follows from the strict monotonicity of the respective trajectory-equilibrium prices with respect to 𝛼 for any 𝛼 > 0. For put options, a mathematical singularity arises at the single point 𝛼 = 𝑅 𝑓 , where the intersection time 𝑥 * is undefined; outside this point, implied 𝛼 is well-defined and unique for 𝛼 ≠ 𝑅 𝑓. The behaviour of the framework under the conditions 𝛼 < 𝑅 𝑓 and 𝛼 = 𝑅 𝑓 is analysed for each instrument, providing a complete characterisation of the parameter space. Convergent numerical inversion algorithms based on the Brent-Dekker method (Brent, 1973) are provided for all three instruments. The paper further establishes an empirical relationship between implied 𝛼 and Black-Scholes implied volatility 𝜎. Since both parameters are independently extracted from the same observed derivative price-𝛼 through the trajectory-equilibrium inversion and 𝜎 through the BSM inversion-their relationship is comparative rather than circular, characterising how two structurally distinct valuation frameworks interpret the same market information. Across 1,420 numerical configurations spanning deep ITM to deep OTM options, maturities from 1 to 30 years, and risk-free rates from 0.5% to 8%, this relationship follows an approximate power-law of the form 𝛼 ≈ 𝑐(𝑇)𝜎 𝛽(𝑇,𝑅 𝑓 ,𝑚) , with 𝑅 2 averaging 0.953 and exceeding 0.975 within the practically relevant range (𝑇 ∈ [1,10] years, 𝑅 𝑓 ∈ [2%, 8%], near-the-money options). The parameters of the power law are characterised analytically within this range, and their limits of validity are discussed explicitly. A proposed empirical framework for the application of implied 𝛼 to market-observed derivative prices is outlined, illustrating the practical computability of the parameter and its potential as a complementary market indicator.

detail.abstract: In complementary-effort teams, agents may shirk or decline to join, fearing others will do so. We construct collective contracts contingent on outcomes and participation that uniquely implement participation and effort at a cost arbitrarily close to the no-strategic-risk benchmark. Acceptance disciplines subsequent effort through forward induction, while participation-contingent terms insure against others' rejection. When outside options are too weak for forward induction, the principal supplements the collective contract with an "inside option." With heterogeneous agents, the result extends to any target coalition, and least-cost contracts take an all-or-nothing form, restoring agents to their reservation payoffs if the coalition fails.

title: Borrowing Constraints, Markups, and Misallocation
affiliations: Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, University of California, Berkeley, University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and University of California, Berkeley

detail.title: Borrowing Constraints, Markups, and Misallocation
detail.abstract:
We document that less constrained firms in an industry have higher markups. This connection between markups and borrowing constraints has important allocative efficiency implications: it lowers the TFP losses from markup dispersion, because looser borrowing constraints help higher markup firms produce more and move their market shares closer to the efficient level. We further document that this relationship is stronger in industries where firms rely more on earnings to borrow, and that markup dispersion is also higher in these industries. We explain all of these patterns using a standard Kimball demand model augmented with borrowing against assets and earnings, and show that the connection between markups and borrowing constraints substantially lowers TFP losses from markup dispersion, especially when firms rely on earnings to borrow.

title: What Changes After the IPO? Real and Financial Effects of Going Public
affiliations: Government of the Republic of Turkey - Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey, Sabanci University and Nazarbayev University

detail.abstract: A firm that goes public acquires two things at once: capital, which is its own, and a public record of its condition, which is available to everyone who deals with it. Using linked administrative data covering the universe of formal firms in Türkiye, we follow newly listed firms, their banks, and the suppliers that sell to them, and establish three sets of results. (i) Listing transforms the issuer. We find that sales rise by about 45 percent within four years, assets and capital expand by roughly a third, and exports respond only after a two-year delay. In addition, measured productivity rises by roughly a quarter within two years and stays there, profitability improves, and R&D spending increases. Firms also reorganize as they grow: managers and high-skill workers account for most of the employment response, low-skill employment does not move, and wages rise only modestly and evenly, leaving the distribution of pay inside the firm unchanged. (ii) Banks reprice the newly public firm. Borrowing spreads fall by about 70 basis points, credit capacity expands, and the number of lending relationships rises, while the debt the firm actually draws changes less. (iii) That repricing does not stop at the issuer. Suppliers exposed to a newly listed customer sell more to that customer but show little change in other customer relationships, employment, or measured productivity. Yet their borrowing spreads fall by roughly 40 basis points, their credit limits increase, and they provide more trade credit to their own customers. We also find that these effects are larger when the IPO customer accounts for a greater share of pre-listing sales and are negligible when the relationship is economically small. Our results suggest that going public changes not only the scale, efficiency, and organization of the issuer, but also the financing conditions of private firms connected to it through production relationships.

title: Full Immunization coverage and its predictors among under five Years children in Ethiopia: A systematic review and meta-analysis
affiliations: LonAdd Consultancy Plc, Jigjiga University, Jimma University, Ethiopia Federal Ministry of Health - Oromia Regional Health Bureau and Ethiopia Federal Ministry of Health - Oromia Regional Health Bureau

detail.title: Full Immunization coverage and its predictors among under five Years children in Ethiopia: A systematic review and meta-analysis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding was received for this study.

detail.abstract:
Background: Vaccination is one of the most effective, cost-effective, and equitable public health interventions for preventing infectious diseases and reducing childhood morbidity and mortality. In Ethiopia, however, achieving these goals remains challenging, with substantial variation in immunization coverage across populations and geographic settings. A comprehensive synthesis of the available evidence is therefore needed to provide an updated national estimate of full immunization coverage and to identify the socioeconomic, geographic, caregiver-related, and health-service factors associated with complete childhood immunization in Ethiopia. 

Methods: A systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted to estimate full immunization coverage and identify its predictors among children under five years of age in Ethiopia. The review protocol was registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) under registration number CRD420261494190.

Result: A total of 46 studies conducted in Ethiopia, involving 68,663 children under five years of age, were included in the meta-analysis. Among these, 35,741 children were reported to be fully vaccinated according to the national Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI) schedule. Using a random-effects model to account for anticipated between-study heterogeneity, the pooled prevalence of full vaccination was 57% (95% CI: 0.51–0.62). Maternal/caregiver educational attainment (primary and secondary education), higher household wealth status, shorter distance to a health facility, urban residence, visits by health extension workers or field workers, maternal knowledge of immunization and the immunization schedule, and maternal/caregiver utilization of health services including one to three or four or more antenatal care visits, postnatal care, institutional delivery, and maternal tetanus toxoid vaccination were significantly associated with full immunization coverage.

Conclusion: Despite global and national commitments to the Immunization Agenda 2030, full immunization coverage among children in Ethiopia remains suboptimal, reflecting a substantial and persistent immunization gap. Policymakers should prioritize: decentralized and outreach immunization services to reach remote and underserved areas; strengthened health extension worker–led household follow-up and systematic tracking of zero-dose and under-immunized children through catch-up services; and integration of immunization counselling and referral within antenatal, delivery, and postnatal care, with intensified efforts to reach children in rural, remote, displaced, and socioeconomically disadvantaged communities.

title: Hot spots of Tuberculosis and Rifampicin-Resistant Tuberculosis in Mongolia
affiliations: National Center for Communicable Diseases, University of Missouri, National Center for Communicable Diseases, National Center for Communicable Diseases, National Center for Communicable Diseases, National Center for Communicable Diseases, National Center for Communicable Diseases and University of Missouri-Columbia

detail.title: Hot spots of Tuberculosis and Rifampicin-Resistant Tuberculosis in Mongolia

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that there are no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: No ethical approval was required for this study as it used retrospective, aggregated (time, location) data for analysis.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding was received for performing this work.

detail.abstract:
Background: Tuberculosis (TB) and rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis (RR-TB) remain a public health challenge in Mongolia. Identifying high-risk areas is important for public health management of this disease; however, conventional incidence rates can be unstable in sparsely populated areas and for rare outcomes such as RR-TB. This study evaluates the sub-provincial level spatial and temporal distribution of TB and RR-TB to identify hotspots and evolving geographic risk patterns.

Methods: A nationwide small-area spatiotemporal analysis was conducted using routine surveillance incident notification data from 2017 to 2024 across 339 soums and districts in Mongolia. Hierarchical Bayesian Poisson regression models were implemented to estimate smoothed posterior relative risks (RR) and identify exceedance probability hotspots (P (RR > 1) > 0.95) while accounting for spatial, temporal, and interaction effects. Model performance was evaluated using the Deviance Information Criterion (DIC) and Watanabe–Akaike Information Criterion (WAIC).

Findings: A total of 22,502 TB and 1,381 RR-TB incident cases were notified during the study period. Despite declining national incidence, both conditions exhibited marked geographic heterogeneity. The Type I interaction model performed best for TB, revealing widespread, temporally shifting high-risk areas. The Type IV interaction model performed best for RR-TB, isolating highly localized, temporally stable high-risk areas. Hotspots were concentrated along the proximity of Mongolia’s central–eastern transport corridor. While hotspots comprised fewer than 10% of administrative units, they consistently accounted for 51–71% of notified TB cases and 72–83% of all RR-TB notifications.

Interpretation: The national TB and RR-TB burden in Mongolia is concentrated within a few geographic hotspots, which can be prioritized for public health interventions. Integrating Bayesian hierarchical modeling into routine programmatic planning establishes a reproducible framework for precision public health. This empirical approach can optimize resource allocation, guide targeted active case detection, and decentralize molecular diagnostics in Mongolia and other expansive, high-burden settings.

title: Firm Investment and the User Cost of Capital: New U.S. Corporate Tax Reform Evidence
affiliations: Stanford University, Stanford University - Hoover Institution and Stanford Graduate School of Business

detail.title: Firm Investment and the User Cost of Capital: New U.S. Corporate Tax Reform Evidence
detail.abstract:
The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 (TCJA) marked the first time in three decades that material changes were made to the corporate tax code of the United States. We use TCJA as a quasi natural experiment to estimate the impact of changes in user cost of capital on investment. Following the method of Auerbach and Hassett (1991), using cross-sectional data we find that the user cost is associated with higher rates of investment consistent with previous studies. BEA asset types with greater reductions in user cost of capital and marginal effective tax rate (METR) after the 2017 TCJA had greater statistically significant increases in their investment rates several years after the tax reform. Specifically, we find the magnitude of a 1 percentage point decrease in user cost is associated with a 1.68 to 3.05 percentage point increase in the rate of investment, larger than prior estimates of the responsiveness of investment with respect to user cost of capital.

detail.abstract: Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) can be exposed by short duration and spatially non-uniform exposure in the fence-line communities that surround petroleum refineries, industrial cooking and rendering plants and waste-to-energy facilities. Regulatory surveillance, necessitating conventional monitoring at fixed sites, may not be the breathing-zone exposure of individuals whose daily micro-and macroenvironmental experiences involve indoor, outdoor, commuting, school, and work. This systematic narrative medium review assesses how affordable personal monitoring can supplant accepted techniques minus being confused with control grade measurement. It combines evidence on PAH physiochemistry, sources, passive and active collecting, silicone wristbands, low-flow pumps, pairing filters and sorbents, optical particle sensors, laboratory investigation, quality control, community management and interpretation of health risks. The suggested tiered system employs cheap screening equipment to determine changes in time and space as well as validates priority discoveries through validated sampling and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry or other similar lab tests. Four scientific figures based on literature characterize the molecular structure, the behavior of partitioning, toxic-equivalency weighting and sensitivity to a method; Four tables characterize analytes, source contexts, monitoring options, and a field protocol. The conclusion of the review is that the exposure coverage and community engagement can be enhanced with the help of low-cost tools yet the PAH specificity remains the issue of chemical sampling and laboratory analysis. Data-quality goals ought to be predefined by credible programs, blank and duplicate use should be documented, a good sampling volume should be recorded, a chain-of-custody kept, uncertainties reported, participant privacy should be ensured, and translation-of-screening-signalsinto cancer-risk appraisal should be avoided.

title: Trade and Industrial Policy in Supply Chains: Directed Technological Change in Rare Earths
affiliations: Harvard University, University of Vienna, University of Mannheim and University of Indonesia (UI)

detail.title: Trade and Industrial Policy in Supply Chains: Directed Technological Change in Rare Earths
detail.abstract:
Trade and industrial policies restricting critical inputs can inadvertently promote foreign downstream industries via a directed technological response. We provide evidence for this mechanism by examining rare earth elements (REEs) – critical manufacturing inputs with highly concentrated production and low substitutability. We show that China’s REE export restrictions in 2010 induced a surge in global innovation increasing REE input-efficiency and exports in REE-intensive industries. A quantitative trade model with Heckscher-Ohlin-based comparative advantage, directed technological change and input-output linkages rationalizes how input-supply restrictions induce REE-enhancing innovation and expand REE-intensive industries abroad. This directed technological response substantially mitigates foreign welfare losses.

title: The Private Value of Innovating for the Government
affiliations: Duke University - Fuqua School of Business, Duke University, Tulane University - A.B. Freeman School of Business and Duke University - Fuqua School of Business

detail.title: The Private Value of Innovating for the Government
detail.abstract:
We quantify the private returns to government R&D contracts awarded to firms. We present new evidence that R&D contracts not only finance innovation but also embed an implicit government guarantee of noncompetitive future procurement for the winning R&D contractor. We measure its private value by analyzing stock market reactions to news about R&D contract awards. Using all federal R&D contracts awarded to U.S. publicly traded firms from 1984 through 2015, we find that the average private return on an R&D contract is 19 times its maximum potential revenue. However, returns are highly skewed, with only 7.5% of firms receiving at least one top-quartile contract. Private returns are linked to future production contracts, but only for noncompetitive awards to vertically integrated or large firms. These results suggest that a procurement regime bundling R&D and production contracts enhances value for firms with production capability. We develop a conceptual framework to clarify this innovation policy lever.

title: Uncertainty through the Production Network: Sectoral Origins and Macroeconomic Implications
affiliations: HEC Montreal and HEC Montreal

detail.title: Uncertainty through the Production Network: Sectoral Origins and Macroeconomic Implications
detail.abstract:
We study how uncertainty propagates through production networks. First, we construct a highly disaggregated, forward-looking measure of industry-level uncertainty using option-implied volatility data for U.S. firms. Second, we identify the effects of higher uncertainty within industries, across the supply chain, and at the aggregate level. We find that heightened uncertainty in upstream industries (e.g., chemical manufacturing, iron and steel mills) behaves like a negative supply shock—raising prices and lowering employment across the production network. In contrast, greater uncertainty in downstream industries (e.g., automotive manufacturing, insurance carriers) behaves like an adverse demand shock, reducing both prices and employment. At the aggregate level, the inflation response depends on where uncertainty originates within the supply chain. A multi-sector model with time-varying sectoral uncertainty demonstrates that production linkages play a central role in explaining these empirical findings.

title: From Tank to Odometer: Winners and Losers from a Gas-to-VMT Tax Shift
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Center for Energy and Environmental Policy Research (CEEPR), Tufts University - Department of Economics and Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT)

detail.title: From Tank to Odometer: Winners and Losers from a Gas-to-VMT Tax Shift
detail.abstract:
With the increase in fuel economy of the personal transportation fleet along with the increased penetration of hybrid and electric vehicles, federal motor vehicle fuel excise tax revenue has been steadily declining. This has led to calls for finding a replacement for this tax. One option is to replace the gas tax with a vehicle miles traveled (VMT) tax. To investigate the impact of such a tax swap, we combine data from the 2017 National Household Transportation Survey (NHTS) and the American Community Survey (ACS). Using machine learning techniques, we generate estimates of VMT and gasoline tax collections at the census tract level. This allows us to explore the distributional implications of this tax swap at a geographically disaggregated level. We find, as have previous researchers, that this tax swap is modestly progressive. Our more granular geographic analysis highlights striking disparities not previously reported. We find that rural areas and census tracts in the center of the country generally benefit from this tax swap, while urban and bicoastal areas generally experience higher taxation. Additionally, Republican-leaning districts, which overlap significantly with rural areas, see marked gains compared to Democratic districts.

title: Stablecoin Runs and the Centralization of Arbitrage
affiliations: Columbia University - Columbia Business School,  and University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: Stablecoin Runs and the Centralization of Arbitrage
detail.abstract:
Stablecoins are cryptoassets which are designed to be pegged to the dollar, but are backed by imperfectly liquid USD assets. We show that stablecoins feature concentrated arbitrage: the largest issuer, Tether, only allows 6 agents in an average month to redeem stablecoins for cash. We argue that issuers' choice of arbitrage concentration reflects a tradeoff: efficient arbitrage improves stablecoin price stability in secondary markets, but amplifies run risks by reducing investors' price impact from selling stablecoins. Our findings imply that policies designed to improve stablecoin price stability may have the unintended consequence of increasing stablecoin run risks.

detail.abstract:
The Bhagavad Gītā opens at the moment of leadership failure. Arjuna — one of the most accomplished warriors of his age, surrounded by his allies, armed with every advantage — collapses. His weapons fall from his hands. He cannot act. The crisis is not military, logistical, or physical. It is cognitive and moral: Arjuna’s identity as a warrior is in direct conflict with his identity as a family member; his Dharma as a Kshatriya is in direct conflict with his love for his kinsmen arrayed against him; his belonging to his tribe is pulling him away from the action that his role and the moment require. Krishna’s response occupies the next seventeen chapters of the text and constitutes, across those chapters, the most penetrating account of leadership under moral complexity and identity pressure that any intellectual tradition has produced.

This paper argues that the Bhagavad Gītā’s teaching is not merely culturally significant for India but is a theoretically superior and practically generative framework for leadership in the specific conditions of the twenty-first century — conditions characterised by cognitive complexity (the Want Architecture’s systematic engineering of desire, belonging, and epistemic environment), identity pressure (the manufactured-belonging dynamics documented in Paper No. 1), institutional trust erosion (documented across every major democracy), and the specific challenge of acting with clarity and ethical commitment under conditions of radical uncertainty about outcomes. The three dominant Western leadership frameworks — Transformational Leadership, Servant Leadership, and Authentic Leadership — are genuine contributions that address the mechanics of leadership in relatively stable environments. None of them is adequate to the Arjuna moment: the moment when the leader’s identity, belonging, and tribal narrative are all pulling toward reactive action that their Viveka tells them is wrong.

The paper introduces the Svadharma Leadership Framework (SLF) — the series’ original contribution in the domain of leadership — comprising five dimensions derived from the Gītā’s specific teachings: Svadharma Clarity (precise understanding of the obligations of one’s specific role), Nishkama Action (action from role-obligation without attachment to outcome), Viveka in Decision (discriminative wisdom under identity pressure), Lokasamgraha (the community-sustaining obligation of leadership), and Sthita-prajna Equanimity (the steady-wisdom baseline that the Attention Economy of Moksha identified as the attentional pinnacle of the series’ counter-architecture, now expressed in the specific context of leading under pressure). Two testable propositions are stated. The paper situates the SLF within the series’ developing architecture and demonstrates that Svadharma Leadership is not an additional framework alongside the series’ counter-architectures but their most natural institutional expression: the leader who has cultivated the series’ counter-architectures — attentional sovereignty (DAI), epistemic resilience (ICRM), and system-design accountability (DAP) — leads differently, and leads better.

Not peer-reviewed. Circulated for scholarly discussion. APA 7. AI Disclosure: AI-based tools assisted with literature search and language editing. All analysis, framework design, and conclusions are the author's own.

title: Collateral and Secured Debt
affiliations: Duke University and Duke University - Fuqua School of Business

detail.title: Collateral and Secured Debt
detail.abstract:
We argue that firms’ assets, especially their tangible assets, serve as collateral restricting both secured and unsecured debt. Secured debt is explicitly collateralized, placing a lien on specific assets, which facilitates enforcement. Unsecured debt is backed by unencumbered assets and thus implicitly collateralized. The explicit collateralization of secured debt entails costs but enables higher leverage. Therefore, financially constrained firms use more secured debt both across and within firms. Our dynamic model is consistent with stylized facts on the relation between secured debt and measures of financial constraints and between leverage and tangible assets, and with evidence from a causal forest.

title: Cigarette Advertising Bans Raised Mortality When Risk Disclosures Ended

detail.title: Cigarette Advertising Bans Raised Mortality When Risk Disclosures Ended

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.

detail.abstract: Governments worldwide ban advertising of harmful products to protect public health, but the health effects of those bans are largely unknown. Here we measure the long-term mortality effects of cigarette advertising bans in ten countries, alongside the American ban’s spillover into Canada. These bans differed in whether they also withdrew mandated risk disclosures. We examine the USA in the most detail, where the 1971 broadcast ban inadvertently reduced the anti-smoking advertisements required since 1967. Two national surveys show increased smoking among Americans who were teenagers in the six years after the 1971 ban. The smoking increase was larger in nonmetropolitan counties with stronger predicted television reception, supporting the loss of anti-smoking advertisements as a mechanism. Using a cancer registry, we show that these same generations were more likely to develop lung and laryngeal cancer. Using three death registries, we estimate that the ban caused 47,000 to 67,000 additional deaths from lung cancer, laryngeal cancer, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. International comparisons show that deaths from smoking increased where cigarette advertising and mandated risk disclosures ended together and decreased where advertising ended without that loss. Similar regulations today for prescription drug advertising in the USA and gambling advertising in Australia risk losing a mandated health message, just as the USA did in 1971.

title: The Structural Transformation of Innovation
affiliations: Dartmouth College, Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of New York and Northwestern University

detail.title: The Structural Transformation of Innovation
detail.abstract:
We document the structural transformation of innovation using historical patent data since the 1850s, along with R&D expenditure and TFP growth for the post-war period. Over time, innovation has shifted from agricultural sectors to manufacturing, and, more recently, to services. We develop and quantify a multi-sector semi-endogenous growth model of structural change in innovation and production, incorporating the classical demand-pull and technology-push drivers of innovation. Sectors differ in their innovation technologies, and the extent to which they benefit from knowledge spillovers (technology-push). Nonhomothetic demand shifts the market shares toward income-elastic sectors along the growth process (demand-pull). A calibrated version of our model replicates the structural transformations of innovation and production observed in the US data. Using the model, we evaluate the future impact of Baumol’s disease on aggregate productivity and find it to be minimal. Our results suggest that aggregate productivity growth may recover in the coming decades as the service sector becomes increasingly innovation-driven.

detail.abstract: Background: Commercial transport is the largest user of liquid fuel in Pakistan, but digital payment adoption in this sector is not well documented. Objective: This study examines the factors that support or limit commercial fuel card use in Pakistan and considers the implications for oil marketing companies and transport policy makers. Methods: The study uses a two stage mixed methods design. It combines industry data from 1991 to 2017, eight executive interviews, a passenger survey with 7,391 respondents in Karachi and Lahore, and a post hoc review of market changes from 2018 to 2026. Findings: Pakistan's transport sector consumed 11.4 million tons of liquid fuel, or 51% of national use. It accounted for 57% of high speed diesel demand and 98% of premium motor gasoline demand. Pakistan State Oil held about 82% to 85% of the B2B fuel card market and 54.8% of the petroleum market. The 2018 forecast expected transport fuel demand to reach about 20 million tons by 2025. Actual demand stayed near 13.5 to 15.0 million tons because of price shocks and weaker economic activity. Fuel payment systems also moved from physical cards and point of sale terminals toward telematics, application programming interfaces, and direct links with corporate enterprise resource planning systems. Conclusions: Oil marketing companies should invest in secure digital fleet platforms rather than card issuance alone. Policy makers should support open data standards and interoperable payment systems at fuel stations.

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors have declared that no competing interests exist

detail.abstract: Kazakhstan Introduction. The persistently low employment rate among persons with disabilities (PWDs) constitutes a pressing socioeconomic challenge for the Republic of Kazakhstan, while the rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies simultaneously presents both novel opportunities and emergent risks for its mitigation. The present study was aimed at conducting a comprehensive analysis of the current state and prospective applications of AI tools for facilitating the employment of PWDs within the Kazakhstani context. Materials and Methods. Methodologically, the investigation drew upon: statistical analysis of aggregated data from government portals (inva.gov.kz, the Bureau of National Statistics, the Ministry of Labor and Social Protection of the Population of the Republic of Kazakhstan) and private recruitment platforms (hh.kz, Enbek.kz); a thematic review of international scientific literature (2020-2026, n = 38 full-text sources); and comparative analysis with Kazakhstan's regulatory and strategic framework. Results. It was established that among approximately 759,000 PWDs in Kazakhstan, roughly 376,000 are of working age, of whom only about 30% are employed. The potential reserve of unemployed PWDs (≈ 265,000) substantially exceeds the combined supply of quota-based and voluntarily designated vacancies (≈ 68,700), which covers merely about 26% of this reserve. Four categories of AI tools relevant to inclusive employment were identified: assistive technologies, intelligent jobmatching platforms, workplace adaptation tools, and career guidance solutions. It is demonstrated that AI possesses ambivalent potential: personalized job matching and compensation for functional limitations coexist with the risks of algorithmic discrimination and the perpetuation of gender disparities. A practical "roadmap" was formulated, encompassing the integration of a specialized PWD module into the "Digital Employment Service", the localization of AI-assisted applications, and the establishment of an employer support platform. Conclusion. It is substantiated that the introduction of AI tools into the domain of inclusive employment constitutes not a technological option but a strategic imperative for building a competitive economy in Kazakhstan.

detail.abstract: This paper presents the generic framework for a national-level model of sustainability. The basic assumption is that there is not one model (or condition) but multiple possibilities; not one path, but a multiplicity of options. The countries of this world are diverse indeed, and the challenges facing them are both generic and idiosyncratic. In appreciation of the complexity and diversity of development, our approach is to depict underlying structural and functional linkages representing' the profile of states, with the objective of exploring possible paths over time in response to structural conditions as well as policy choices.

detail.title: Collusion through Common Leadership
detail.abstract:
This paper studies whether common leadership, defined as two firms sharing executives or board directors, contributes to collusion. Using an explicit measure of labor market collusion from unsealed court evidence, we find that the probability of collusion between two firms increases by 11 percentage points after the onset of common leadership, a ninefold increase over the baseline rate. These results are not driven by closeness of product or labor market competition. Our findings are consistent with the increasing attention toward common leadership under Clayton Act Section 8.

title: The Return to Adaptation in a Changing Climate
affiliations: Columbia University, Graduate School of Arts and Sciences, Department of Economics, Columbia University - Columbia Business School, Economics and Peking University - Guanghua School of Management

detail.title: The Return to Adaptation in a Changing Climate
detail.abstract:
We quantify the economic return to adaptation in a changing climate. Our approach exploits the fact that extreme-weather arrivals are nonhomogeneous: we first estimate each country’s time-varying disaster arrival rate, then test whether per-disaster damage declines when risk is elevated—a key feature of risk-dependent adaptation. We apply this to tropical cyclones across 48 countries over 1980–2019. Indeed, cyclones do significantly less damage when the arrival rate has risen above its historical baseline. The finding survives placebo permutations, lagged-disaster controls, and two-way-fixed-effects critiques. Welfare gains reach several percent of GDP for the most exposed economies and scale sharply under climate projections.

title: What are the Costs of Weakening Shareholder Primacy? Evidence from a U.S. Quasi-Natural Experiment

detail.title: What are the Costs of Weakening Shareholder Primacy? Evidence from a U.S. Quasi-Natural Experiment
detail.abstract:
We study the economic consequences of weakening shareholder primacy using Nevada Senate Bill 203 as a quasi-natural experiment. A difference-in-differences analysis shows that affected Nevada firms experienced a decline in firm value of more than 4%, as measured by Tobin’s q. Rather than responding with stronger governance to reassure capital providers, affected firms worsen their governance. We document significant real effects through the investment channel: treated firms undertake worse acquisitions and exhibit reduced efficiency in both capital expenditures and R&D spending. Furthermore, weakening shareholder primacy does not improve how stakeholders are treated, as environmental and social performance worsen.

detail.abstract: Despite the increasing relevance of multiparty alliances, existing research remains fragmented and predominantly organized around functional purposes or structural forms, overlooking the relational dynamics among alliance partners. Such an omission prevents a systematic understanding of what fundamentally distinguishes multiparty alliances from their dyadic counterparts and how different types of multiparty alliances vary from one another. This paper addresses this gap through a systematic review of research from leading management journals published between 1990 and 2025. Adopting an interdependence-based view, we offer two main insights. First, the presence of more than two partners introduces three categorically distinct features compared to dyadic alliances: a change in membership, a change in reciprocity patterns, and the emergence of faultlines. Each of these features poses distinct challenges. Second, and more importantly, we show how pooled, sequential, and reciprocal forms of interdependence shape the emergence, evolution, and consequences of these relational features, thereby explaining systematic variations across multiparty alliances. Building on these insights, we develop an integrative framework that clarifies the distinctiveness of multiparty alliances and identifies key mechanisms and boundary conditions. This framework informs a future research agenda to redirect scholarly attention to the unique relational dynamics within and across multiparty alliances.

title: Expectations Formation with Fat-Tailed Processes: Evidence and Theory
affiliations: , Capital Fund Management, Capital Fund Management and Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Sloan School of Management

detail.title: Expectations Formation with Fat-Tailed Processes: Evidence and Theory
detail.abstract:
This paper studies expectations formation when the underlying process has fat tails. Using a large sample of firm sales growth expectations, we document three facts: (i) the relationship between forecast revisions and future forecast errors is strongly non-linear, (ii) the distribution of sales growth has fat tails, and (iii) extreme values of sales growth tend to mean-revert. We formally show that these three facts are consistent with a model in which the underlying process is non-Gaussian, but forecasters fail to recognize this fully. We estimate this model and show it quantitatively explains our three facts. Finally, we show the model is consistent with evidence from an online forecasting experiment where the underlying process is non-Gaussian and the non-linearity in the momentum of stock returns.

title: Tax Avoidance as an R&D Subsidy: The Use of Cost Sharing Agreements by US Multinationals
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania, Stanford University and Stanford Graduate School of Business

detail.title: Tax Avoidance as an R&D Subsidy: The Use of Cost Sharing Agreements by US Multinationals
detail.abstract:
We use administrative corporate tax data from the IRS to study a particular form of tax avoidance for US multinational corporations (MNCs). This strategy relies on cost sharing agreements (CSAs), which govern joint R&D efforts conducted with foreign affiliates and allow US MNCs to shift profits by moving intellectual property abroad. We analyze an unexpected 2005 Tax Court ruling that additionally allowed MNCs with CSAs to engage in cost shifting: by excluding employee stock option compensation costs from CSAs, the ruling allowed MNCs to allocate these formerly-shared costs entirely to their US parent corporations. This in turn increased the domestic tax deduction associated with R&D expenses, generating a tax shield that lowered the after-tax cost of domestic R&D. We show that the regulatory change increased market value, R&D investment, and cost shifting margins among US MNCs with CSAs following the ruling. Our results demonstrate how tax minimization strategies can translate into real changes in innovative economic activity.

title: Effectiveness of supervisory activities in mitigating banks’ commercial real estate risk
affiliations: ,  and European Central Bank (ECB)

detail.title: Effectiveness of supervisory activities in mitigating banks’ commercial real estate risk
detail.abstract: We assess the effectiveness of supervisory activities in mitigating credit risk stemming from banks’ commercial real estate portfolios. We analyse two activity types deployed by European banking supervisors: (a) on-site inspections, which assess in depth banks’ risk-taking and internal controls, but can only be selectively applied, and (b) off-site targeted reviews, which survey risk management practices across institutions, are less intrusive but are applied more widely. Using quarterly confidential supervisory data for large euro area banks between 2020 and 2024, we employ a Difference-in-Differences framework with an event-study design to capture the effects of these activities on the coverage ratio of banks’ commercial real estate portfolios. We find that on-site inspections are followed by persistent increases in coverage ratios, while targeted reviews are associated with immediate improvements which are significant but short-lived. The results highlight the complementary nature of the two activity types, which have different outreach possibilities and effects.

detail.title: Singapore’s Silicon Statecraft: Doctrinal Independence Through Substitution Under US Extraterritorial Export Controls

publicationDetails.detailsText: SMU Centre for Digital Law Research Paper Forthcoming

detail.abstract: This Article examines how Singapore manages US pressure over semiconductor diversion without adopting US extraterritorial export-control logic. Taking AI-server diversion cases as its starting point, it contrasts a US regime that follows controlled items, end users, affiliates, and computing access across borders with Singapore’s territorial, list-based framework, anchored in the multilateral non-proliferation baseline beyond which US controls have moved. It introduces the ‘hub economy’ to explain that divergence: unlike chokepoint economies, asked to restrict what they produce, hub economies are asked to police what they host, handle, and route. Alignment turns on political judgment, not legal capacity: the Article argues that Singapore regards the costs to its strategic autonomy and hub standing as too high. It preserves ‘doctrinal independence’ by retaining multilateral categories and practices ‘doctrinal substitution’ by reaching diversion through general criminal law and, potentially, cybercrime law. Transactions through Singapore are constrained not by the regulatory divergence but by extraterritorial US controls, license conditions, and anticipatory firm compliance. Whether this balance holds remains open: remote-access controls, proposed legislation concerning chip traceability and corporate affiliation, and Pax Silica may narrow the space for non-alignment. The findings illuminate how States manage asymmetric extraterritorial pressure without converting it into domestic legal obligation.

detail.abstract:
Demographic transition theory describes a sequence it has never explained. Caldwell’s 1997 call for a unifying theory with a causal imperative — one capable of saying when a fertility decline will begin and what trajectory it will follow — remains unanswered thirty years on, and the evolutionary literature has largely responded by classifying modern low fertility as a malfunction: an adaptive mechanism stranded by environmental novelty.

This monograph develops the alternative I proposed in 2006. Selection optimises verifiable fitness — the number of offspring whose arrival at reproductive maturity the progenitor survives to observe. Fertility is then what a budget buys: N = (Θ* − φ) / (LS · γ), where γ is the cost of one competitive child as a share of dyad income, φ the share committed to the old-age and health provision that keeps the observation window open, LS the probability a birth survives to maturity, and Θ* the total fitness budget. Because no dyad has a fractional child, N is an integer and observed national rates are mixtures.

Nothing here is maladaptive. The Sahel at six children and Seoul at half of one are the same calculation under different prices.

Across nine countries the fitness budget Θ* is far more stable than its components — a coefficient of variation of 10.3 per cent against 44 per cent for γ, permutation p = 0.003 — an invariance no other theory predicts. Its estimated value is approximately 0.94 of dyad disposable income. The paper reports this alongside the specification errors and one withdrawn observation found in attempting to break it.

Three original positions are falsified and the failures are diagnostic. Sweden’s fertility fell to a record 1.43 with its family policies intact, because γ moved to housing while φ rose with ageing. The predicted floor of one child per dyad was breached by Korea at 0.75, which the integer reading absorbs: zero is a rung, and childlessness is the left tail of the income distribution meeting a cost floor. And γ proves uncorrelated with income among rich countries — Korea at 0.43 on $62,000, France at 0.12 on $61,000 — because γ measures the intensity of intra-generational competition. On the OECD’s net childcare cost measure Korea is among the cheapest countries in which to have small children; on total child-rearing cost it is the most expensive in the world. Both are true, and the divergence explains why childcare-centred pronatalism fails.

The framework has no restoring force and predicts no floor at replacement. The monograph closes with fourteen dated predictions for 2026–2076, each with an explicit failure condition, separately preregistered: global fertility below 2.0 before 2035, world population peaking at 9.0–9.7 billion between 2055 and 2070 against the UN’s 10.3 billion in the mid-2080s, East Asia’s modal family size reaching one child before 2040, and most of sub-Saharan Africa below replacement by 2070.

detail.title: All Programming Languages: A Historical, Taxonomic, and Comparative Review of Human–Computer Expression

detail.abstract: Programming languages are the formal media through which humans express computational ideas to machines. Since the emergence of theoretical models of computation in the 1930s and practical high-level languages in the mid-twentieth century, programming languages have diversified into thousands of general-purpose, domain-specific, educational, scripting, systems, functional, object-oriented, logic, data-oriented, hardware-description, and query languages. This review synthesizes the historical development, classification, design principles, implementation strategies, application domains, and future direction of programming languages. Because no single paper can literally enumerate every programming language ever created, this study treats "all programming languages" as a research domain: a global ecosystem of languages, paradigms, specifications, communities, tools, and computational philosophies. The paper argues that programming languages evolve through recurring tensions between abstraction and control, safety and performance, simplicity and expressiveness, portability and hardware specificity, and human readability and machine efficiency. The review concludes that the future of programming languages will be shaped by memory safety, concurrency, formal verification, artificial intelligence assistance, domain-specific languages, interoperability, and humancentered design.

detail.abstract: This Chapter reviews empirical methodologies studying the impact of global warming on economic indicators in India. We begin with an analysis of global climate dynamics, which includes definitional debate of level and growth effects, using climate econometrics to highlight the methodological issue in temperature-GDP econometrics, and summarising methodological discussion on differentiation between weather and climate change. The chapter then evaluates India's vulnerability to climate shocks, detailing macroeconomic impacts on critical sectors such as agriculture, health, and productivity, and reviews the evolution of India's environmental policies. We further review the role of fiscal, regulatory, and monetary policies in facilitating climate adaptation and mitigation. Additionally, we explore diverse econometric approaches for estimating climate change impacts, including cross-sections and panel methods. This review highlights the urgency of coordinated international action and the need for India to implement robust climate policies to ensure sustainable economic growth and fulfil its emission reduction targets.

title: Endogenous monetary policy effectiveness
affiliations: European Central Bank (ECB) and London School of Economics

detail.title: Endogenous monetary policy effectiveness
detail.abstract: How does the effectiveness of monetary policy vary over the policy cycle? Do tightenings and loosenings have symmetric effects on the macroeconomy? This paper addresses these questions using a nonlinear empirical framework that allows financial exposure to evolve endogenously in response to macroeconomic conditions and monetary policy changes. We provide new evidence on how monetary policy effectiveness varies over the policy cycle and across economic states. We find that i) monetary policy transmits more strongly to the real economy in periods of elevated private-sector financial exposure; ii) tightening cycles increase financial exposure in the short run, which in turn amplifies the effect of further interest rate increases, whereas loosening cycles lower financial exposure, increasingly dampening the effect of interest rate cuts; iii) tightening during economic downturns further intensifies debt-servicingpressures, making monetary policy even more potent; instead, when the tightening occurs during expansions, monetary policy effectiveness is not materially affected.
