detail.abstract: Decision-making is a fundamental process through which individuals select a single behavioural alternative from two or more competing alternatives. Although existing theories have explained decision-making from rational, bounded rational, dual-process, emotional, reinforcement-learning, and neurocognitive perspectives, a unified framework describing the regulatory architecture through which an existing psychological state governs the progression of decision-making remains limited. This paper introduces the Mesa 2:1 Theory of Decision-Making, a conceptual model proposing that decision-making is governed by an existing Current Regulatory State (CRS). The Mesa 2:1 Theory does not attempt to explain the antecedent factors responsible for the formation of the Current Regulatory State. Rather, it explains how an existing Current Regulatory State regulates the progression of decision-making from multiple behavioural alternatives to two dominant alternatives and ultimately one Final Determination. The proposed regulatory architecture conceptualises decision-making as a dynamic process progressing through Psychological Regulation, Cognitive Generation, Regulatory Evaluation, and Progressive Regulatory Filtering. The theory proposes that, regardless of the number of behavioural alternatives initially generated, Progressive Regulatory Filtering culminates in a terminal stage of decision-making in which two dominant behavioural alternatives remain immediately before Final Determination. One of these alternatives subsequently achieves Regulatory Dominance and is selected for behavioural execution. Final Determination represents the selection of the behavioural alternative expected to provide the Individual Highest Attainable Psychological Equilibrium (IHAPE) by creating or enhancing psychological comfort and/or reducing psychological discomfort under the prevailing Current Regulatory State and existing internal and external conditions. This regulatory orientation may operate as Comfort-Oriented Equilibrium-Seeking under relatively unconstrained conditions or as Survival-Prioritized Equilibrium-Seeking when external constraints, threat, or immediate survival demands become dominant. Behaviour subsequently produces outcomes and consequences that may influence future Current Regulatory States through Outcome-Consequence Modifiability. As a proposed general conceptual theory of human decision-making, the framework provides a process-oriented regulatory architecture applicable wherever behavioural selection occurs among competing alternatives P a g e | 2 and offers a foundation for interdisciplinary research and practical applications. As a conceptual theory, the framework requires empirical investigation through behavioural, experimental, longitudinal, computational, and neurocognitive research.

title: Patenting the Future

detail.title: Patenting the Future

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none
declarations.ethicsApproval: n/a
declarations.funderStatement: none

publicationDetails.detailsText: Texas A&M Law Review, Vol. 15, forthcoming 2027

detail.abstract:
This Essay examines a fundamental asymmetry in patent law: while patentability is evaluated at the patent application's filing date, infringement is evaluated at the time of infringement. This temporal misalignment allows patentees to paradoxically enforce patents against subsequent improvements or that were neither disclosed nor contemplated by the initial inventor at filing. This conflicts with two foundational requirement in patent law: that inventors both provide public notice of the claimed invention and enable a skilled artisan in the technical field to make and use the full scope of the claimed invention at the time of filing. Through the doctrine of equivalents (DOE), courts permit initial inventors to capture later-developed variants as infringements, even when such variants would fail statutory notice and disclosure requirements if claimed in the original patent application. This approach to the DOE causes tension between two essential patent policies: adequately rewarding pioneering inventors while preserving meaningful incentives for subsequent improvers. 

This Essay proposes a recalibrated equivalence analysis that considers both parties' contributions: the initial patentee's enabling disclosure at filing and the technical merit of the subsequent improvement at the time of its development. This approach distinguishes between trivial technological advances warranting equivalence (and infringement) and substantial technical advances that do not. Adopting this approach would strike the right balance between the competing interests of initial inventors and subsequent improvers while also honoring patent law's commitment to public notice and disclosure.

title:
SAFETY OF MACHINE LEARNING MODELS

IN REAL-WORLD ENVIRONMENTS:

RELIABILITY AND ROBUSTNESS AGAINST ATTACKS

detail.title:
SAFETY OF MACHINE LEARNING MODELS

IN REAL-WORLD ENVIRONMENTS:

RELIABILITY AND ROBUSTNESS AGAINST ATTACKS

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests or personal or financial relationships with any individuals or organizations that could have influenced, or could be perceived to have influenced, this research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this study because it did not involve human participants, patients, animals, or the collection of personal data. The study consisted of controlled computational experiments using machine learning models and a systematic review of previously published scientific literature.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
The use of ML models in critical environments, including self-driving cars, medical decision-making, monetary transactions, and critical infrastructure management, has turned the robustness and reliability of such models from desirable properties into safety requirements. The model that works perfectly on the clean dataset and completely fails when there is a change in environment, an adversarial attack, or noise in the hardware cannot be seen as inefficient; rather, it could be potentially dangerous. This work conducts a comprehensive study on the safety of ML models in practice, covering both the robustness of the models in practical environments and the security of the models against adversarial attacks

Based on an empirical benchmark study, which comprises 240 controlled experiments conducted within 8 architectures of machine learning models, 6 methods of adversarial attacks (including FGSM, PGD, Carlini-Wagner, DeepFool, Backdoor, and Adversarial Patch), and 5 types of defense mechanisms, together with a systematic literature review involving 95 scientific papers published between 2018 and 2024, this work introduces a novel Safety-Reliability-Robustness (SRR) framework for assessing the safety of machine learning models. Experimental results suggest that adversarial training proves the most efficient defense technique, which delivers robust accuracy of 71.4% when under attack compared to 42.8% for unsecured models (Cohen's d = 2.31, p < 0.001), whereas the Backdoor method displays the lowest rate of detection (3.2/10), and Carlini-Wagner attacks deliver the highest effectiveness against undefended models. Regression modeling indicates that robust accuracy (β = 0.487), reliability score (β = 0.341), and defense method (β = 0.228) are the principal factors determining the safety of ML models, explaining 86.9% of variance of the safety score (R² = 0.869).

title: Service Provider Competence, Motivation, and Resource Availability as Determinants of Quality Healthcare Delivery:A Cross-Sectional Study at Makeni Regional Hospital, Sierra Leone

detail.title: Service Provider Competence, Motivation, and Resource Availability as Determinants of Quality Healthcare Delivery:A Cross-Sectional Study at Makeni Regional Hospital, Sierra Leone

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No external nor internal relationships to have influenced our study or independence.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethical approval was sought and received from the Ethical Review Board of the Sierra Leone Ethics and Scientific Review Committee. An informed consent form was issued to each respondent to seek their consent, assure them that their contribution to the study will be confidential, and that the data provided can only be used for the purpose of the study. The respondents were also informed that no form of financial incentive will be given to them for being part of the study – and that their choice of not being part of the study cannot stop them from getting any benefit that may come because of the study.
declarations.funderStatement: Self-Funded: No external funders.

detail.abstract: Quality healthcare delivery in low- and middle-income countries remains constrained by workforce and resource limitations. This study assessed service provider competence, service provider motivation, and resource availability as determinants of quality healthcare delivery at Makeni Regional Hospital in Northern Sierra Leone, from the service providers' own perspective. A cross-sectional study, descriptive in type, was conducted among 155 service providers, with sample size determined using the Yamane formula. Structured questionnaires were administered and analyzed using STATA to assess the relationship between competence, motivation, resource availability, and quality healthcare delivery. Most service providers (74.8%) reported possessing the required professional skills, and 91.6% perceived that competent staff resulted in improved delivery of quality healthcare; 94.8% associated competent personnel with improved patient outcomes. Motivation levels were markedly lower: only 7.1% of respondents were highly motivated, 16.1% were motivated, and 40.65% were somewhat motivated, while all respondents (100%) agreed that motivation influences quality of care delivery.  Resource availability showed the strongest association with quality outcomes, with 99.4% of respondents affirming that adequate resources affect quality healthcare delivery and 95.5% affirming that adequate resources result in improved delivery of quality healthcare; gaps were noted in bed capacity (45.8% reporting inadequacy) and equipment. Service provider competence, motivation, and resource availability were all found to significantly determine the delivery of quality healthcare at Makeni Regional Hospital, with motivation representing the weakest of the three despite high levels of provider competence. Continuous professional development, formal motivation policies, and improved resource allocation are recommended to strengthen quality healthcare delivery.

title: Big Data and Artificial Intelligence in Sustainable Entrepreneurship: Economic Performance Analysis and Market Entry Strategies

detail.abstract: Emerging economies marked by institutional deficiencies and elevated informality encounter considerable ambiguity over the impact of digital ecosystems on macroeconomic and entrepreneurial results. This research investigates the correlation between national artificial intelligence (AI) and Big Data ecosystem factors, the absorption of high-tech workers, and overall economic scale within South Asian economies. Utilizing a country-year panel dataset spanning from 2015 to 2025, the analytical approach combines two-way fixed-effects linear regression with an investigative supervised Random Forest regression model. The empirical results indicate that national AI adoption rates by enterprises, AI readiness metrics, and comparative AI market depth show statistically significant positive correlations with the share of AI-related jobs. In contrast, at a fixed total ecosystem scale, an increased concentration of venture capital allocated to AI firms has a detrimental correlation with net AI employment share. In macroeconomic models, short-term fluctuations in digital ecosystem metrics within a country have no statistically significant correlation with overall Gross Domestic Product when baseline national attributes and temporal disturbances are accounted for. Exploratory assessments of feature significance regularly highlight operational business adoption and policy preparedness as key determinants over financial capital contributions. Theoretically, these results broaden the Resource-Based View and institutional theory to the macro-ecosystem scale, suggesting that widespread technological adoption and institutional support are more closely associated with high-tech labor absorption than mere speculative capital concentration. Constrained by its macro country-year analytical framework, the research is unable to determine firm-level survival odds or micro-level founder cognition. This research provides an empirically based, ecosystem-level evaluation illustrating the co-evolution of national digital preparedness and institutional factors with the absorption of high-tech labor markets in emerging economies.

title: Calibrating AI Automation and its Labor Market Impacts, Preliminary and Incomplete
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania - School of Social Policy & Practice

detail.title: Calibrating AI Automation and its Labor Market Impacts, Preliminary and Incomplete

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict
declarations.funderStatement: No funder

detail.abstract: We are early in the latest AI technological revolution, and there are vastly different projections circulating about the impact of AI on the labor market; most of these projections assume labor automation happens on a fixed schedule. I revisit this question by calibrating a model where labor automation is an endogenous outcome driven by the accumulation of AI capital. The speed of accumulation of AI capital is calibrated based on hyperscalers' and data-center investment. The model has an intelligence sector, composed of intelligence industries, where AI capital represents a (small) share of the sector's capital; this sector automates labor as more AI capital becomes available. The physical sector, composed of the rest of the industries, uses ordinary labor and capital, and does not have the option to automate labor. As AI capital grows, the intelligence sector automates, and workers quit into unemployment. Workers eventually find a job in the physical sector, where physical capital starts to grow in order to respond to the increased labor supply that raises its marginal productivity. The model incorporates three frictions: unemployment, a cap on physical capital investment rate, and an adoption friction for AI. I calibrate the model to the 2024 US economy. If AI capital grows through a series of limited booms, unemployment increases by at most 1.4 percentage points over 20 years. Even if AI capital keeps doubling every year, as assumed in the aggressive scenario of the central case, there is no increase in unemployment in the first two years, consistent with limited effects observed on unemployment so far. Unemployment then increases by 8.4 percentage points after 7 years, while average worker labor income (including zero income for the unemployed) decreases by 5.8%, and the labor share decreases by 13 percentage points. After automation in the intelligence sector completes (year 7), leaving only strictly necessary workers there, unemployment decreases, wages increase sharply (+47.5% at 10 years), and the labor share overshoots its initial value. Without frictions, labor income instead rises monotonically. Across plausible parameter values, the depth of the income trough and the size of the ten-year wage gain depend most strongly on the growth rate of AI capital; most other parameters play a smaller role. This pins both automation and labor market effects to the growth rate of AI capital, which is therefore a key variable to watch.

title: Privacy-Preserving Credit Risk Analytics
affiliations: Shandong University and Shandong University

detail.title: Privacy-Preserving Credit Risk Analytics

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no competing interests.

detail.abstract: Cross-institutional collaboration in credit risk modeling offers considerable potential to enhance predictive performance and foster financial stability, but it is frequently constrained by privacy concerns and regulatory barriers. This paper presents a practical framework for privacy-preserving inter-bank logistic regression based on secret sharing within a Secure Multi-Party Computation (MPC) setting. Our approach enables multiple banks to jointly train a default prediction model without revealing raw client data or individual outcomes, thereby preserving data privacy and complying with data governance requirements. We implement a fully decentralized MPC protocol and evaluate it on real-world credit datasets, demonstrating that the resulting models achieve predictive performance comparable to that of models trained on plaintext data.

title: Evaluating the Participation of Proactive Scouting Agents in Real-time Human Team Meetings
affiliations: Unanimous AI, Unanimous AI,  and Carnegie Mellon University

detail.title: Evaluating the Participation of Proactive Scouting Agents in Real-time Human Team Meetings

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Three members of the research team, Hans Schuman, Miles Bader, and Louis Rosenberg are employed by Unanimous AI.
declarations.funderStatement: No outside funding was used.

detail.abstract: An open research question is whether the addition of conversational AI agents to real-time discussions among human teams enhances group performance. This study tested the value of adding proactive scouting agents to teams engaged in collaborative forecasting tasks. These agents were designed to (i) monitor the groupwise discussion in real-time, (ii) identify critical information gaps in the group deliberation, (iii) autonomously find and retrieve relevant information, and (iv) express the acquired content into the conversation using emulated groupwise human etiquette. In a controlled set of trials, small human teams of 4 or 5 members were tasked with collaboratively predicting the outcome of 34 Major League Baseball (MLB) games, either by forecasting the winning team or by predicting the total number of runs scored. In half the trials, the groups were assisted by proactive scouting agents. The other half were human-only deliberations. When tasked with predicting the winning team, the addition of proactive scouting agents to group discussions significantly increased forecasting accuracy, reducing the mean-absolute error by 18% (p=0.006) and improving raw predictive accuracy from 60% to 76% (p=0.050). These results demonstrate that adding proactive scouting agents to real-time group conversations can significantly increase team performance so long as participants possess baseline forecasting skill. In addition, 86% of participants in post session surveys (N=116) indicated that scouting agents were helpful to group forecasting efforts vs trials without these agents (p<0.001).

title: Strategic Goods and the Changing Geography of Geoeconomic Power
affiliations: University of Oklahoma - Department of Economics, University of Oklahoma and

detail.title: Strategic Goods and the Changing Geography of Geoeconomic Power

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: Firat Demir thanks financial support from the Carnegie Corporation of New York for financial support (grant number G-PS-23-60603).

detail.abstract: We develop a new measure of strategic economic power that captures leverage arising from dependence on strategically important goods that are difficult to replace. Combining bilateral trade, domestic production, product-level substitution elasticities, and a harmonized classification of 338 arms and dual-use products, we measure power across nearly 3,000 goods and every country pair from 1995 to 2024. We document a major reorganization of global strategic power. China's share rose from 3% to 30%, driven overwhelmingly by dual-use goods, while the U.S. retains a larger arms component. China also increasingly occupies product-level chokepoints and has gained dominant supplier status in 80 of 176 importer markets. Greater bilateral strategic dependence is associated with closer UN General Assembly voting positions. Finally, sanctions shift supplier power toward non-Western countries, while sanctioners' relative power remains below its pre-sanction level after restrictions are lifted.

title: GLOBAL - The Political Theory of Orthodoxy

detail.abstract: This paper develops GLOBAL as a normative political theory connecting Orthodox Christian personalism with democratic authority, monetary institutions, and access to productive resources. Its central claim is that democratic authority over Collective Monetary Issuance, an enforceable individual right to instruct Individual Monetary Issuance under common eligibility conditions and auditable rules, and access to productive independence are constitutive dimensions of political freedom. Monetary organization therefore concerns the distribution of political power itself. GLOBAL joins three mechanisms: binding democratic mandates organized through KRITIS; interest-free collective and individual monetary issuance under publicly authorized rules; and access to a first necessary productive base, complemented by protected participation in positive business results during dependent employment. The argument distinguishes theological inspiration from public justification and biblical analogy from historical evidence. It presents a minimal accounting framework separating issuance, repayment, monetary cancellation, and the collective coverage of good-faith debt remission. This framework identifies necessary accounting conditions without claiming macroeconomic sufficiency. Comparison with personalism, republican freedom, property-owning democracy, and polycentric governance clarifies the proposal's contribution as an institutional synthesis rather than an unprecedented discovery of economic democracy. The paper argues that GLOBAL is defensible as a research programme only if equal citizenship is independent of religious belief, majority decisions remain constitutionally limited, productive access does not become compulsory entrepreneurship, and monetary and digital mechanisms remain open to independent testing. It concludes with a staged programme for evaluating distributional effects, fiscal burdens, administrative discretion, and democratic security.

title: A Graph-encoded Fourier Neural Operator for Velocity Field Reconstruction from Surface Pressure Measurements
affiliations: , Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST), Wuhan University of Technology, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST)

detail.title: A Graph-encoded Fourier Neural Operator for Velocity Field Reconstruction from Surface Pressure Measurements

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This study is supported by the State Key Laboratory of Climate Resilience for Coastal Cities at HKUST (Project No. ITC-SKLCRCC26EG01), the National Natural Science Foundation of China (Project No. 52441803, W2511050), the Hong Kong Research Grants Council (RGC) General Research Fund (Project No. 16211821), and the Shenzhen Science and Technology Program (KJZD20230923115210021, GXWD20231129111527001).

detail.abstract: Inferring a full spatial field from measurements confined to accessible surfaces is a challenge in engineering, and predicting the velocity field around multiple obstacles from surface pressure is a representative instance in wind engineering. This work proposes the Graph-encoded Fourier Neural Operator (GFNO), which combines graph-based boundary encoding with Fourier-based global field decoding to address this reconstruction problem. GFNO is systematically benchmarked against four representative architectures, Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), Fourier Neural Operator (FNO), and Graph Neural Operator (GNO), on two complementary datasets derived from multi-obstacle bluff-body aerodynamics. Dataset I consists of transient velocity snapshots from a fixed three-obstacle configuration. Dataset II spans 3,360 mean-flow cases with varying obstacle layouts and wind directions. On Dataset I, GFNO achieves an RMSE of 0.031, approximately 67% lower than the next-best model. On Dataset II, GFNO achieves an RMSE of 0.058, approximately 16% lower than the nextbest model. Additional experiments assess robustness under varying sensor densities, obstaclemasking scenarios, and training data volumes. GFNO remains accurate down to 8 sensors per obstacle, and masking the most informative obstacle surface raises RMSE by 71%, revealing strongly asymmetric information contributions across surfaces. A training-ratio sweep further reveals a crossover in inductive bias. FNO outperforms GFNO at low training ratios through implicit spectral regularization, while GFNO overtakes FNO once sufficient training data become available. These findings provide systematic guidance for architecture selection under a common benchmark, and the observed crossover between spectral and geometric inductive biases may extend to other sparse-to-full-field problems in engineering.

keywords: Generational Economic Transfer Model (GETM): Measuring Generational Economic Influence Across Wealth

detail.abstract:
This study introduces the Generational Economic Transfer Model (GETM) which is a framework for
measuring generational economic influence. The model consists of four main factors: existing wealth,
transferred wealth, productivity and technology, and demographic participation.
GETM is expressed as: GEI_g=(W_g+T_g)×P_g×D_g
where (W_g) is existing wealth, (T_g) is transferred wealth, (P_g) is the productivity and technology
multiplier, and (D_g) is demographic and labor-force participation.
The paper applies GETM to Baby Boomers, Generation X, and Millennials plus Generation Z using
available data. The goal of GETM is not to make an exact prediction of the future. Instead, it is a simple
and testable framework that helps to study how wealth, inheritance, technology, productivity, and
demographic participation may change economic influence among the generations.

detail.abstract: This study investigates the effects of Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) and corruption on economic growth in Tunisia. Using bivariate copula theory, the empirical results indicate that FDI has a positive and significant impact on economic growth, while corruption is negatively associated with growth performance. To further explore the transmission mechanisms, multivariate copula models (C-vine and D-vine) are employed. The results suggest that FDI fosters economic growth through technology transfer, enhanced performance of domestic firms, and improved financial development. In contrast, corruption adversely affects public finances, discourages foreign investment, and undermines political stability. These findings provide relevant policy implications for governments and regulatory authorities in developing economies.

detail.abstract: The present study investigates the transformative character of digital finance and financial technology (fintech) in supporting financial inclusion in Pakistan and discusses their impact in terms of income inequality critically. Pakistan is also experiencing tremendous expansion in the digital financial service category in the last ten years that is comprised of mobile money, digital payments and alternative credit scoring due to growth in mobile and internet penetration, favorable regulatory environment and new fintech solutions. Improved access to cheap financial services has the potential to strengthen the marginalized groups, boost entrepreneurship, and ease the process of adopting the formal financial system. Nevertheless, this paper also emphasizes risks that could potentially arise on the high pace of digitalization of finance. Using empirical data based on national surveys, fintech adoption data, and examples of the Pakistani digital finance ecosystem, the study appraises the effect of digital finance on economic participation behaviour by various groups of people, based on income. Results indicate that although digital financial services can potentially lessen the risks of inclusion and help eradicate poverty, policy interventions and design principles is the key to reducing risks.

detail.abstract: This study explores how the performance of India's leading IT companies TCS, Infosys, HCL Technologies, Wipro, Tech Mahindra, and Mphasis shapes movements in the USD/INR exchange rate between January 2015 to December 2024. While most research looks at how currency changes affect IT firms, this paper shifts focus to the reverse: can IT stock rallies or declines influence the rupee's value? The IT sector, being heavily export-oriented and a magnet for foreign portfolio investments, plays a critical role in India's external sector stability. Using high-frequency stock and exchange rate data, the study applies econometric tools such as regression models, causality tests, and GARCH-family volatility models to capture both short-term shocks and long-term patterns. It also considers asymmetric effects and global events like oil price swings or policy shifts that may amplify volatility. The findings aim to provide fresh insights into the two-way relationship between IT stocks and the rupee, offering practical value for policymakers managing currency risk, investors making sectoral bets, and IT firms planning hedging strategies. By highlighting the IT sector's influence on India's currency dynamics, the study adds a new 2 dimension to financial econometrics literature and deepens our understanding of India's position in an interconnected global economy.

detail.title: When Better Repayment Does Not Mean Less Debt:Evidence from a Credit-Repayment Experiment
detail.abstract: This study examines whether behavioural score visibility and gain–loss framing alter repayment behaviour in a repeated consumer-credit setting, and whether ap parently stronger repayment of a loan corresponds to genuine portfolio-level delever aging. Participants completed a 24-period simulated personal-loan repayment task in a randomised 2×2 design crossing gain versus loss framing with displayed versus hidden behavioural score feedback. The main online sample comprises 448 Prolific participants across two sequential waves, with an additional laboratory sample of 193 participants used for selected robustness analyses. In the factorial analysis, score visibility reduces repayment volatility on average across framing conditions, while producing no detectable reduction in final total debt, cumulative interest, or overdraft duration. A central exploratory pattern is overdraft-financed repayment, interpreted at the portfolio level as debt substitution: 46% of online participants make at least one loan repayment that itself draws on overdraft credit before the income shockshock, substantially reducing the loan while increasing overdraft exposure and interest costs without significantly reducing total debt.

detail.abstract: Africa-focused equity indices are, in most cases, constructed on the basis of listing geography or domicile, and the revenue-based measures that extend beyond listing geography combine firms domiciled in Africa with firms domiciled elsewhere. Neither approach isolates a relationship central to the African ownership gap: the revenues that firms domiciled outside Africa earn from African customers, while the equity claims on those revenues are constituted outside the continent. This paper introduces the Africa Foreign Revenue Index (AFRI), a methodology for measuring that relationship at the firm level. AFRI restricts its universe to listed firms incorporated outside the fifty-four sovereign states of Africa and reports two measures for each firm: African Revenue Exposure (ARE), the proportion of consolidated revenues derived from African customers, and African Revenue Value (ARV), the absolute value of those revenues in United States dollars. Estimation relies exclusively on public documents and is organized through a four-tier confidence architecture that classifies each firm according to the quality of its disclosure. For firms that report Africa only within a combined region, the paper introduces a bounded decomposition in which verifiable floors and ceilings, derived from subsidiary accounts and regulatory disclosures, constrain each estimate, and a fully disclosed public reference estimate is published alongside the calibrated estimate. The paper sets out universe construction, estimation, uncertainty banding, a proposed index construction and governance framework, and specifies a hold-out validation design whose results are reserved for subsequent work. AFRI measures the revenue side of the ownership gap; measurement of the ownership side is identified as a priority for future research.

title: AI-driven Supply Chain Optimization for Enhancing Resilience against Global Disruptions

detail.title: AI-driven Supply Chain Optimization for Enhancing Resilience against Global Disruptions

detail.abstract: This paper will discuss the ways in which artificial intelligence (AI) can help supply chains to be resilient to global disruptions, such as pandemics, geopolitical crises, transportation congestion, natural calamities, and demand crises. The study integrates the previous research on the subject of machine learning, predictive analytics, intelligent agents, Industry 4.0 technologies, and responsible deployment of AI to evaluate how AI can enhance supply chain power to predict, absorb, and resilience to disruptive events. The synthesis suggests that AI may enhance disruptive prediction by detecting new risk behavior, enhance supplier risk assessment based on ceaseless evaluation of operational as well as external information, streamline inventory allocation amid uncertainties of demand, and assist in dynamic logistical routing in instances where transportation networks are limited. In addition, AI-based decision systems have the potential to enhance the speed of recovery by delivering information in a timely manner, focus on essential resources, and aid adjustment in response to various supply chain networks. Nevertheless, the advantages of AI are limited by arising, long-term issues with the quality of data, cybersecurity risks, insufficient organizational preparedness, integration issues, and accountability of robot-made decisions. Such challenges suggest that adoption of technology does not necessarily mean that resilience will be increased and they should be met with the proper adoption of governance, qualified people, quality data infrastructure and effective risk management practices. This paper thus contends that AI is more of a decision support option than a replacement tool to human opinion. The best implementation of AI is in conjunction with human decision-making, organizational governance, and bigger resilient supply chain plans that can ensure firms effectively react to complex and fast-changing disruptions (Mandava, 2025; Batta, 2024; Awujoola et al., 2024).

title: Coordinate Cut Deficits and Hall Certificates for Three-dimensional Local Repair

detail.title: Coordinate Cut Deficits and Hall Certificates for Three-dimensional Local Repair

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: Minimum-disturbance repair arises when a small set of displaced objects must be reassigned to legal receiving sites while preserving an existing three-dimensional layout. Motivated by engineering-change-order (ECO) legalization in 3D integrated circuits, we study the unitcapacity endpoint model under positive weighted Manhattan distance. For arbitrary repair cardinality, we derive an exact cut-deficit identity: the repair cost equals the sum of the three one-dimensional optimal transport costs plus twice the weighted amount of bidirectional traffic across coordinate cuts. Hence attainment of the coordinate lower bound is equivalent to simultaneous satisfaction of a finite family of cut constraints. Each cut constraint deletes a complete bipartite rectangle from the source-site graph, so zero deficit is equivalent to the existence of a perfect matching after all such deletions. We then determine the sharp local certificate numbers for repair cardinalities q = 2, 3, 4. If κ 3 (q) denotes the largest, over positive-deficit cardinality-q instances in three dimensions, of the minimum number of coordinate-cut constraints needed to certify that no zero-deficit repair exists, then κ 3 (2) = 2, κ 3 (3) = 3, κ 3 (4) = 5. For q = 3, every nontrivial cut reduces to a mandatory or excluded edge; this yields a complete five-type obstruction classification. For q = 4, the structure is qualitatively different: cuts can delete genuine rectangles, and Hall deficiencies of type 2 × 3 or 3 × 2 appear. We prove that six cuts are never minimally necessary. The proof uses the nested structure of one-dimensional prefixes and a two-color parity argument across the three coordinate directions. An explicit cardinality-four instance requires five cuts, proving sharpness. Exact pseudocode returns the minimum repair cost, all optimal assignments, and a smallest certificate for q ≤ 4. Independent computation is used only as validation. It exhausts all 4,683 weak orders of six labeled endpoints and all 545,835 weak orders of eight labeled endpoints on one axis, verifies the smallest 3D cube instances, and checks all 5,488 combinatorial candidates for a six-cut 2 × 3 obstruction. No computational enumeration is used in the proofs. The result isolates a closed discrete repair kernel with a direct application to minimum-disturbance 3D ECO legalization while leaving mixed cell sizes, obstacles, routing, timing, and capacity coupling outside the model.

title: Financial Incentives and School Dropout: An Impact Evaluation of the "Pé-de-Meia" Program via Difference-in-Differences with Treatment Intensity

detail.title: Financial Incentives and School Dropout: An Impact Evaluation of the "Pé-de-Meia" Program via Difference-in-Differences with Treatment Intensity

detail.abstract: This paper evaluates the causal impact of the Pé-de-Meia program (PPM) on high school dropout rates in Brazilian municipalities. To address the nationwide scope of the policy, we exploit variation in local treatment intensity, utilizing a municipal panel spanning from 2018 to 2024. Employing a Difference-inDifferences (DiD) framework with two-way fixed effects and municipal-level clustered standard errors, we find that the program led to a statistically significant decrease of approximately 3.8 percentage points in municipal dropout rates among treated localities and 3.1 to 5.2 percentage points in regional dropout rates among treated localities. Controlling for local socioeconomic vulnerability through the proportion of households registered in the Unified Registry (Cad Único), the findings confirm robust policy efficacy. Furthermore, regional interaction models indicate that the mitigating effect of the financial incentive operates uniformly across major geographic regions.

detail.title: Validity and Reliability Establishment for Questionnaire-Based Research Studies

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not required

detail.abstract: Questionnaire-based surveys are widely used in health, social, behavioral, nursing, management, and educational sciences, yet a substantial share of studies rely heavily on Cronbach's alpha as the sole reliability index, a practice increasingly identified as inadequate and often misinterpreted. This primer provides step-by-step guidance for assessing validity and reliability across four commonly mishandled psychometric domains. Content validity requires item-level CVI (I-CVI ≥ 0.78) and scale-level CVI (S-CVI/Ave ≥ 0.90) from ≥ 6 experts using CVR and CVI. Construct validity is assessed via Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA; factor loadings ≥ 0.40, n ≥ 200) and Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA; CFI > 0.95, RMSEA < 0.08, SRMR < 0.08), alongside convergent (AVE > 0.50; CR > 0.70) and discriminant validity (HTMT < 0.85). Internal consistency benchmarks are α ≥ 0.70 acceptable, α = 0.80-0.89 good, α ≥ 0.90 excellent, and α > 0.95 indicating redundancy, with McDonald's omega (ω) and 95% CI recommended as a superior alternative. Test-retest reliability favors ICC over Pearson's r, with ICC < 0.50 poor, 0.50-0.74 moderate, 0.75-0.89 good, and ≥ 0.90 excellent, assessed in n = 30-100 over 1-4 weeks. The full validation follows a five-phase framework-item generation, expert review, pilot testing (n = 30-60), main validation (n = 200-500), and cross-validation aligned with COSMIN and APA Standards (2014). No single index is sufficient; multi-method assessment is essential for rigorous, publishable research.

detail.abstract:
This case study examines the structural barriers that prevent Nigerian agricultural products from achieving price competitiveness in the Chinese market, using a failed attempt to export 200 litres of palm oil from Nigeria to a retail buyer in Zhenjiang, Jiangsu Province, in May 2025. The product cost was NGN360,000, while logistics and delivery to China amounted to NGN2.5 million, more than six times the product value.

The Chinese buyer's market price ceiling of 60 RMB per litre placed the landed cost of NGN14,300 per litre far above what the market would bear, and the transaction did not proceed. Through researcher-participant observation and cost structure decomposition, the study identifies five findings: the dominance of logistics costs, the absence of economies of scale, the role of domestic supply deficits, the importance of established trade relationships and infrastructure, and the limitations of tariff policy as a tool for promoting trade. The case contributes transaction-level data to the literature on Nigeria-China trade and supply chain management, demonstrating that the barriers to Nigerian agricultural exports are not primarily about tariffs or product quality but about the cost of moving goods across distance and the infrastructure and relationships that determine that cost. Recommendations are directed toward policymakers, export promotion agencies, and individual exporters.

title: The Law of Structural Outsourcing: Efficiency, Fragility, and the Clinical Counterpoint of Abundance

detail.title: The Law of Structural Outsourcing: Efficiency, Fragility, and the Clinical Counterpoint of Abundance

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no conflicts of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Evolutionary progress is frequently conceptualized as an additive process; however, evidence across genomic, cellular, reproductive, and technocentric scales reveals a counter-trajectory: strategic deletion, epigenetic silencing, and structural outsourcing. Differentiated neurons encrypt over 90% of their genome, outsourcing survival to vascular and glial partners. Genomic lineages have routinely purged synthetic pathways for essential amino acids and vitamins, outsourcing nutritional security to ecological abundance. Reproductively, autonomy has been progressively surrendered from ancestral asexuality to highly specialized sexual dimorphism. At the subcellular scale, structural microdeletions of the Y chromosome outsource male fertility to autosomal scaffolds, establishing an evolutionary reliance on external clinical interventions when genetic compensation fails. This systemic outsourcing yields extreme metabolic and computational efficiency, but introduces a profound vulnerability-the Master Domino Effect-wherein the failure of centralized external scaffolds triggers cascading collapses. The counterbalance to this fragility lies in the Law of Abundance: distributed ecological webs, nutritional redundancy, and technological plurality act as universal buffers that transform precarious dependencies into resilient mutual safety networks. Clinical practice vividly illustrates this dialectic: nutritional collapse, infertility, and cognitive offloading to artificial intelligence highlight unprecedented structural vulnerabilities, while biodiversity, assisted reproductive technologies, and hybrid human-AI reasoning systems buffer systemic failure. Complexity, therefore, advances not by internal accumulation, but by structural outsourcing sustained through environmental abundance.

title: The Branded-Prescribing Gap Associated With Industry Payments Did Not Narrow During the COVID-19 Pandemic

detail.title: The Branded-Prescribing Gap Associated With Industry Payments Did Not Narrow During the COVID-19 Pandemic

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study used publicly available, physician-level administrative data and involved no patient-level records, intervention, or interaction; institutional review board approval and informed consent were therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Industry payments are associated with physician prescribing, but whether payment associated prescribing differences narrow when promotional activity declines remains unclear. This study examined whether the branded-prescribing gap between physicians with high general payments and those with no recorded general payments in 2019 narrowed during 2020-2021. Medicare Part D prescribing data (2016-2024), Open Payments data (2019-2024), and National Plan and Provider Enumeration System records were linked. The cohort included 295,725 physicians eligible in all nine years; physician-years with suppressed outcomes (26.3%) were excluded from branded-share analyses. Physician fixed-effects models estimated changes in the prescribing gap relative to 2019, and equivalence tests, added after the event-study estimates were examined, assessed whether these changes were small relative to the baseline gap. Mean general payments to high-payment physicians fell 46% in 2020. Nevertheless, the branded-prescribing gap increased by an average of 0.183 percentage points during 2020-2021 (90% confidence interval, 0.136-0.229). This increase was statistically distinguishable from zero but small relative to the baseline gap of 6.75 percentage points, falling within the strictest fixed equivalence margin of ±0.34 percentage points; because the gap had risen by about 0.56 percentage points from a stable 2016-2018 level into 2019, the year used to define payment groups, this conclusion is specific to the 2019 reference. Secondary analyses showed substantial heterogeneity across payment groups and specialties. The payment-associated prescribing gap persisted during a substantial decline in measured industry payments. Payments measure promotional activity indirectly, and concurrent pandemic-related changes limit causal interpretation. These findings support persistence of the observed association without establishing that previous promotional contact caused enduring prescribing habits.

detail.title: Strategic Adjustment of Environmental CSR under Political Uncertainty: Substantive and Stakeholder-Facing Engagement

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Political uncertainty creates a strategic tension between preserving flexibility and remaining responsive to external stakeholders. We argue that firms navigate this tension by selectively adjusting environmental efforts across activities that differ in commitment and external visibility. Exploiting close local elections in Korea, we find that firms modestly increase aggregate environmental CSR but substantially alter its composition: they reduce resource-intensive substantive activities, increase more flexible stakeholder-facing (symbolic) activities, and leave internal environmental systems largely unchanged. The symbolic shift is stronger among firms facing greater external scrutiny. These findings suggest that firms respond to political uncertainty not by uniformly expanding or contracting environmental engagement, but by changing its composition, highlighting compositional adjustment as an important form of strategic adaptation under uncertainty.

title: Boundary Control Authority: Who Holds the Right to Set Work-Life Boundaries, and Whether It Can Be Withdrawn

detail.title: Boundary Control Authority: Who Holds the Right to Set Work-Life Boundaries, and Whether It Can Be Withdrawn

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder and CEO of Sovera, a consultancy that advises organizations on workplace design and employee experience, including topics addressed in this paper. No financial support from Sovera or any client was involved in the underlying research or the preparation of this manuscript.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The underlying study was reviewed by the University of Pennsylvania Institutional Review Board and determined exempt (Exempt Category 2), protocol number 859388, approved September 30, 2025. All participants provided informed consent prior to interviews and surveys, and data were de-identified to protect participant confidentiality.

detail.abstract: Boundary theory describes how individuals manage the line between work and personal life along a continuum from segmentation to integration, and a substantial literature has established boundary control, the degree to which individuals can manage those boundaries to fit their identities and preferences, as the mechanism through which flexibility policies are meant to work. Kossek, Perrigino, and Lautsch's (2023) review of 338 studies found that only one in five measured boundary control at all, and none measured control over permeability. Drawing on a sequential multimethod study of 35 full-time working parents in medium and large U.S. organizations who experienced workplace model shifts after March 2020, this paper argues that a further distinction governs integration quality: boundary control authority, defined as who holds the authority to decide when, where, and on whose terms work crosses into personal life, and whether that authority can be withdrawn. In the study, integration was experienced as sustainable when the working parent held that authority (24 participants, 69%) and as exploitative when the organization held it (13 participants, 37%), regardless of how permeable the arrangement was. Return-to-office mandates and monitoring technologies were the most concentrated expressions of organizational control. The paper defines the construct, distinguishes it from boundary control as currently measured, from boundary preference, and from job autonomy, develops five propositions centered on revocability, and proposes that control authority determines whether an organizational support functions as a resource or as a demand.

title: Proposer-Invariant Floors in Certified Discovery
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Proposer-Invariant Floors in Certified Discovery

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Nothing to declare.
declarations.funderStatement: This research is self-funded.

detail.abstract: Does a stronger search leave less signal hidden? At orthogonal designs the answer is no, and the reason is a floor: the concealable signal mass admits a lower bound that no discovery pipeline goes below. We define pipelines, a proposer that selects hypotheses on one part of the data and a calibrated gate that certifies on the rest, and prove that every test of null size at most alpha admits a deterministic mask of mass kappa min(B, h_P)^2 (1 - o(1)) that passes it, where B is the amplitude budget, kappa the support size, and h_P = sqrt(2 log P), uniformly over all tests. The floor is therefore invariant to the proposer, and it does not move when the gate's calibration fails. The fielded instrument, a Benjamini-Hochberg gate over coordinate statistics, attains the floor at first order, so no pipeline on the same data improves on it. That is the headline, and a reader who needs only the headline can stop here. The remainder develops the account. Validity is a property of the gate and its data lineage rather than of the search. Realized certification can order two architectures oppositely to their worst-case values. The dark fraction obeys a vocabulary law min(1, 2 log P / B^2), saturating at P*(B) = e^{B^2/2}, beyond which the entire budget can be concealed from every test. An appendix fixes the definitional apparatus, pipelines, calibration, certificates, and three accountings of dark mass, that the process-level theory builds on. The theory at general Gram matrices is deferred to a sequel and gated by an open needle law stated here.

title: Active Shooter Preparedness and Soft-Target Protection in U.S. Homeland Security
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Active Shooter Preparedness and Soft-Target Protection in U.S. Homeland Security

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Active shooter preparedness and soft-target protection are important components of counterterrorism and homeland security in the United States. Soft targets, including schools, shopping centers, transportation facilities, religious institutions, entertainment venues, and public events, are particularly vulnerable because they often have large crowds and limited security controls. Counterterrorism strategies therefore emphasize prevention, preparedness, rapid response, and recovery. Effective preparedness begins with identifying potential threats through intelligence sharing, behavioral threat assessment, risk analysis, and cooperation between federal, state, and local authorities. Security agencies can work with private organizations to develop emergency action plans, improve communication systems, conduct preparedness exercises, and establish procedures for evacuating or sheltering civilians. Physical security measures, such as controlled access, surveillance systems, lighting, protective barriers, and trained security personnel, can also reduce vulnerabilities without unnecessarily restricting public access. Rapid response is equally important. Law enforcement, emergency medical services, fire departments, and facility personnel require coordinated training to respond effectively during an active shooter incident. Public awareness programs can teach individuals how to recognize suspicious behavior and respond appropriately during emergencies. Ultimately, protecting soft targets requires a collaborative counterterrorism approach involving government agencies, communities, businesses, and the public. Continuous risk assessment, information sharing, training, and technological innovation can strengthen U.S. homeland security and reduce the potential impact of terrorist and targeted violence.

declarations.funderStatement: Active shooter preparedness and soft-target protection are important components of counterterrorism and homeland security in the United States. Soft targets, including schools, shopping centers, transportation facilities, religious institutions, entertainment venues, and public events, are particularly vulnerable because they often have large crowds and limited security controls. Counterterrorism strategies therefore emphasize prevention, preparedness, rapid response, and recovery. Effective preparedness begins with identifying potential threats through intelligence sharing, behavioral threat assessment, risk analysis, and cooperation between federal, state, and local authorities. Security agencies can work with private organizations to develop emergency action plans, improve communication systems, conduct preparedness exercises, and establish procedures for evacuating or sheltering civilians. Physical security measures, such as controlled access, surveillance systems, lighting, protective barriers, and trained security personnel, can also reduce vulnerabilities without unnecessarily restricting public access. Rapid response is equally important. Law enforcement, emergency medical services, fire departments, and facility personnel require coordinated training to respond effectively during an active shooter incident. Public awareness programs can teach individuals how to recognize suspicious behavior and respond appropriately during emergencies. Ultimately, protecting soft targets requires a collaborative counterterrorism approach involving government agencies, communities, businesses, and the public. Continuous risk assessment, information sharing, training, and technological innovation can strengthen U.S. homeland security and reduce the potential impact of terrorist and targeted violence.

detail.abstract: Soft targets and crowded places-shopping centers, houses of worship, entertainment venues, schools-present a uniquely difficult homeland security challenge because their defining civic and commercial value depends on remaining accessible and unfortified, characteristics that also make them attractive targets for active shooters and other mass-casualty attackers. This paper examines U.S. federal efforts to support active shooter preparedness and soft-target protection, tracing the evolution of DHS guidance and resources since the 2017 Las Vegas mass shooting, and assessing the specific challenges of extending federal security support to an enormous, decentralized population of privately owned and operated venues. Drawing on Tahirbayli's (2025) analysis of U.S. homeland defense gaps, the paper argues that soft-target protection illustrates the limits of a voluntary, resource-guide-centered federal support model when applied to a threat category whose potential targets vastly exceed what any level of government can directly secure.

title: Abuse Without Dominance in Africa? Some Tentative Thoughts on Article 11 of the AfCFTA Competition Policy Protocol

detail.title: Abuse Without Dominance in Africa? Some Tentative Thoughts on Article 11 of the AfCFTA Competition Policy Protocol

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.
declarations.funderStatement: The author is a Global Research Program Fellow of the National Research Foundation of Korea and acknowledges the support of JSPS KAKENHI Grant Number JP24H00013.

detail.abstract: Article 11 of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) Competition Protocol prohibits the abuse of economic dependence (AED) and several blacklisted gatekeeper (or core platform) practices, while envisaging a designation procedure for the latter. These prohibitions operate independently of Article 9 on abuse of dominance. Such a legal architecture raises some interpretative questions regarding, among others, the interplay between AED and the prescriptive obligations for gatekeepers, the relationship between general and digital AED under the AfCFTA, the specific parameters and legal effects of designation, and the interaction between AED and the abuse of dominance. Drawing on the author's remarks at the recent AfCFTA Stakeholders' Engagement Webinar, this article addresses these questions from a broader competition law perspective, advancing three (tentative) arguments: first, subjecting digital AED, as opposed to general AED, to an ex ante regulatory framework requires rigorous justification; second, designation parameters must be calibrated to capture pronounced, tangible structural issues within African markets; and third, beyond theoretical complementarity, caution is required to prevent AED from serving as an enforcement shortcut that practically displaces dominance assessments.

title: The Algebra of Certificates: Lineage, Composition, and the Price of Reuse in Certified Discovery
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Algebra of Certificates: Lineage, Composition, and the Price of Reuse in Certified Discovery

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Nothing to declare.

detail.abstract: When can later work build on a certified finding, confirming it, refining it, combining it with others, or handing a subset to a reader, without re-verifying it, and what exactly is lost when the discipline that permits this is violated? We answer with five rules carrying exact prices. Validity is a property of data lineage alone: any measurable search on data disjoint from the test rows preserves the gate's guarantee, and a hereditary lineage record is what makes the consumption of earlier certificates safe. Sequencing on fresh rows is free, and fresh confirmations multiply error rates. Shared lineage is priced exactly: re-testing a certified member at a fixed level on its own certifying rows is vacuous in the sparse regime; screening and then gating the survivors on the same rows runs the gate at level q/s, where s is the screen's null pass rate, 3.15 times the nominal level for a one-standard-error screen, with a one-line repair; and the selection-adjusted interval of a certified member never crosses zero. Aggregation requires a global budget: certificate sets do not union at a common level even on fresh data, and the online false discovery rate methodology supplies the budget layer. Refinement is the one operation that lowers a certification threshold, and direction refinement inside a certified window is valid on the certifying rows themselves, with familywise control across the certified ledger. The rules assemble into a small type system for building on certified findings, and the program's two-tier instrument is its canonical instance.

detail.abstract:
Sustainable investment has moved from a specialist activity to a mainstream component of investment practice, creating new ethical and professional challenges for investment professionals. This paper presents a suite of CFA UK case studies designed to help practitioners navigate contentious situations in sustainable investment using the CFA Institute Code of Ethics and Standards of Professional Conduct as the core reference framework. The cases are organised by professional role, covering buy-side analysts, corporate issuers, sales and marketing professionals, sell-side analysts, portfolio and fund managers, private wealth advisers, and specialist ESG professionals.
The case studies address recurring ethical risks in sustainable finance, including the reliability of ESG data, greenwashing, green hushing, selective disclosure, conflicts of interest, suitability, performance presentation, stewardship, record retention, and the treatment of sustainability-related material non-public information. They also illustrate how ethical duties may apply beyond minimum legal or regulatory requirements, particularly where sustainability claims are qualitative, incomplete, unaudited, disputed, or difficult to compare across jurisdictions.
The paper is intended as a practitioner-oriented educational resource. It does not provide jurisdiction-specific legal or regulatory advice. Instead, it uses realistic scenarios to support professional judgement, ethical reflection, and better conduct in sustainable investment decision-making.

detail.abstract: India's retail investor base has expanded rapidly on the back of Unified Payments Interface (UPI)-linked broking apps, discount brokerages, and algorithm-driven robo-advisory platforms, yet participation has not been matched by a commensurate rise in the quality of investment decisions. This paper develops and specifies an integrated, empirically testable model of the relationship between digital financial literacy (DFL) and investment decision quality (IDQ) among Indian retail investors, positioning financial risk tolerance and behavioural biases (overconfidence and herding) as parallel mediators and perceived digital trust and security as a boundary-condition moderator. Grounded in the OECD/INFE digital financial literacy framework, the Lyons and Kass-Hanna (2021) multidimensional conceptualisation of DFL, and behavioural finance theory, the paper models DFL as a second-order reflective-formative construct comprising digital financial knowledge, digital financial skills/self-efficacy, digital financial awareness, and digital financial attitude. Nine hypotheses are advanced and a 44-item, five-point Likert instrument is proposed, adapted from validated OECD/INFE, Ravikumar et al. (2022), and behavioural-finance scales. Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) in SmartPLS 4 is specified as the analytical technique, following the two-stage measurement then-structural assessment protocol of Hair et al. (2019), with formal criteria for reliability, convergent validity, discriminant validity (HTMT), collinearity, bootstrapped path significance, mediation, moderation, and out-of-sample predictive power (PLS predict). To be completed following primary data collection from a minimum effective sample of 385– 460 active Indian retail investors, determined via the inverse square root and 10-times rules and confirmed through G*Power minimum-R² power analysis. Unlike the substantial existing literature that treats conventional financial literacy as the principal antecedent of investment decisions in India, this paper (i) operationalises digital financial literacy – rather than traditional financial literacy – as the focal antecedent construct; (ii) tests a dual-mediation structure a rational-capacity path through risk tolerance and a bias-attenuation path through overconfidence/herding) within a single model; and (iii) introduces digital trust and cybersecurity perception as a moderating boundary condition unique to app-mediated retail investing, addressing gaps explicitly flagged in Ravikumar et al. (2022), Agarwal et al. (2025), and Jain et al. (2023).

keywords: Divergence and Non-Divergence of Debt to GDP Ratio

detail.abstract: It is often said that, to prevent the ratio of government debt to GDP from diverging (i.e., growing indefinitely), the nominal economic growth rate must exceed the interest rate (the so-called Domar condition). But is this really the case? In this note, using a simple model, we analyze how-when we take into account that government debt creates private financial assets, which (or the interest income derived from them) increase consumer demand-the conditions required to prevent the ratio of government debt to GDP from diverging become less stringent, and that such divergence does not occur in the first place. Furthermore, this note examines the implications of government debt in a pure managed currency system.

title: Production Structure and Consumption Dynamics in Rural Economies

detail.title: Production Structure and Consumption Dynamics in Rural Economies

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No competing interests to declare.
declarations.funderStatement: STEG.

detail.abstract: I study how the structure of production shapes interest rates and consumption dynamics in a canonical general equilibrium model with uninsurable risk. The structure of production governs income shares and depreciation rates across productive assets, which determine whether precautionary savings are absorbed through asset accumulation or through declines in interest rates. I apply the model to explain the consumption dynamics of rural households in developing economies. Because rural production is land-intensive and land is a non-depreciating factor of production, the rural sector sustains high interest rates and effective self-insurance. This mechanism jointly explains three puzzling features of rural economies: high consumption insurance, low intergenerational mobility, and low aggregate savings rates.

title: Understanding Patenting Disparities via Causal Human+Machine Learning
affiliations: and Stanford University

detail.title: Understanding Patenting Disparities via Causal Human+Machine Learning
detail.abstract:
We develop an empirical approach for analyzing multi-dimensional discrimination using multimodal data, combining human perception measures with language-embedding-based, nonlinear controls for latent quality to relax restrictive assumptions in causal machine learning. Applying it to the U.S. patent examination process, we find that, ceteris paribus, applications from female inventors are 1.8 percentage points less likely to be approved, and those from Black inventors are 3 percentage points less likely—inconsistent with legally prescribed criteria. Jointly studying multiple bias dimensions and their intersections for the first time, we uncover new biases, including an affiliation bias—individual inventors are disadvantaged by 6.6 percentage points relative to employees of large, public firms, a disparity larger than any demographic gap. Moreover, innovation quality, location, and other factors can mitigate or compound discrimination, and the disparities interact: for example, racial gaps vanish among public-firm employees, masking more severe discrimination against individuals. Existing theories such as homophily cannot fully explain the results, but a simple model of correlation neglect does.

title: Serial Acquisitions in Tech
affiliations: National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER), Boston University - Questrom School of Business, Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute (RPI) - Lally School of Management and University of Maryland - Robert H. Smith School of Business

detail.title: Serial Acquisitions in Tech
detail.abstract:
We examine serial acquisitions in the technology sector from 2010 to 2023. Defining serial acquisitions based on a granular S&P industry taxonomy, we find that they account for 24–37% of majority-control tech M&A, with over half completed by public firms. Followon targets in a series are generally larger and older than the initial acquisition, and among public acquirers, starting a series is associated with higher market value and greater innovation value, but not with significant changes in market competitiveness. Among deals with valid transaction values, over half of serial deals exceed the reporting threshold of the U.S. Hart–Scott–Rodino (HSR) Act. However, in below-threshold acquisitions, acquirers primarily target their core business category. Accounting for the cumulative value of a series would, in most cases, keep the timing of HSR review unchanged or modestly accelerate it, but when it does accelerate it, review could occur several deals or years earlier, potentially yielding important benefits in markets with long acquisition sequences. Finally, while Google/Alphabet, Amazon, Facebook/Meta, Apple and Microsoft (GAFAM) stand out from the rest of the sample for more frequent serial acquisitions, some other large acquirers display similar patterns.

detail.abstract:
Amidst interconnected environmental and human wellbeing challenges, multilateral agreements and global movements have begun acknowledging the longstanding roles of Indigenous peoples and local communities (IPLCs) in conservation and sustainable management of ecosystems and natural resources. One potential tool and emerging frontier for supporting this role more actively and inclusively lies in everyday environmental heritage (EEH). Here, we develop guidance for operationalising this concept through systematic, culturally appropriate assessments that identify and prioritise EEH manifestations on the community level.

We conceptualise EEH as social assemblage and formulate a six-step participatory assessment methodology that involves the systematic contextualisation and identification, specification, and selection of EEH manifestations. We illustrate our approach through a case study in northern Thailand, where many IPLCs have experienced prolonged tensions with modernist rural development agendas and top-down state conservation policies for tropical forest protection. Building upon participatory ethnographic research involving 75 Indigenous participants in four Hmong and Pgaz K’Nyau communities in Chiang Mai Province (implemented between 03/2022 and 05/2024), we illustrate the uses of community-drawn maps, social structure maps, annual calendars, heritage record forms, and EEH evaluation forms for prioritising heritage practices that have the potential to support conservation.

We contend that the EEH Assessment Methodology can actively support EEH with a view towards local policy challenges while remaining grounded in and respectful towards the lived realities and internal heterogeneities of communities. Our work underlines the potential of EEH as a tool for promoting inclusive and sustainable locally-led conservation and development.

title: How Much Tax Do US Billionaires Pay? Evidence from Administrative Data
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley, University of California, Berkeley, University of California, Berkeley - Department of Economics and University of California, Berkeley - Department of Economics

detail.title: How Much Tax Do US Billionaires Pay? Evidence from Administrative Data
detail.abstract:
We estimate income and taxes for the wealthiest group of US households by matching Forbes 400 data to the individual, business, estate, and gift tax returns of the corresponding group in 2010–2020. In our benchmark estimate, the total effective tax rate—all taxes paid relative to economic income—of the top 0.0002% (approximately the “top 400”) averaged 24% in 2018–2020 compared with 30% for the full population and 45% for top labor income earners. This lower total effective tax rate on the wealthiest is substantially driven by low taxable individual income relative to economic income. First, the C-corporations owned by the wealthiest distributed relatively little in dividends, limiting their individual income tax unless they sell their stocks. Second, top-owned passthrough businesses reported negative taxable income on average in spite of positive book income, further limiting their individual income tax. The top-400 effective tax rate fell from 30% in 2010–2017 to 24% in 2018–2020, explained both by a smaller share of business income being taxed and by that income being subject to lower tax rates. Estate and gift taxes contributed relatively little to their effective tax rate. Top-400 decedents paid 0.8% of their wealth in estate tax when married and 7% when single. Annual charitable contributions equalled 0.6% of wealth and 11% of economic income in 2018–20.

detail.title: Andō Shōeki's Economic Philosophy of Direct Cultivation and Self-with-others

detail.abstract: Japanese Edo period thinker Andō Shōeki (1703-1762) is primarily read as a philosopher of nature, yet his major work Shizen shin'eidō [The Way of Functioning of the Truth of Nature] contains a radical and systematic critique of political economy. This paper examines Shōeki's economic thought through the lens of four newly translated passages from Volume 25 of Shizen shin'eidō (Sections 22-25). Central to his thought are two concepts: chokkō (直耕, direct cultivation) and the principle that "the myriads of people are all one" (banmin ichi). This paper argues that for Shōeki, chokkō functions as both a labor theory of value and a normative economic principle: legitimate economic life is direct, productive labor in accord with nature, while all other forms of consumption are defined as fukō (non-cultivation), donshoku (insatiable voracity), and tōdō (stealing the Way). His second principle, self-with-others (gosei 互性 and banmin wa mina isshin), provides an ontology of economic interdependence that rejects hierarchical differentiation and anticipates contemporary theories of the commons and ecological economics. Six original diagrams illustrate the five processes of shizen, the metabolic circuit of chokkō, taxonomy of economic parasitism, gosei network ontology, seasonal self-acting world, and comparative analysis of Tokugawa hierarchy versus Shōeki's egalitarian commons.

detail.abstract: This preprint employs a methodological approach developed by W. S. Jevons and A. L. Chizhevsky. Years within solar cycles were numbered according to the standard convention in solar astrophysics, grouped, and compared against values of the geomagnetic Ap index. Application of the superposed epoch method revealed a nonlinear (parabolic) relationship between macroeconomic dynamics and cosmophysical factors. For the first half of the average solar cycle (years 1-6; 36 years of observations), the coefficient of determination for the parabolic model was R² = 0.88, with the peak of global GDP growth occurring at Ap = 11.24. For the second half of the average cycle (years 7-12; 29 years of observations), the coefficient of determination was also 0.88, while the maximum of global GDP growth shifted to an Ap value of 12.63. The results obtained mathematically demonstrate the existence of a single geomagnetic optimum for global business activity within the Ap index range of 11.24-12.63. This phenomenon is explained by a universal psychophysiological mechanism: deviations of the Ap index from this "comfort zone"-whether toward desynchronizing "magnetic quiet" or toward magnetic storms-disrupt the population-level balance of serotonin and melatonin, thereby suppressing emotional tone as well as consumer and investment activity.

title: The Passthrough of Treasury Supply to Bank Deposit Funding
affiliations: University of Southern California - Marshall School of Business, Columbia University - Columbia Business School and Amazon.com, Inc.

detail.title: The Passthrough of Treasury Supply to Bank Deposit Funding
detail.abstract:
We demonstrate the passthrough of Treasury supply to bank deposits through bank market power. We show that a larger Treasury supply crowds out deposits with disproportionate effects in more competitive deposit markets. A larger Treasury supply further curtails bank lending and affects bank funding structure. The explanatory power of Treasury supply is not driven by other shocks to deposit demand and supply. In comparison, monetary policy rate hikes have a larger impact on deposit funding in more concentrated markets, consistent with the deposits channel of monetary policy. Our empirical findings are rationalized in a model of imperfect deposit competition.

title: How Do Banks Compete? Evidence from Advertising Videos
affiliations: , University of British Columbia (UBC) - Division of Finance and

detail.title: How Do Banks Compete? Evidence from Advertising Videos
detail.abstract:
This paper studies how banks compete through a novel lens: the content of advertising videos. Using video embeddings, we identify three competitive dimensions: pricing, service quality, and trust-building emotional appeals. We build a framework connecting advertising content to franchise value and monetary policy transmission. Empirical evidence is consistent with model predictions. Banks with high local market shares compete on service and trust while downplaying pricing. New entrants compete primarily on pricing. Banks lacking pricing or service advantages lean on emotional appeals. Non-price advertising strengthens the deposit franchise, enabling banks to maintain wider spreads during monetary tightening and shaping monetary transmission.
