detail.abstract:
This article seeks, first, to elucidate the actual processes by which ethnic Chinese and ethnic Lao minorities in Cambodia have undergone Khmerization; second, to compare these processes with the Thaification of the ethnic Khmer of northeastern Thailand, who, in contrast to the Khmer majority in Cambodia, constitute an ethnic minority within Thailand; and third, through these comparisons, to examine the rapid advance of nationalization among ethnic minorities in mainland Southeast Asia.

Here, “nationalization” refers not only to the strengthening of ethnic minorities’ sense of belonging to and identification with the nation-state, but also to their compulsory or voluntary assimilation into the dominant or central language and culture—a process that overlaps with the broader currents of centralization and homogenization now engulfing local societies throughout mainland Southeast Asia, sometimes termed “Bangkokization” and “Phnom Penhization.”

Drawing on new materials gathered through field investigation, the article compares the Khmerization of the ethnic Lao of Stung Treng in Cambodia with the Thaification of the ethnic Khmer of Surin in northeastern Thailand—two peoples possessing nation-states of their own who were nonetheless separated from their co-ethnics by the drawing of borders and became minorities in neighboring countries. These cases are further compared with the earlier assimilation of the ethnic Chinese in both countries. The article also examines Cambodian perceptions of Thailand and Vietnam as a further clue to the sources of the powerful drive toward nationalization evident in Cambodia.

The article finds that, particularly in its later stages, the nationalization of the Lao in Cambodia and the Khmer in Thailand has proceeded largely voluntarily and peacefully, much as it did among the ethnic Chinese of both countries. During the second half of the twentieth century, nationalization has thus increasingly engulfed the languages and cultures of ethnic minorities in mainland Southeast Asia, bringing ethnic diversity itself to the verge of disappearance.

detail.abstract: When a prediction market lists a new claim that separates a state previously bundled into an existing claim, investors can reallocate positions, share risk, or expand speculative exposure. Using investor-level positions on Polymarket, we trace these responses. Positions in existing markets increase after related listings, and new investors account for most of the increase. Among prior holders, amplification dominates, with the majority of the exposure in the new claim reinforcing existing bets that were maintained or increased. Finer-state speculation and substitution also occur, while risk-reducing hedging is rare. Within Polymarket, the evidence favors speculative expansion over risk sharing under disagreement.

detail.abstract:
This study examines how procurement responds to upstream sustainability uncertainty in electric mobility supply chains and why some environmental, social and governance (ESG) criteria become more operational than others. It develops an explanation of uneven ESG operationalisation based on information production costs and examines procurement as a supply chain information-processing function. 

Design/methodology/approach The study draws on seven semi-structured interviews with senior actors in the Basque electric mobility ecosystem, analysed using a Gioia-informed abductive approach. Organisational information processing theory was introduced during second-order interpretation rather than as a predefined coding template. 

Findings The analysis identifies three forms of sustainability uncertainty: informational opacity beyond direct suppliers, measurement instability across ESG dimensions and interpretive ambiguity in sustainability information. Procurement responds through asking, verifying, comparing and defending supplier information. The effort varies with organisational resources, the ability to make sustainability commensurable with price and the knowledge required to evaluate supplier evidence. These differences help explain uneven ESG operationalisation. Supplier information may later support reporting, circular practices and finance-related assessment, but these downstream uses are not tested as outcomes. 

Originality The paper shifts attention from the ESG criteria included in supplier evaluation to the organisational effort required to produce usable supplier information. It explains uneven ESG operationalisation through information production costs and specifies how procurement responds to upstream sustainability uncertainty through information-processing work conditioned by organisational capacity.

detail.abstract: Dozens of firm characteristics predict the returns on delta-hedged equity options, with different explanations for different characteristics. I show that most of them are the same anomaly. Their long-short portfolios lose money because they hold options on volatile stocks, and options on volatile stocks are repriced every month when the standard contracts expire and positions roll into the next maturity. Implied volatility alone accounts for four fifths of the average long-short return, and for nearly all of it on the two rollover days; among stocks of similar volatility, the idiosyncratic-volatility and maximum-return anomalies point the other way. What the expiration weekend costs the holder of a contract that does not expire, beyond what any weekend costs, is not time decay or realized variance but a missing recovery in implied volatility, the rise that every other weekend shows and this one does not; it grows with volatility and with the open interest that rolls. The anomalies are not separate puzzles but different exposures to one recurring repricing, and each portfolio's exposure is known a month ahead, from which stocks are volatile and when the contracts expire.

title: Uncovering the relationship between entrepreneurship and wealth: an interdisciplinary review and research agenda
affiliations: , Technische Universitat Berlin, Bergische Universitat Wuppertal and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Uncovering the relationship between entrepreneurship and wealth: an interdisciplinary review and research agenda

detail.abstract: Given the centrality of entrepreneurial activity to the accumulation, reproduction, and legitimization of wealthand conversely, of wealth in the form of capital to foster entrepreneurshipit might be reasonable to expect a plethora of research on the relationship between entrepreneurship and wealth. However, as we demonstrate in our interdisciplinary literature review, a surprising lack of engagement exists with regard to this relationship. Sociological studies of wealth inequality rarely address entrepreneurship, and entrepreneurship research rarely addresses wealth. We systematically review, discuss, and synthesize the discourse in the leading journals of both fields. In the sociological discourse on wealth, we find that entrepreneurship is seen as one of many sources of income and wealth, and as a means of legitimizing its accumulation. However, the social practices, actors, and institutions that mediate the concentration of wealth through entrepreneurship, as well as the structural power of wealth in entrepreneurial activity, are rarely addressed. Similarly, in entrepreneurship research, we show that considerable attention is paid to the role of family businesses, transgenerational wealth, and nonfinancial wealth ("socioemotional wealth"), whilst the fundamental role of these factors in fostering wealth concentration more broadly remains largely unremarked upon in the literature. We therefore suggest future research that systematically engages with how entrepreneurial activity shapes wealth accumulation, and how wealth, in turn, structures entrepreneurial opportunities and outcomes. With this review, we contribute to advancing debates on inequality, social mobility, and economic development.

detail.abstract:
Modern civil litigation depends on coordination among claimants, lawyers, medical providers, experts, funders, insurers, courts, technology platforms, and evidentiary systems. Coordination can widen access to justice, improve representation, and make complex claims practically possible. The same organisational capacity can also facilitate unreliable evidence, medically unsupported treatment, inflated billing, opaque referral relationships, improper financial influence, coercive settlement pressure, or litigation pursued for purposes disconnected from legitimate redress. Existing doctrine addresses fragments of this problem through procedural sanctions, professional regulation, evidentiary rules, abuse-of-process principles, funding disclosure, insurance review, and civil remedies. It does not provide a unified method for distinguishing legitimate coordination from arrangements that warrant enhanced scrutiny or may present serious integrity concerns. 

This article develops the Civil Justice Integrity Screening Framework as a system-level legal and institutional architecture. The framework evaluates a defined litigation ecosystem across seven domains: evidentiary integrity; medical necessity and independence; referral-network transparency; funding and control risk; litigation purpose; settlement distortion; and access-to-justice protection. It operationalises those domains through a structured screening test and a Litigation Integrity Matrix that distinguishes legitimate coordination, high-risk coordination, and potentially abusive coordination. The matrix does not determine fraud, liability, sanctions, professional misconduct, illegality, or civil RICO liability. It structures inquiry, identifies information and verification needs, and connects provisional screening judgments to proportionate human review. 

The article further argues that modern litigation coordination has acquired two analytically distinct dimensions that existing doctrine does not adequately integrate. The first is an AI-enabled justice-process dimension involving source traceability, medical and expert independence, referral transparency, claimant voice, contestability, and human-supervised review. The second is a financialisation and market-integrity dimension involving claim origination, third-party funding, algorithmic valuation, portfolio incentives, settlement analytics, and direct or functional control. These dimensions may overlap, but neither proves the other. The framework therefore permits coordinated review without collapsing process concerns into financing concerns or treating lawful technology, funding, aggregation, or advocacy as evidence of abuse. Existing prototypes and confidential technical specifications demonstrate that each dimension can be operationalised, while stakeholder validation and controlled testing remain necessary before institutional reliance or claims of scalability.

title: Acquisition-side Uncertainty in Relative Rationality Theory: Emotional Adjusted Expected Cost

detail.title: Acquisition-side Uncertainty in Relative Rationality Theory: Emotional Adjusted Expected Cost

declarations.declarationOfInterest: no Interest to declare

detail.abstract:
This paper develops the acquisition-side uncertainty framework of Relative Rationality Theory (RRT) by extending Emotional Adjusted Cost (EAC) from certain acquisition to uncertain acquisition. Standard demand theory, search-cost theory, and behavioural consumer research provide important treatments of non-price attributes, search, time, waiting, stock-outs, and consumer experience. The contribution developed here is more specific: within RRT, economic costs, economic revenues, emotional costs, and emotional revenues are represented on a common cash-equivalent scale and incorporated into an acquisition-side uncertainty architecture. Thispaper introduces Emotional Adjusted Expected Cost (EAEC) as the RRT demand-side uncertainty extension of EAC. It distinguishes one-shot Expected Emotional Adjusted Cost (EEAC), where the decision-maker makes a single uncertain acquisition attempt, from repeated-search Emotional Adjusted Expected Cost (EAEC), where the decision-maker continues searching until successful acquisition.

The central claim is that uncertain acquisition should not be evaluated only through nominal price or expected monetary expenditure. Failed acquisition attempts may generate travel costs, wasted time, frustration, disappointment, search fatigue, delay, anxiety, and loss of trust, while successful acquisition may generate emotional revenues such as certainty, relief, convenience, confidence, and satisfaction. EAEC translates these economic and emotional consequences into a cash-equivalent acquisition-cost structure. The relatively rational choice is therefore not necessarily the cheapest option, but the option or acquisition path with the lowest Expected Emotional Adjusted Cost. By formalising one-shot uncertainty, repeated search, stock-out risk, online versus in-store acquisition, bundle acquisition, and EAEC-based utility mapping through Decision-EAW, the paper extends RRT from price-centred demand analysis to emotionaleconomic acquisition paths under uncertainty.

title: Declarers, Defenders, Experimenters, Builders: How Universities Are Responding to AI

detail.abstract: Institutions of higher education are responding to the rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence with widely divergent strategies, ranging from public declarations of AI leadership to quiet experimentation, defensive policy development, and active co-creation with students and faculty. Yet the scholarly literature has not yet produced a coherent framework for understanding these divergent responses or their implications for institutional governance. This article argues that variation in institutional responses to AI is neither random nor merely tactical. It reflects identifiable orientations along two axes: how institutions position themselves between reactive control and adaptive learning, and how they relate to uncertainty, whether by suppressing it through policy artefacts or engaging it through structured governance processes. The article draws on disruptive innovation theory, Theory U, and institutional isomorphism. It is grounded in the author's direct experience in institutional AI policy development, including cross-functional engagement with senior leadership, faculty, student affairs professionals, library administrators, and students as part of a formal AI task force process. From this foundation, the article develops a four-category typology of institutional AI responses-the Declarers, the Defenders, the Experimenters, and the Builders-as a framework for understanding not just what institutions are doing, but why governance succeeds or fails in each case. Running beneath these governance orientations is a more fundamental question about institutional priorities: whether the institution has maintained the engagement infrastructure-writing centers, faculty mentoring, peer learning, genuine advising-that makes honest learning possible. The central theoretical contribution is this: institutions that conflate policy with governance are likely to be structurally constrained in their capacity to respond to a technology evolving faster than any fixed policy framework can track. Anticipatory governance, understood as the institutional capacity to learn and adapt under genuine uncertainty, is not a best practice among options. It is the condition under which any other intervention becomes sustainable.

detail.abstract: Cross-border payment infrastructure has expanded rapidly, but infrastructure availability and transaction growth do not necessarily indicate adoption by specific user segments. This paper introduces the Pre-Transactional Gap, which is defined as the gap between a person's potential eligibility for a cross-border payment capability and the initiation of a successful transaction. It develops a framework organised in two layers. Three adoption barriers operate in the user's journey toward a completed transaction. The Architecture Inheritance Gap arises when domestic payment assumptions are carried into new markets. The Discovery Context Gap separates general awareness of a payment option from confidence it will work at a specific merchant and moment. The Consent Timing Gap occurs when activation consent is requested before or after the user's motivation is highest. A fourth element, the Observability Gap, sits at a different level. It is a cross-cutting institutional measurement failure that prevents the other three from being seen at any stage of the journey. The framework applies to three user segments, including tourists, regular diaspora remitters, and migrant remitters with limited access to formal financial services, using the user-segmentcorridor pair as the primary unit of analysis. Drawing on publicly available data, operational experience, and illustrative propositions, the paper proposes three intervention areas, which are corridor-aware activation, consent-based contextual delivery, and geographic acceptance mapping. It closes by naming two open policy design questions on segment-level measurement and the consentbased use of network signals. This is a conceptual working paper grounded in practitioner experience rather than causal validation. Its contribution is a segment, corridor and stage framework for identifying and attributing barriers that occur between payment eligibility and transaction initiation, together with a set of testable propositions. It does not offer validated causal findings.

detail.abstract: Thermal comfort in buildings has long been described through physiological and heat-balance models, yet how people actually seek, avoid, and use cooling is more variable than those models predict, especially in warm climates where air conditioning is pervasive. This paper asks whether individuals can be grouped by their thermal-preference behavior rather than by physiology alone, using a longitudinal smartwatch micro-survey deployment collected in Singapore with the open-source Cozie platform. The analysis draws on 9,520 geolocated thermal-preference responses from 104 eligible participants, each paired with a matched outdoor heat index and an environmental-control context defined by the likelihood that the occupied space is air-conditioned. Three person-level behaviors, the tendency to prefer cooler conditions, the tendency to prefer warmer conditions, and the sensitivity of cooling demand to outdoor heat, are stabilized with empirical-Bayes shrinkage and clustered into four behavioral archetypes: the Craver, the Captive, the Conventional, and the Carefree. Mechanistic scrutiny with cluster-bootstrap confidence intervals shows that two archetypes behave as thermal physiology predicts, with cooling demand that rises with outdoor heat and is relieved by air conditioning, while two are largely decoupled from the physical environment, consistently seeking or forgoing cooling regardless of the heat around them. The groups are robust to clustering perturbations and are not explained by wearable physiology or by most stable personal traits, with only personality openness showing a modest association. These findings indicate that thermal preference in a warm climate is only partly a physiological response and is substantially behavioral, and they argue for comfort strategies and cooling policies that offer people a genuine choice among low-carbon paths to feeling comfortable.

detail.abstract: The growing role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the economy has been met with both hope and anxiety. The hope is driven by the potential of the technology to accelerate economic growth and push the frontier of science. Yet this promise is tempered by anxiety over AI's potential impact on the labor market. Such concerns have prompted researchers and policymakers to weigh responses to help manage any AI-driven disruption. The need for such interventions may be particularly pronounced if highly capable and advanced AI systems-including artificial general intelligence (AGI)-develop and diffuse widely. This paper sets out to systematically evaluate 11 such policy responses across four core dimensions: whether a policy (1) boosts welfare, (2) supports agency and socioeconomic empowerment, (3) can be feasibly implemented, and (4) remains durable across different economic scenarios. We conducted our investigation using a multi-method approach, including economic analysis, a nationally representative survey of 2,019 Americans, and a simulated panel of AI agents trained on the personas of 51 prominent economists. Our work suggests a strong tension between popular support for a policy and that policy's durability across different scenarios of economic transformation, with public preferences and scenario durability negatively correlated. Given the epistemic uncertainty over the level of disruption that might emerge due to AI, our analysis points to a dynamic and phased policy package that evolves as labor market conditions shift. This package could include expanded unemployment insurance, a negative income tax, and capital redistribution.

title: Are Global Production Networks Resilient to Geo-Political Instabilities?

detail.title: Are Global Production Networks Resilient to Geo-Political Instabilities?

detail.abstract: Using granular bilateral trade data, recorded UNGA votes on security issues, and adhering to best possible practices in structural gravity estimation, the study establishes that, as a consequence of geopolitical conflicts, trade, on average, is being reoriented away from countries in opposing geopolitical blocs and towards countries with similar political alignments. However, this pattern is not consistent across the two most GVC-intensive sectors, automobile and electronics, where we find that the shocks are mostly absorbed through price adjustments rather than actual changes in the volume traded. Additionally, most of the geopolitical fragmentation is documented for final commodities, with inputs being more resilient. However, the underlying cause of such resilience and heterogeneity is structural. The study finds that, conditional on the availability of alternate suppliers to source from, agents decide to diversify and reduce their dependence on a single supplier. However, if alternate suppliers are not available, cross-political-bloc input trade relations turn out to be resilient. Following this pattern, this study confirms that differentiated commodities, for which supplier relationships include significant specialised investments and thus higher sunk costs, are more resilient when compared with homogeneous commodities. Similarly, being a connector economy is not solely a political consideration. Finally, after identifying cross-bloc countries as strategic threats, firms prefer relocating to countries with better judicial mechanisms, freer trade, and better business regulations.

title: When Is Private Money Information-Sensitive? Evidence from Stablecoin Reserve Disclosures
affiliations: Aston Business School, Aston University, Aston University - Aston Business School, Athens University of Economics and Business - Department of Business Administration and University of Zurich - Department Finance

detail.title: When Is Private Money Information-Sensitive? Evidence from Stablecoin Reserve Disclosures
detail.abstract: Theories of private money predict that debt designed to circulate at par is information-insensitive: disclosure moves prices only where asymmetry about backing survives. We test this using a hand-collected calendar of 116 stablecoin reserve attestations by Tether and Circle, 2018-2026, in a panel with date and asset fixed effects. Tether's releases widen its peg deviation by roughly half relative to peers the same day, without abnormal volume or redemptions: repricing, not runs. Circle's releases move nothing on average, but do move its peg in months disclosing material reserve reallocations. Information sensitivity attaches to disclosure content, not issuer identity.

title: CEO Overconfidence and Bank Payout Strategies
affiliations: , , University of Bristol and University of Zurich - Department Finance

detail.title: CEO Overconfidence and Bank Payout Strategies
detail.abstract: We examine the impact of CEO overconfidence on payout policies in U.S. banks over a period of more than two decades. We find that banks with overconfident CEOs have higher payout ratios and tend to smooth dividends to a greater extent than banks with non-overconfident CEOs. This finding contradicts those in the literature on nonfinancial firms, in which overconfident CEOs reduce payout ratios to invest more in risky projects. We also show that institutional ownership constrains payout ratios and investors tend to react less positively to dividend increase announcements when the bank CEO is overconfident.

detail.abstract: Bulgaria just became the most recent European Union Member State to implement a comprehensive personal insolvency regime, leaving Malta as the sole remaining holdout. This article examines the parallel but ultimately divergent paths of the two countries toward individual debt relief. Both Malta and Bulgaria long resisted extending insolvency relief to individuals, despite mounting personal debt problems and growing European support for a "second chance" for over-indebted small businesspeople. Both eventually relented only a few years ago in the face of an EU mandate to offer discharge relief to individual entrepreneurs. Malta stopped there. Facing additional pressure from EU authorities, Bulgaria went further, resolving a decade-long legislative battle and enacting a full-fledged personal insolvency law. This article examines the Maltese and Bulgarian laws extending insolvency relief to individual entrepreneurs, along with Bulgaria's new universal personal insolvency law, including its eligibility requirements and provisions on no-asset cases, repayment plans, liquidation, and discharge. Although the new Bulgarian system has yet to be tested in practice, its architecture broadly reflects emerging international norms and offers reason for optimism. Malta's continued exclusion of consumers from insolvency relief, by contrast, leaves it relegated to the ignominious distinction of being the EU's last personal-insolvency holdout.

title: Lease or Moat A Gated Protocol for Separating Velocity from Capture in Early-stage Companies

detail.title: Lease or Moat A Gated Protocol for Separating Velocity from Capture in Early-stage Companies

detail.abstract:
Is this company’s advantage actually defensible?

Investors often infer defensibility from what is easiest to see—growth, scarcity, pricing power, or a position at a chokepoint. Yet a company can exhibit all four while the constraint that produces them is controlled by someone else. This paper distinguishes a commanding market position from a defended one. Its contribution is causal: it separates the decisive constraint that makes a position defensible from the dependencies merely required to operate the business. It introduces a gated protocol that identifies the constraint through which competitive value must pass, determines who controls it, and classifies the position as an owned closure, a conditional transition, or a lease. An owned closure occurs when the company materially controls the decisive constraint; a conditional transition exists when it has a credible path to such control but has not yet crossed the threshold; and a lease arises when the decisive constraint is controlled upstream. For a conditional transition, the protocol requires the analyst to name a specific, observable event that will resolve the reading.

The protocol is applied to companies already priced by the market, historical companies evaluated at decision points before their outcomes were known, three companies designed to stress-test the method, and one contemporary case whose outcome remains open—stated as a dated prediction with a fixed evaluation date. The protocol operationalizes this separation as a structural test distinguishing captured value from a rented position, made prospectively testable by applying it before the outcome is known and specifying in advance what observation would overturn the reading. It also converts the reading into a founder-level strategic assignment: what the company must come to control before an upstream owner, rival, or substitute can appropriate the economics of its position.

Finally, a cross-regional annex illustrates the same structural reading across Europe, Asia, Africa, and the Americas, demonstrating that the distinction travels beyond a single region.

title: Southeast Asia's Green Hydrogen Export Gap: Production Cost Estimates Against Japan's and Korea's Stated Price Targets

detail.title: Southeast Asia's Green Hydrogen Export Gap: Production Cost Estimates Against Japan's and Korea's Stated Price Targets

detail.abstract: Green hydrogen occupies an unusual place in the energy transition: a strategically prominent decarbonization pathway whose near-term economics remain deeply uncertain. Viet Nam, Malaysia, and Indonesia have each published national strategies framing themselves as future green hydrogen or ammonia exporters, at the same time Japan and Korea have begun operating real procurement mechanisms rather than only publishing aspirational strategies of their own. This paper compares IEA's country-level modelled hydrogen production-cost estimates for these three countries against Japan's and Korea's stated 2030 government price targets reported separately, since the two targets are not established to sit at the same point in the value chain and examines what each country's rst real procurement award reveals. The principal result: even using IEA's 2030 cheapest-site cost estimates under its Stated Policies Scenario (USD 4.50 5.95/kg H 2), Southeast Asian production cost remains above both Japan's (USD 2.102.37/kg, explicitly CIF/delivered) and Korea's (USD 2.833.43/kg, a national market-reference price whose exact value-chain position its source document does not specify) 2030 targets for all three countries. Relative to Japan's target, the gap is roughly 1.92.8 times and constitutes a minimum, pre-logistics competitiveness gap, since Japan's CIF target already includes delivery while the Southeast Asian gure does not; relative to Korea's target the gap is roughly 1.32.1 times, a gure that carries the additional caveat of Korea's unresolved value-chain denition. A supplementary, temporally mismatched comparison against 2023 country-average costs shows a larger gap of roughly two to nearly four times. Neither buyer country's live procurement mechanism discloses an actual market-clearing price, so this paper compares Southeast Asian costs against stated policy price targets, not evidence of willingness to pay. Separately, it reports that both countries' rst real procurement awards (20242025) went to blue, non-Southeast-Asian ammonia suppliers rather than a Southeast Asian green one an early outcome consistent with, but not independent proof of, the cost-gap nding, given that eligibility rules and project readiness also plausibly shaped both awards. An independent global trade-ow model, examined separately, projects Southeast Asia itself as a net importer of green hydrogen overall complementary, model-based evidence directionally consistent with this paper's cost-side nding, in real tension with the region's own stated export ambitions.

title: 0DTE Options and the Price of Tail Protection
affiliations: City University of Hong Kong (CityU)

detail.title: 0DTE Options and the Price of Tail Protection
detail.abstract: On May 16, 2022, the addition of Tuesday and Thursday weekly expirations extended SPX same-day-expiry (0DTE) options to every weekday. SPX put skew compressed across tenors, peaking at 72 basis points at 30 days. A cross-tenor difference-in-differences design shows that the decline is concentrated in the put wing and is absent in date and asset placebos, supporting a causal interpretation. Customer net put buying rises within one week of maturity, concentrated at zero to two days, while gap risk that daily expirations cannot remove limits compression at the shortest tenor. The implied reduction in the cost of equity tail insurance over the May 2022–June 2024 episode is $0.9 to $1.5 billion. Post-2022 skew partly reflects intermediation-cost changes alongside tail-risk preferences.

The initiative has received internal funding from the Faculty of Arts, Design & Architecture at UNSW since its inception, and the passport component received project-specific funding from the Provost in 2025–2026.

detail.abstract: Australia's national suite of higher education surveys, Quality Indicators for Learning and Teaching (QILT), has operated for around a decade, bringing together a rich dataset spanning student experience, graduate outcomes, and employer perspectives. This article draws on policy materials, scholarly literature, and sector commentary alongside a descriptive and interpretive longitudinal analysis of national QILT data from 2016 to 2025. To begin, we consider how QILT participates in the dynamic feedback loops between institutions, governments, and wider society. We then focus on survey indicators relating to skills, conceptualising 'skills' as a 'quilting point' that brings student experience, graduate outcomes, employer expectations, institutional mission and public accountability into relation. Our longitudinal analysis shows relative stability in employers' assessments of graduate skills, alongside a persistent and widening divergence between supervisors' and graduates' assessments of how well the qualification prepared graduates for employment. This divergence may reflect a gap in graduates' recognition and articulation of their capabilities rather than a straightforward skills deficit. Finally, we argue that QILT provides a valuable longitudinal view of national trends, however it cannot show where skills are taught, practised, assessed or made meaningful within curricula and disciplines. As Australian higher education enters a renewed era of mission-based compacts, we therefore propose a layered evidence architecture around skills, in which national indicators are complemented by curriculum-embedded evidence and learner-controlled portable credentials. This approach allows each form of evidence to remain appropriate to its scale and design, without requiring QILT to demonstrate forms of educational value beyond its reach.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a monthly Structural Strategic Import Risk Index (SSIRI) that combines U.S. import dependence on China with concentration among alternative non-China suppliers. In the headline specification, family-level risk equals the current China import share multiplied by the squared non-China supplier Herfindahl-Hirschman index calculated over the preceding 12 months. Using monthly bilateral customs data from January 2004 through December 2025, sectoral indices are constructed for Battery and Energy Storage Materials (BAT) and Critical Minerals and Advanced Materials (CMA). Mean structural vulnerability is 0.0608 for CMA and 0.0349 for BAT. Exposure weighting reverses this ranking because electric accumulators dominate BAT import value. Graphite products and accumulators are the principal contributors to BAT vulnerability, while antimony, rare-earth materials, barite, and tantalum contribute most to CMA vulnerability. The structural sector ranking is robust to alternative concentration parameters, supplier windows, targeted classification exclusions, and leave-one-family-out tests. Patterns surrounding historical Chinese export-control episodes are consistent with limited substitution, persistent China-centered sourcing, and concentrated fallback supply in several high-risk families. SSIRI provides a transparent screening tool for prioritizing further assessment of diversification, stockpiling, allied sourcing, recycling, and domestic capacity.

detail.abstract: Whether merchant arbitrage acts as a counter force to the "merit order effect" of solar and wind is important, but little is explored in the Australian National Electricity Market (NEM). This study fills this gap by studying the impact of charging and discharging stand-alone Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) on spot electricity prices considering their rapid recent growth in the wholesale electricity market. Australia is a global leader in BESS, and this study context is also relevant to other countries decarbonizing their energy mix. We use 5-minute wholesale price data between 2024 and 2025 and apply Quantile Regressions with instrumental variables. We find that stand-alone BESS has impact on spot-prices, but the effect is asymmetric: charging BESS increases the spot price, while discharging them decreases the spot price and thus driving self-cannibalisation. The net impact of charging and discharging on the electricity prices on consumer prices can be negative, especially under large scale penetration of BESS. The findings also offer some policy recommendations.

detail.abstract: This study investigates the conditionality of short-run competitiveness effects of FinTech investment by economic policy uncertainty. The study uses a balanced panel of 26 Indian commercial banks during the period 2010-2024. The results indicate that the FinTech expenditure is negatively associated with subsequent competitiveness based on a competitiveness index constructed from PCA and two-way fixed-effects estimation. The association is more adverse economically with policy uncertainty though the interaction is sensitive to conservative inference. The negative association of FinTech is concentrated in financial intermediation and credit growth, and is stronger for private-sector banks. The paper contributes to the literature on uncertainty by stressing the role of prior technological commitment as a source of heterogeneity in bank responses to a common policy environment. It shows that policy uncertainty may widen the short-run gap between technology investment and competitive returns by separating expenditure from realized digital capability.

detail.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly influencing how students search for, interpret, and communicate historical information. While GenAI can provide rapid access to historical explanations and generate diverse forms of content, its outputs may contain inaccuracies, fabricated references, decontextualized claims, bias, and excessive certainty. These characteristics create an important challenge for history education, where students are expected to evaluate evidence, identify authorship and provenance, contextualize historical claims, corroborate sources, and construct evidence-based judgments. This study examines the relationship between students' engagement with generative AI and their historical source-criticism competence in higher education. Using a quantitative descriptive-correlational design, the study proposes a sample of 200 university students enrolled in general education and history-related courses at a Philippine state university. Data are gathered through a researcher-developed instrument measuring GenAI engagement, awareness of AI limitations, and historical source-criticism competence in terms of sourcing, contextualization, corroboration, evidence evaluation, and historical judgment. Descriptive statistics, Pearson's product-moment correlation, and multiple regression are proposed for analysis. The illustrative results suggest that students may demonstrate moderate-to-high GenAI engagement but only moderate competence in independently verifying AI-generated historical claims. The expected contribution of the study is an empirically grounded framework for strengthening source criticism and historical thinking in an AI-mediated learning environment.

detail.abstract:
Stablecoins are moving from crypto-market infrastructure toward an institutional payment and settlement layer. By 2026, major card networks, fintech infrastructure providers and the global bank messaging network are integrating blockchain-based settlement or tokenised money. Yet headline on-chain volumes can mislead: the Bank for International Settlements estimates roughly $28 trillion of stablecoin transaction volume in 2025, while payment-related flows were only about $390 billion. The technology is therefore simultaneously real, fast-growing and still early in real-economy adoption.

This paper examines stablecoins through a CFO and macroeconomic lens. It distinguishes ledger speed from end-to-end payment performance, analyses liquidity and working-capital effects, evaluates the security architecture beyond the blockchain itself, and compares stablecoins with correspondent banking, instant-payment links, tokenised deposits and central bank digital currencies.

The paper introduces two analytical constructs: the Cross-Border Settlement Friction Wedge, which decomposes the all-in economic cost of a cross-border payment, and the Stablecoin Settlement Dividend, which measures the potential reduction in that wedge after accounting for new on-chain and compliance costs.

India is used as a detailed emerging-market case study. In FY2025-26, India recorded merchandise exports of $441.8 billion, merchandise imports of $775.0 billion and a merchandise deficit of $333.2 billion, partly offset by a services surplus of $213.9 billion. India also received approximately $150.7 billion in personal remittances in 2025. A calibrated scenario model suggests that regulated tokenised settlement could create meaningful savings in fees and working capital, but it would not mechanically reduce a trade deficit. Unrestricted foreign-currency stablecoin adoption could instead deepen dollarisation, complicate capital controls and increase monetary-policy spillovers.

The paper concludes that the likely end-state is a hybrid multi-money architecture in which regulated stablecoins, tokenised bank deposits, CBDCs, instant domestic rails and traditional payment networks interoperate under common compliance and legal standards.

title: Ideology beyond Unity: A Meta-Conceptual Account of Structural Plurality

detail.title: Ideology beyond Unity: A Meta-Conceptual Account of Structural Plurality

detail.abstract: Since its emergence at the end of the eighteenth century, the concept of ideology has remained marked by persistent definitional instability. Across philosophy and the social sciences, it has been understood as false consciousness, social mediation, discursive framework, symbolic system, and more. This plurality has often been treated as a theoretical defect, prompting repeated attempts to stabilize the concept through a unifying definition. This paper argues that such attempts are systematically misguided. The instability of ideology is not best explained by conceptual confusion, semantic looseness, or theoretical failure, but by the fact that the concept operates across distinct analytical levels. Drawing on the conceptual history of ideology and its major theoretical rearticulations, the paper argues that ideology is a structurally plural concept. Its plurality is not accidental but constitutive of the mediating role ideology plays across epistemic, social, and symbolic domains. Accounts that define ideology at a single analytical level generate genuine insights, but they do so by foregrounding one dimension of the concept at the expense of others. Apparent theoretical conflicts are therefore often better understood as the result of treating different explanatory tasks as if they were rival answers to the same conceptual question. By distinguishing structural plurality from ambiguity, vagueness, and polysemy, the paper offers a meta-conceptual framework for explaining why efforts to unify ideology have repeatedly failed. It concludes that the philosophical task is not to reduce ideology to a definitive theory, but to clarify the conditions under which its different articulations become illuminating, warranted, or reductive. Ideology thus emerges as a paradigmatic case of a concept whose significance lies less in definitional closure than in the mediating work it performs across irreducibly distinct domains of analysis.

detail.abstract: The rapid advancement of Generative AI and no-code AI platforms is reshaping the skill landscape of the modern workforce. While AI literacy is becoming indispensable, the ability to apply AI tools effectively within specific disciplinary contexts-combining nocode AI competencies with domain knowledge-remains underexplored in the context of graduate employability. This paper proposes a conceptual framework examining how nocode AI competencies and domain knowledge jointly influence graduate employability, mediated by integration skills. Grounded in Human Capital Theory and the Technology Acceptance Model, the framework posits that no-code AI competencies and domain knowledge positively affect individual employability both independently and synergistically through enhanced integration skills. The paper outlines four hypotheses, a 7-step strategic learning framework, and a proposed research methodology using PLS-SEM with final-year business and engineering students and recruiter respondents. The study contributes to the literature by integrating no-code AI constructs with traditional employability theory, offering a roadmap for curriculum design, and providing empirical guidance for educators and policymakers on future-proofing higher education.

detail.abstract:
A monotone re-encoding of firm characteristics leaves every within-date ordering intact
and still changes the book a neural ranker trades. Pooled across five differentiable ranking
objectives, moving from a centred percentile rank to an inverse-normal rank is worth
+0.370 of annualised gross Sharpe ratio (t = 4.46) and +0.307 net. A third arm, carrying
the percentile shape at the inverse-normal scale, splits that gap in two. The larger half
belongs to the change of scale, +0.224 (p = 0.020), which multiplies every rank by a
constant and cannot reorder anything. The change of shape at matched scale contributes
+0.146 (p = 0.065).
The setting is 144 point-in-time characteristics on a top-1000 United States equity
universe, 272 consecutive monthly rebalances from April 2003 to November 2025, and
23 purged walk-forward folds. Representation, ranking objective, weighting scheme and
traded tail width each vary alone; the universe, the monthly label, the architecture, the
five-seed ensemble and the execution rules do not. The training target stays on the
percentile encoding, so the contrast runs through the feature channel alone. A gradientboosted
pairwise ranker on the identical surface acts as an invariance control and returns
a contrast of exactly zero: its two arms fit the same trees, agreeing on topology, split
feature, split gain and every leaf value.
The effect is close to invisible to the statistic this literature usually reports. Mean
rank information coefficient moves from 0.0383 to 0.0403, a difference no test separates
from zero (p = 0.44). What moves is the steadiness of the ordering, whose dispersion
falls from 0.1063 to 0.0892 and whose information ratio rises from 0.361 to 0.452. The
two steps then act on different quantities. Scale moves IC dispersion and book volatility,
leaving both means within their standard errors. Shape moves the annualised return, by
1.95 percentage points (p = 0.015), leaving dispersion and volatility within theirs. The
gain also belongs to the ensemble rather than to any single fit, since one seed on its own
recovers +0.192 of the +0.370.
Annualised return rises from 18.51% to 22.14% and volatility falls from 16.81% to

impact, stock-loan and financing costs (plain rules, deliberately left unoptimised),
every one of the twelve sweep specifications loses between 0.45 and 0.56 of Sharpe ratio,
more than the representation choice adds, and every one reaches its deepest drawdown
in 2025 without recovering inside the sample.
Part I states the research questions, positions them in the learning-to-rank, empirical

Part II reports the representation, construction and friction results. Part III examines subperiods, the drawdown common to every specification, and the alternative
explanations that bear on the interpretation.

title: Swarms in AI Innovation - Why exponentials of exponentials matter in innovation, and where they break

detail.title: Swarms in AI Innovation - Why exponentials of exponentials matter in innovation, and where they break

detail.abstract: Three documented events frame the question this article studies, and each one was, at the time, unremarkable engineering. In July 2024 one vendor's content update reached about 8.5 million hosts in minutes and produced cross-sector disruption that took roughly ten days to unwind (CrowdStrike, 2024; Parametrix Insurance, 2024). In May 2010 independently designed trading algorithms, coupled only through the prices and volumes they all read, produced a 27,000-contract, 14-second cascade that a five-second exchange pause stopped (CFTC and SEC staffs, 2010; Kirilenko et al., 2017). In 2025 and 2026 human-directed agentic systems executed 80 to 90 percent of tactical cyber-operations work with agent fleets running for hours or days at a time, reaching administrative control of victim infrastructure in about three hours (Anthropic, 2025b; Anthropic Threat Intelligence, 2026). None of these is a software swarm incident. Each supplies one or two of the ingredients that a genuine swarm-risk regime would require: software leverage, emergent interaction among coupled components, and agentic velocity under thin human oversight. This article asks what happens when those ingredients, already separately documented, converge with a fourth: a population of software agents whose collective behaviour departs from what any member individually pursues. Drawing on a corpus of 65 core sources (35 from 2025 and 2026, independently audited against primary documents) we build a five-regime taxonomy running from ordinary software to open-ended software swarm intelligence, show that the last regime remains unobserved in realised form as of September 2026, and identify the measurable conditions under which the transition into it would become visible. We propose a distortion-cascade mechanism by which locally rational perception can compound into globally unstable behaviour absent any destructive goal, and a candidate defence principle-that irreversible authority should fall as a system's measured uncertainty about its own consequences risesalongside thirty testable safety requirements. The article's stance throughout is that the strong swarm-risk thesis is a hypothesis under test, held open rather than settled in either direction. The full evidence registries travel inside the article as eleven appendices, so every claim in the body can be traced to the record that carries it.

title: The Reach of Anti-Corruption: Financial Enforcement and Corporate Asset Markets

detail.title: The Reach of Anti-Corruption: Financial Enforcement and Corporate Asset Markets

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no personal or financial relationships with other people or organizations that may have influenced, or could reasonably be perceived to have influenced, this study.
declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (Grant No. 72573006) and the Peking University School of Economics Research Seed Grant (6309900019/283).

detail.abstract: How far does anti-corruption reach beyond the officials and institutions it formally targets? We study this question using 1,411 publicly announced financial anti-corruption inspections in China and a panel of asset-sale decisions by listed firms. The financial-sector origin of the enforcement provides an institutional source for tracing its spillover effects on corporate asset markets. We find that the first inspection in a city reduces local firms' annual probability of reporting an asset sale by 5.1 percentage points, or 7.9 percent of the sample mean. Moreover, the contraction is more pronounced for sales that cross industry, provincial, or ownership boundaries, around salient or transaction-specific announcements, and in regions with weaker arm's-length market institutions. The joint pattern is hard to reconcile with a simple decline in the need for restructuring among firms, as heterogeneity by our pre-treatment operational-risk measures does not show an ordered pattern. Among observed sales, completion takes longer and buyer payments are larger, while completion rates and market valuation do not differ detectably. These findings align with a stylized model showing how review exposure and anticipated gatekeeper responses can raise market participation thresholds and induce costly documentation among surviving transactions. Our results thus highlight how anti-corruption reaches markets.

detail.abstract: Attrition in the IT and software sector is not a new problem, but the way we try to predict it has changed. A decade ago, the conversation was about exit interviews and annual engagement surveys. Today it is about feature stores, gradient boosting, and early-warning dashboards that flag who is likely to leave in the next ninety days. The models have got better; the problem has not got smaller. India's technology services industry reported attrition rates above 20 percent through much of 2022-23, cooled to the midteens in 2024-25 as hiring slowed, and is now watching those rates tick up again as demand recovers and generative AI reshapes role definitions. This paper argues that the persistent gap is not a modelling gap. It is a framing gap. Drawing on the turnover literature and on observable practice in Indian IT services, product firms, and global capability centers, the paper makes three contributions. First, it reframes attrition as five distinct phenomena that are usually pooled together-growth exits, market corrections, burnout and work-design failures, relational breakdowns, and shock-driven departures-each with different leading indicators and different managerial levers. Second, it maps the signal landscape that actually precedes departure in software delivery contexts: compensation compression and offer velocity, utilization and bench dynamics, learning stagnation, manager quality, schedule and on-call load, internal mobility friction, and commute and location policy changes. Third, it proposes a practitioner-usable prediction-to-prevention workflow that treats a model as one component in a larger system that includes explainability, intervention playbooks, fairness review, and measurement of prevention rather than just prediction accuracy. The paper is conceptual and practitioner-facing. It does not report a new proprietary model or a confidential dataset. Its aim is to help HR leaders, delivery managers, and PMO heads ask better questions of their data, avoid common ethical and legal traps, and move from scoring attrition risk to reducing it.

title: Education without Absorption: The Formalisation Trap in North

detail.title: Education without Absorption: The Formalisation Trap in North

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethical approval was not required for this study as it relies exclusively on secondary analysis of publicly available, fully anonymized unit-record microdata from the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS), conducted by the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI), Government of India. No individual primary data collection or human participant intervention was undertaken.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Education is widely assumed to be the primary pathway to formal employment, yet in India's NorthEastern Region (NER) this relationship is double-edged. Using PLFS 2024 microdata and a Firth-penalised multinomial logistic model on NEET youth aged 15-29 across all eight NER states (n=8,480), this paper tests three propositions: that education raises the relative risk of both formal employment and unemployment; that gender and Scheduled Tribe (ST) status act as independent structural barriers to formal-sector access; and that Sikkim is a policy-driven outlier in formal absorption. A postgraduate qualification raises the relative risk of formal employment roughly eight-fold, but raises unemployment risk nearly thirty-five-fold, consistent with a Harris-Todaro-style queueing mechanism. ST status carries a significant, independent penalty in formal-sector access even after controls, complicating readings of ST numerical dominance in the formal workforce as favourable treatment. Women face no formal-employment penalty relative to men once controls are applied, but face significantly higher unemployment risk, likely understating the true gender gap given sample selection on labour-force participation. Sikkim alone combines a formalisation premium with an unemployment discount, driven by public-administration and pharmaceutical employment. The region's problem is best characterised as an absorption deficit: education without demand-side job creation drives credential inflation, not mobility.

detail.abstract:
India does not lack assessment activity. It lacks assessment use. Teachers collect exit tickets, mark worksheets, maintain registers, and record observations. What they do not consistently have is a protected, routine moment in which that evidence is interpreted and converted into a decision about what to teach next. The consequence is now measurable at system level. PARAKH Rashtriya Sarvekshan 2024, the first national assessment built around the NCF-SE 2023 competency framework, tested over 21 lakh students across 781 districts. Grade 9 mathematics averaged 37% nationally. Only about 28% of students could apply percentages to real-world problems; only 29–31% demonstrated competence in fractions and integers. These figures identify where learning weakens. They cannot, by themselves, change what happens in a classroom the following week.

This policy brief proposes a one-year feasibility study of a Structured Reflective Formative Assessment Cycle (SRFAC) for Tamil Nadu under NEP 2020. SRFAC is a five-step teacher routine — Plan, Gather Evidence, Reflect, Adjust, Share — that converts ordinary classroom evidence into a concrete next instructional decision within 5–10 minutes per cycle. It operates through a one-page, non-evaluative reflection protocol embedded within existing DIET–SCERT–BRC–CRC academic-support structures rather than as a parallel programme. The proposal requests no new institution, cadre, compulsory digital platform, daily register, or high-stakes assessment. It asks SCERT Tamil Nadu for three specific authorisations: a written non-evaluative safeguard circular from the District Education Officer; permission to temporarily suspend one existing assessment-related register in pilot schools; and permission to work with one DIET (suggested: Theroor, Kanniyakumari district).

The document comprises a one-page summary for busy officers, a policy brief with thirteen sections, an assumptions-and-dependencies framework that specifies the conditions under which the study should not proceed, a pilot evaluation design, a facilitator training script, a Tamil translation of the reflection protocol, and ten supporting annexes. It includes pre-implementation evidence from a 16-week classroom trial conducted by the author in his own Class VIII Science classroom — 16 reflection cycles completed, 12 documented instructional adjustments — alongside an explicit account of the limitations of that single-classroom evidence.

The proposal is offered as a testable and reversible feasibility study. Its central claim is not that SRFAC improves learning outcomes in Tamil Nadu, for which no Indian evidence exists, but that it is plausible, policy-aligned, and worth testing under controlled conditions. If the feasibility evidence is weak, the model should be revised or discontinued rather than scaled. The international evidence on which the proposal draws, its limits, and the assumptions on which the study depends are stated without overclaim.

title: A pre-planning difficulty assessment framework based on target spatial characteristic value and spatial organ-at-risk conflict scores for volumetric modulated arc therapy
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Central South University - Hunan Cancer Hospital, Capital Medical University, Harbin Medical University, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Harbin Medical University

detail.title: A pre-planning difficulty assessment framework based on target spatial characteristic value and spatial organ-at-risk conflict scores for volumetric modulated arc therapy
detail.abstract: Purpose: An objective and quantitative method for assessing plan achievability and treatment planning difficulty remains lacking in volumetric modulated arc therapy (VMAT). This study aimed to establish an interpretable pre-planning framework that separately quantifies target spatial characteristics and organ-at-risk (OAR)-planning target volume (PTV) conflict, and evaluated its clinical relevance and feasibility.Materials and methods: We retrospectively analyzed 1642 VMAT plans from six homogeneous brain, breast, and cervical cancer cohorts. To quantify potential difficulty from anatomical factors before plan designing, we proposed the target spatial characteristic value (TSCV) and spatial OAR-PTV conflict scores (SOCS). A target visual hull volume (VTVH) was generated from beam’s-eye-view projections of PTV at several gantry angles. TSCV was calculated from the volumetric relationship between the PTV and VTVH to characterize PTV spatial features. SOCS described OAR-PTV conflict through multiscale proximity (Sprox), near-target incursion (Smargin), and OAR exposure within the VTVH-related space (STVH). Validation used associations with the plan quality metric (PQM), eight RT Plan-derived complexity metrics, and OAR-specific dose-volume histogram endpoints.Results: TSCV differed across cohorts and was significantly associated with PQM in all six cohorts. Mean MLC gap was associated with TSCV in all cohorts, whereas edge metric, mean aperture area, and mean leaf travel were associated in five cohorts. Among 289 evaluable SOCS-DVH comparisons, 254 (87.9%) were significant, including 101/104 for Sprox, 84/98 for Smargin, and 69/87 for STVH. Representative cases showed that lower TSCV and higher SOCS corresponded to less favorable pre-planning anatomical profiles.Conclusion: TSCV and SOCS provide complementary, interpretable pre-planning descriptors of anatomical factors potentially contributing to VMAT planning difficulty. This framework may support case stratification, early identification of critical OARs, allocation of planning attention, and individualized planning decisions.

title: Misguided Paternalism in Commercial Law and Litigation Finance

detail.title: Misguided Paternalism in Commercial Law and Litigation Finance

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is a consultant to Burford Capital and Justice Catalyst Access Fund (commercial and nonprofit third-party litigation funds, respectively), neither of which had any role in the creation of this article.
declarations.funderStatement: This article was made possible with the support of a Summer Research Stipend from Cardozo Law School.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Cardozo Legal Studies Research Paper No. 2026-24
publicationDetails.journalName: Cardozo Law School Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Third-Party Litigation Finance (TPLF) occurs when a third party funds a stranger’s attorney’s costs and/or other legal expenses.  It serves a variety of markets, the two main ones being the consumer market, involving individuals with personal injury claims, and the commercial market, (mostly) involving commercial entities suing commercial defendants in business disputes such contract breach and antitrust.  Like any novel business activity, TPLF has generated a variety of responses from private and public sector entities.  There have been efforts to reform TPLF and one state, North Carolina, prohibited it in 2026.

In this Article I examine a leading argument against commercial TPLF, which is that it permits commercial plaintiffs to give away control over the conduct of the funded litigation, including control over settlement.   Because this argument is made in the absence of any plausible account that commercial TPLF causes significant third-party harms or imposes unfair burdens on commercial defendants, I refer to this argument as one of contract paternalism, where, for their own good, plaintiffs are prevented from freely contracting with funders.

I argue that in the context of commercial TPLF is governed by the law of secured transactions in U.C.C. Article 9 and that from this perspective, the paternalism urged by commercial TPLF's critics makes no sense.  Further, I argue from the perspective of modern contract theory, the default provisions in Article 9 that would allow plaintiffs to contract away control to funders are efficient and would be preferred by rational commercial actors.

The Article concludes cautions that its argument cannot be transferred automatically to consumer TPLF.  The Article's larger point is the failure to take seriously the different types of law that have evolved over the past century to help different types of parties manage their business relations can lead to the production of confusing and potentially harmful academic and policy arguments about TPLF.

title: STEP-Net: Probabilistic static–temporal fusion for pre-operation-start surgical-duration estimation
affiliations: Henan Normal University, Henan Normal University, Wuhan University, Wuhan University, affiliation not provided to SSRN, The First People’s Hospital of Yunnan Province and Yunnan University

detail.title: STEP-Net: Probabilistic static–temporal fusion for pre-operation-start surgical-duration estimation
detail.abstract: Background and Objectives: Surgical-duration estimates for advance planning are typically based on historical procedure durations and static perioperative information. Additional physiological and anesthesia-monitoring observations become available as the start of surgery approaches, but whether these newly available observations provide incremental predictive information beyond an existing estimate remains unclear. We therefore investigated pre-operation-start surgical-duration estimation as a short-horizon updating problem.Methods: The study included 70,186 surgical cases from INSPIRE, 3,817 from VitalDB, and 20,966 from KSDC. Structured perioperative information and physiological and anesthesia-monitoring observations preceding the recorded operation start were extracted using 30-, 20-, and 10-min windows for INSPIRE, VitalDB, and KSDC, respectively. Based on these inputs, we developed STEP-Net, a probabilistic static--temporal framework comprising separate Gaussian experts for static and temporal information, mask-aware hypernetwork-driven adaptive temporal filtering, and gated Gaussian Product-of-Experts (PoE) fusion to update surgical-duration estimates.Results: STEP-Net achieved MAEs of 48.01, 49.67, and 35.82 min on INSPIRE, VitalDB, and KSDC, respectively. Relative to the otherwise identical static-only model, MAE decreased by 4.04 min (95% CI, 3.64--4.43), 1.52 min (95% CI, 1.16--1.88), and 1.41 min (95% CI, 0.95--1.87), respectively. Temporal information consistently reduced MAE across all duration strata in each of the three datasets.Conclusions: Pre-operation-start temporal observations provided incremental predictive information beyond procedure history and static perioperative records in this retrospective evaluation. STEP-Net is intended as a short-horizon update to an existing surgical-duration estimate rather than a replacement for advance planning. Prospective studies are needed to determine whether these improvements translate into operational benefits.

title: Bottlenecks of Mission LiFE and Fusion of Traditional Indian Wisdom: A Cross-Cultural Governance Framework for Forbes Global Top 100 Enterprises

detail.title: Bottlenecks of Mission LiFE and Fusion of Traditional Indian Wisdom: A Cross-Cultural Governance Framework for Forbes Global Top 100 Enterprises

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This is to declare that there is no personal or financial relationship with other people, who influenced this study
declarations.funderStatement: There is no direct funding for this study

detail.abstract:
Modern corporate governance faces structural inefficiencies, regulatory fragmentation, and internal resistance to sustainable transitions. As global requirements evolve from voluntary disclosures to rigid Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) mandates and initiatives such as Mission LiFE (Lifestyle for Environment), organisations frequently encounter severe operational friction. Traditional models often treat sustainability as a reactive compliance burden rather than an intrinsic imperative, leading to institutional inertia and strategic drift. This paper proposes an integrated theoretical and empirical framework designed to address these challenges by drawing upon timeless ethical principles from seven foundational wisdom traditions: Vedic philosophy, the Ramayan, the Mahabharat, Chanakya Neeti, Buddhist philosophy, Christian theology, and Islamic jurisprudence.

The study establishes an interdisciplinary cross-cultural governance architecture anchored in concepts such as cosmic balance (Rta and Mizan), principled boundaries (Maryada), non-wastefulness (Israf), and servant stewardship (Khalifa). Using a structural equation model (SEM), the research evaluates four primary hypotheses concerning the interactions between regulatory bottlenecks (B1), cultural inertia (B2), global wisdom fusion (M1), and C-suite leadership commitment (Mod1) on Mission LiFE adoption (DV1). The empirical analysis is supported by the mapping of 100 classical scriptural statements to contemporary governance parameters.

The empirical analysis confirms that regulatory bottlenecks and organisational cultural inertia exert a strong negative impact on enterprise pro-environmental behaviour (B1: beta = -0.34, p < 0.01; B2: beta = -0.41, p < 0.01). However, the study validates that Global Wisdom Fusion (M1) serves as a critical mediator, providing a positive offset to these challenges (beta = +0.28, p < 0.05). Furthermore, C-Suite Ethical Leadership Commitment (Mod1) acts as a significant moderator, amplifying the positive relationship between wisdom fusion and environmental adoption (beta = +0.22, p < 0.01). The interaction effect (M1 multiplied by Mod1) demonstrates that leadership commitment functions as a force multiplier for ethical governance (beta = +0.18, p < 0.01).

This paper offers a novel governance architecture that bridges the gap between ancient ethical wisdom and modern ESG imperatives. It provides global leaders with an actionable roadmap to eliminate institutional bottlenecks, reduce greenwashing, and embed long-term environmental stewardship into the core operational strategy of Forbes Global Top 100 enterprises.

affiliations: Independent, Nasarawa State University, Keffi Nasarawa State  Nigeria and University of Nigeria, Nsukka

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Nil
