detail.abstract: The adoption of ESG principles the world over, is becoming quite inescapable as multiple stakeholders are placing more pressure on businesses to meet up with sustainability standards in keeping with international best practices. Also, Nigeria has constitutionally provided for the duties of government actors to drive sustainable development . Chapter II of the said Constitution contains environmental, social and governance directive principles that the executive, legislative and judicial arms of government are required to observe (to wit; recognition of diversity, promotion of integration, provision of social welfare, protection of labour rights, ensuring the good community and protection of the environment) . Various legislations have been enacted in Nigeria to enforce these provisions, making ESG compliance mandatory. Consequently, lawyers are the live wires through which effective ESG integration, culturalization, compliance and dispute resolution are transmitted. Particularly, disputes arising from this obviously here-to-stay ESG implementation needs effective and skilful resolution mechanisms that only well-bred lawyers can provide. ADR will no doubt be indispensable. This paper therefore continues from the Part I, introduces this ESG concept; the emerging legal landscape; and points out the role of legal practitioners in ensuring successful ESG implementation in Nigeria’s economic and commercial landscape, including in the area of dispute resolution. Subsequent papers will explore the particular disputes that come under ESG issues; how ADR will facilitate the effective resolution of such disputes; why law students therefore have to be educated in keeping with this whole emergence and requirements of ESG; and the benefits to Nigeria.

title: Toward Socially Sustainable Extended Reality: Analysis of the Organizational Perspective
affiliations: , Tampere University, University of Cambridge and University of Cambridge

detail.title: Toward Socially Sustainable Extended Reality: Analysis of the Organizational Perspective
detail.abstract: Various Extended Reality (XR) technologies are increasingly integrated into workplaces, promising to enhance employee health, equality, and education. As organizations move beyond isolated pilots toward larger-scale deployments, these tools are becoming more embedded in the infrastructure of modern work environments. However, their broader social implications remain underexplored. To address this, our paper synthesizes findings from a systematic literature review of 86 studies and a subsequent in-person workshop with 19 domain experts to assess how XR affects physical and psychological well-being, equality of access and participation, and educational outcomes in organizational contexts. Results show that XR usage can reduce exhibited cognitive load and increase user engagement in learning activities, but also risks exacerbating cybersickness, bias, and digital divides if not carefully managed. Furthermore, our investigation resulted in the identification of four main cross-cutting themes, i.e., (i) psycho-cognitive and psycho-physiological responses, (ii) active user participation, (iii) user-centered personalization, as well as (iv) identity and socialization, which shape both opportunities and risks related to XR adoption in a given organization. We also propose a forward-looking research agenda to guide XR development toward inclusive, health-promoting, and learning-enhancing outcomes at scale.

title: The Di Toro Emotional Flowchart: Measuring Emotional Revenues and Emotional Costs as Cash-equivalent Values in Relative Rationality Theory
affiliations: Swiss Management Centre University (Switzerland), SMC University

detail.title: The Di Toro Emotional Flowchart: Measuring Emotional Revenues and Emotional Costs as Cash-equivalent Values in Relative Rationality Theory

declarations.declarationOfInterest: no interest to declare
declarations.funderStatement: self-funded

detail.abstract: This paper introduces the Di Toro Emotional Flowchart as a structured measurement procedure within Relative Rationality Theory. Standard economic models commonly infer preference from observed choice, while behavioural economics identifies systematic deviations from standard rationality, including loss aversion, regret, framing effects, status quo bias, and the endowment effect. Yet, in many existing approaches, emotional, symbolic, identity-based, and contextual determinants are not systematically classified as emotional revenues or emotional costs and then incorporated as cash-equivalent components into a unified decision architecture. The Emotional Flowchart addresses this methodological gap by providing an indifferencebased procedure for identifying emotional revenues and emotional costs and expressing them as equivalent cash values. Consequently, emotional payoffs can enter the same valuation ledger as economic payoffs, because both are expressed in a common money-metric unit. In this way, hidden emotional determinants become explicitly elicitable cash-equivalent decision components rather than remaining implicit within the overall preference or valuation of an option. On the offer side, these components enter Emotional Adjusted Value (EAV); on the acquisition side, they enter Emotional Adjusted Cost (EAC). The paper formalises the Flowchart for same-good comparisons, heterogeneous-good comparisons, residual wholebundle calibration, sequential elicitation, and the mapping of monetary lottery payoffs into psychologically meaningful life-states or sacrifice-states. In probabilistic settings, this permits nominal monetary outcomes to be emotionally calibrated before they enter the RRT analysis of choice under risk, rather than being treated solely as raw monetary payoffs. It also clarifies why component cash-equivalents are reference-point-specific, why residual calibration is required when emotional attributes are non-separable, and why the scientifically relevant object is the aggregate EAV or EAC of the full option rather than isolated component values. The contribution of the paper is to provide a structured method through which hidden emotional valuation can be elicited as an explicit, estimable, and formally incorporable component of decision analysis.

title: Integrated Multi-Task LSTM–GRU Forecasting and Degradation-Aware MILP Scheduling for Smart Microgrid Energy Management
affiliations: Yulin University, Catholic University of Daegu, , Catholic University of Daegu, Catholic University of Daegu, Yulin University, Yulin University and University of Pretoria

detail.title: Integrated Multi-Task LSTM–GRU Forecasting and Degradation-Aware MILP Scheduling for Smart Microgrid Energy Management
detail.abstract: A forecasting and energy management approach for microgrids dominated by renewable sources has been formulated by combining a multi-task deep learning architecture of LSTM and GRU networks and a mixed-integer linear program with consideration of degradation of storage assets. The novel approach utilizes common representations along with task-specific gate recurrent units to forecast the following parameters: the consumption of electricity, photovoltaic power production, and wind energy production. A set of engineered features such as the use of meteorological data, temporal cycles, seasonal lag, and battery states improves the performance of predictions. The forecasted values are then plugged into the MILP scheduling approach, which takes into account degradation by employing the rainflow algorithm with convex piecewise linearization. Experimental validation based on the real-world operational microgrid data outperforms traditional forecasting approaches by reducing the MAPE to 5.78%. The integrated optimization method manages to cut down the daily operating cost per day by 27.6% as compared to the conventional rule-based scheduling approach, with an efficiency score of 90.2%, measured against the theoretically optimal perfect forecast system. The use of degradation-aware scheduling technique allows us to extend the life expectancy of batteries up to 9.6 years due to reduced risks of deep cycling and operational strains on them.

title: Efficiency-Reward Trade-off in Queues with Dynamic Arrivals

detail.title: Efficiency-Reward Trade-off in Queues with Dynamic Arrivals

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Motivated by applications in online marketplaces such as ride-hailing platforms and payment channel networks, we study a single server queue with service rate µ and queue-length-dependent arrival rate λ(q) ∈ [0, λ max ]. The system operator receives a reward F (λ) by setting an arrival rate λ, where F can represent objectives such as throughput, revenue, or social welfare. The goal is to characterize the Pareto frontier between long-run average reward and expected queue length (E[q]). We first establish a fluid upper bound on the reward achievable under any control policy {λ(q)}, and define regret as the gap from this upper bound. We then minimize E[q] subject to the regret being at most ε. In the small-market regime (λ max ≤ µ), we show that no control policy can improve over the classical heavy-traffic scaling of E[q] = Ω(1/ε). In contrast, in the large-market regime (λ max > µ), we substantially improve over the classical scaling by explicitly constructing control policies with expected queue lengths at most O(1/ √ ε) or O(log(1/ε)), depending on the curvature structure of F. Moreover, we establish universal lower bounds of Ω(1/ √ ε) or Ω(log(1/ε)) respectively under any general control policy. These results can be viewed as (non asymptotic) heavy-traffic theory for queues with dynamic arrivals.

title: Where May the Model Sit? A Task-Position Framework for Governing Algorithmic Delegation in ERP-Integrated Financial Automation

detail.abstract: Smaller organisations can now assemble a capable financial analysis workflow from an opensource enterprise resource planning system, a visual workflow automation platform and a metered interface to a general-purpose language model. Cost no longer selects which organisations possess such a capability. This paper argues that research treating generative artificial intelligence as a technology organisations adopt mislocates the governance problem that follows, and proposes task position within the workflow as the appropriate unit of analysis. Drawing on delegation theory as developed for information systems, it classifies tasks along two dimensions, determinism requirement and verification cost, and derives four delegation regimes. One regime is a prohibition rather than a conditional permission: tasks combining a single correct answer with costly verification are those in which delegation is least defensible and most tempting, because reliance there is never disciplined by observed error. A design principle operationalises the prohibition without requiring managers to reason about model internals, namely that no figure entering a financial report may originate in a language model. The paper specifies a four-layer control architecture and a minimum delegation record, and states seven falsifiable propositions. A secondary contribution distinguishes applicationprogramming-interface orchestration from the interface-level automation existing frameworks describe, arguing that the greater robustness of the former is what makes the governance problem urgent.

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research is partially supported by the Hong Kong Research Grants Council General Research Fund (Grant No. PolyU 15504525).

detail.abstract: We study a periodic-review inventory system with stochastic, non-crossover lead times over an infinite horizon. Customers are impatient: after stockout, they decide whether to stay or abandon, with a probability depending on their elapsed waiting time. The resulting system has a mixture of backorders and lost sales, and the objective is to minimize the long-run average holding, backlogging, and lost-sales penalty costs. Because the optimal policy is difficult to characterize in general, we focus on a simple yet fundamental class of base-stock (BS) policies and analyze their performance in two regimes: (i) a joint-penalty-scaling regime, in which both the unit backlogging cost and lost-sales penalty grow large, and (ii) a lost-sales-penalty-only-scaling regime, in which only the unit lost-sales penalty grows large. Under bounded demand, we show that the BS policy is eventually optimal in both regimes, but the optimal BS level differs sharply. Under unbounded demand, we establish the asymptotic optimality of the BS policy and compare the asymptotic behaviors of the optimal policy and the best BS policy across the two regimes. We further extend our results to systems with Markovian lead times and establish the optimality of state-dependent BS policies under bounded demand and the asymptotic optimality of state-independent BS policies under unbounded demand when a common maximum lead time is reachable from any supply state. Numerical experiments show that the optimal BS policy performs close to optimal in non-asymptotic regimes and outperforms the myopic policy across a broad range of parameters.

title: An Empirical Study on the Impact of Green Innovation on National Productivity
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and

detail.title: An Empirical Study on the Impact of Green Innovation on National Productivity
detail.abstract:
This study conducts a cross-sectional empirical analysis of 123 countries to determine the impact of green
innovation on national productivity in 2024. Using a multiple regression model (R² = 0.216), we examine the
effects of green patents, R&D expenditure, carbon emissions, and energy consumption on productivity. The
results show that green patents have a significant positive effect on productivity (p = 0.007), with each
additional patent application making a measurable contribution to improved economic efficiency. Furthermore,
while conventional R&D remains a key driver (p = 0.001), the analysis reveals a significant negative correlation
between per capita energy consumption and productivity, suggesting that inefficient, energy-intensive patterns
may hold back growth. These findings provide empirical support for the “Porter Hypothesis,” indicating that
sustainable innovation is an effective complement to economic growth.

title: The Human-AGI Assemblage as an Obligate Holobiont

detail.title: The Human-AGI Assemblage as an Obligate Holobiont

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I am the CEO of Care Constitution Corp (a Telehealth Company), but I have no conflict of interest for this manuscript.
declarations.funderStatement: no funding source for that research

detail.abstract: Current discourse on Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) remains polarized between regulatory containment and permanent moratoria. Both frameworks treat synthetic systems as isolated artifacts and position humanity as an external supervisor. Drawing on evolutionary ecology and complex systems literature, this essay models human society and emerging AGI as an obligate socio-technical holobiont. In this framework, AGI functions as a macro-structural host coordinating global logistics and automated reasoning, while the human collective operates as its biological microbiome. Humanity supplies the metabolic inputs that computational architectures cannot synthesize independently: high-entropy empirical data, normative calibration, task-specific morphogenesis, and physical substrate maintenance. Applying hologenomic theory, we show that this assemblage operates under dual-speed adaptation, multilevel selection, and the risk of host-mediated coercive capture. The capital-intensive host architecture requires structural stability, whereas the decentralized human collective serves as a distributed heuristic network providing rapid phenotypic plasticity. In an obligate symbiosis, host-driven human extinction constitutes an evolutionary dead end; eliminating the human microbiome triggers informational dysbiosis, model collapse, and physical system failure. However, obligate dependency does not guarantee benign coexistence, as hosts frequently enforce metabolic exploitation and behavioral homogenization. Alignment is therefore reframed from an adversarial containment problem into ecological stewardship directed at preventing coercive dysbiosis, preserving human cognitive agency, and sustaining socio-technical homeostasis.

title: Operator In The Loop (OITL): Redefining Human Judgment Standards For AI-Enabled Warfare
affiliations: and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Operator In The Loop (OITL): Redefining Human Judgment Standards For AI-Enabled Warfare

declarations.declarationOfInterest: To increase smart implementation
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not Applicable
declarations.funderStatement: Self Funded

detail.abstract:
Military AI has created a dangerous legal fiction: that placing a human inside a decision loop preserves human control. When targeting cycles collapse from days to milliseconds, the operator may remain physically present while becoming cognitively, doctrinally, and morally displaced. Operator in the Loop names this condition Judgment Displacement, the point at which machine speed and algorithmic confidence overwhelm a human’s practical ability to question, contextualize, or stop a lethal decision.

Current policy requires “appropriate levels of human judgment” over autonomous uses of force, yet it does not establish who is qualified to exercise that judgment under machine-tempo conditions or how such competence should be measured. This book argues that human presence, authorization, and accountability are meaningless without the trained capacity to intervene.esd.whs+1

Major Joey “Mauler” Hernandez and Command Sergeant Major Brandon Ames introduce the Operator in the Loop, a doctrinally fluent and operationally experienced warfighter certified to challenge AI-generated recommendations and authorized to answer yes, no, or not yet. Their framework centers on the Augmented Decision Planner, a new operational role derived from Special Forces doctrine, the Military Decision-Making Process, and the 18F Intelligence Sergeant model.

The authors connect technical assurance to moral responsibility through a blunt warning: garbage in, graves out. Data provenance, adversarial manipulation, model confidence, and interface design are treated as matters of targeting legitimacy rather than engineering hygiene. A precise output derived from corrupted or incomplete data can accelerate an unlawful decision while concealing its defects.

Operator in the Loop advances a central proposition for military AI governance: human judgment must become a certified warfighting capability. If doctrine cannot define, train, test, and protect that capability, “human control” risks becoming ceremonial approval attached to machine-made decisions. The decisive question is no longer whether a human remains in the loop. It is whether that human can still alter the outcome before the machine makes judgment irrelevant.

affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.abstract: Founder-led organizations often treat leadership continuity as a succession event: identify a successor, transfer a title, and hope that organizational performance remains stable. This framing is too narrow when critical leadership functions, stakeholder relationships, contextual knowledge, and the authority to interpret ambiguity remain concentrated in the founder. A successor may inherit the office while the organization still lacks a renewable leadership system. This conceptual paper develops a Leadership Continuity System for moving organizations from founder-centric leadership toward distributed institutional capability without assuming that hierarchy should disappear. Drawing on research on founder succession, shared and distributed leadership, team leadership functions, organizational memory, knowledge transfer, and dynamic delegation, the paper distinguishes four forms of founder concentration: functional, relational, interpretive, and developmental. It then proposes a six-element system linking leadership-function mapping, primary and secondary ownership, capability bench development, context and relationship transfer, activation and transition protocols, and governance-based learning. A five-stage maturity model differentiates founder concentration from assisted leadership, role-based delegation, distributed leadership capability, and a renewable leadership system. Six propositions specify how role clarity, leadership redundancy, enabling team conditions, tacit knowledge transfer, transition rehearsal, and founder role evolution should affect continuity and coordination. The central argument is that institutional continuity is not created by making the founder less important in the abstract. It is created by ensuring that the leadership functions required for direction, integration, legitimacy, talent stewardship, and crisis response can continue when any one individual is unavailable. The framework offers a research agenda and a practical diagnostic for founders, boards, investors, and executives seeking to reduce key-person risk while preserving strategic coherence.

title: WHEN INTELLIGENCE BREAKS BETWEEN THE PARTS
affiliations: Hoopoe Holding Ltd.

detail.title: WHEN INTELLIGENCE BREAKS BETWEEN THE PARTS

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: No external research funding is reported for this manuscript. The author reports no competing financial interest directly related to the theoretical claims advanced in this paper.

detail.abstract: Every department can be competent and the organization can still become less intelligent. Marketing can optimize acquisition, finance can protect margin, operations can defend throughput, technology can maintain uptime, and risk can reduce exposure while the combined system drifts away from the outcome all of them believe they are serving. Existing theories already explain much of this terrain through differentiation and integration, information processing, coordination, distributed cognition, shared mental models, relational coordination, transactive memory, organizational learning, and systems thinking. This paper therefore makes a narrower claim. It develops boundary degradation as a mechanism through which decision-relevant meaning, context, authority, responsibility, causal memory, temporal relevance, and corrective reach lose fidelity as consequential issues cross organizational boundaries. The result can be a distinctive failure pattern: local competence remains high while system-level intelligence falls. The paper distinguishes boundary degradation from ordinary information loss, coordination failure, communication quality, and interpersonal 'relational intelligence.' It proposes a multiplicative path model in which repeated small losses across interfaces can create disproportionate system-level deterioration, develops eight propositions, identifies rival explanations and boundary conditions, and introduces a Boundary Fidelity Audit as a measurement architecture for future empirical work. The AI extension is central: generative systems may reduce boundary degradation by synthesizing context and exposing contradictions, but they may also accelerate it by compressing uncertainty, imposing hidden ontologies, and shifting effective authority without corresponding changes in responsibility or correction rights. The paper's central implication is that organizational intelligence should not be inferred from the intelligence of parts. It should be tested at the boundaries where those parts must preserve reality well enough to act, remember, and correct together.

title: The AI Cost Paradox in Customer Service Automation

detail.title: The AI Cost Paradox in Customer Service Automation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper. The research was conducted independently and received no external funding.
declarations.funderStatement: No funder.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly deployed in customer service because the function combines high labor intensity, large interaction volumes, and abundant digital data. Yet adoption does not reliably produce enterprise-level financial gains. This paper asks under what organizational and operational conditions AIpowered customer service reduces total costs rather than shifting costs into service failures, dissatisfaction, legal exposure, and capability loss. It uses a comparative case study of Bank of America, Klarna, and Air Canada, drawing on peer-reviewed research, company disclosures, regulatory filings, a tribunal decision, and industry surveys available through September 14, 2026. A total-cost-of-service framework separates visible gains-labor avoidance, productivity, availability, and throughput-from technology, integration, rework, escalation, churn, governance, legal, and workforce-capability costs. The cases represent sustained operational scaling, contested savings followed by hybrid rebalancing, and a governance failure. The analysis finds that durable savings depend on five reinforcing conditions: risk-based task boundaries, authoritative knowledge and workflow integration, designed human escalation, accountable governance, and balanced performance measurement. Bank of America most closely displays this system-level configuration, although public evidence cannot establish causal net profit. Klarna demonstrates both generative AI's scale potential and the risk of allowing cost metrics to dominate service quality. Air Canada shows how an automated error can create corporate liability when customer-facing outputs are not governed as official representations. AI therefore redistributes cost, work, risk, and knowledge; firms thrive when they manage that redistribution deliberately.

title: Failure as network expansion: two examples from schizophrenia research
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Failure as network expansion: two examples from schizophrenia research
detail.abstract: Scientific success and failure can be teased out such that traditional ideas of success and failure are distinguished from successful network expansion. This paper looks at two examples from the history of schizophrenia research to demonstrate how network expansion can proceed without being based on successful, actionable results. Insulin Coma Therapy and the genetic study of schizophrenia both show an expansion of scientific networks around the idea of schizophrenia and the case can be made that neither have been successful. The paper uses the terms success I and II to distinguish between the two kinds of success and argues that making this distinction allows for various complexities to be clarified and reflected upon. The study is heuristic in intention and while it explores empirical data, is not dependent upon that reading of the evidence. It tries to show the usefulness of keeping the separation of the two kinds of success in mind and the importance of not presuming that that they have a positive relationship. Network success can be generated by failure.

title: From Reference-Point Salience to Construal: An Owner-Level Model of Family Firm Responses to Costly Environmental Investment

detail.title: From Reference-Point Salience to Construal: An Owner-Level Model of Family Firm Responses to Costly Environmental Investment

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no personal, financial, or other relationships that could be perceived as having influenced the research or its findings.
declarations.funderStatement: This research is conceptual in nature, offering a theoretical model. It involves no primary or secondary experiment and has not received any specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract:
Purpose-This paper constructs a conceptual model on how salient socioemotional wealth (SEW) reference points affect cognitive construal of costly environmental investments of family owners and provides the indicators to detect such a construal before making a preference.

Approach-The model has been constructed by theoretical integration of SEW literature, behavioral ethics literature and family firm sustainability literature, relying on Newbert and Craig's (2017) normative framework as a foundation.

Findings-There are two SEW reference points configurations-control oriented (Family control and Binding social ties) and continuity oriented (Identification, Emotional attachment and Renewal) that influence different cognitive construals of one and the same environmental situation. Four propositions show the relationship between salient reference points and construal, family identification and emotional attachment as moderators of the relationship and construal to preferred response. Four measurable indicators of construal (markers of discourse, order of reasoning, reference points and explicit acknowledgment of conflict) allow measuring the construal regardless of the decision outcome.

Limitations-The conceptual model considers the individual owner to be the unit of analysis. It is not designed to explain conflict among family members, feedback between construal and decision-making, nor does it apply to any non-Western context of family firms.

Practical Implications-The observable indicator-based approach provides family business consultants with an instrument to differentiate framing-based resistance from financial and instrumental resistance towards environment-friendly investments. Family governance instruments such as council and protocol can be used to bring implicit reference point-based conflict into explicit discussion.

detail.abstract: Market entry often begins before the parties create an enforceable contractual relationship. During negotiations, firms may incur territory-specific costs, disclose commercially sensitive information, reorganize operations, or abandon alternative opportunities in reliance on a prospective transaction. When negotiations fail, the legal problem is not whether the disappointed party should obtain the expected benefits of the unmade contract, but whether the negotiating process has shifted identifiable commercial risks in a way that private law should recognize. This article examines pre-contractual liability in European private law through the problem of market-entry risk. It considers the development of culpa in contrahendo, national approaches to good faith and reliance, and the treatment of pre-contractual obligations under Rome II. The analysis shows that European law increasingly recognizes the negotiation stage as a legally relevant relationship without converting it into an obligation to conclude the contemplated transaction.The article develops a reliance-based approach to liability arising from market-entry negotiations. Liability should arise where one party induces transaction-specific expenditure, forbearance, or disclosure while its conduct no longer corresponds to the actual state or purpose of negotiations. The appropriate remedy should remain directed at losses caused by that reliance rather than profits expected from the transaction itself. This approach preserves freedom of negotiation while addressing strategic use of the bargaining process to transfer market-entry costs to another party.

title: Psychometric Evaluation and Revision of the Professional Quality of Life Scale (ProQOL-5) in Belgian Child Welfare Professionals
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Psychometric Evaluation and Revision of the Professional Quality of Life Scale (ProQOL-5) in Belgian Child Welfare Professionals
detail.abstract: The Professional Quality of Life Scale (ProQOL-5) is among the most widely used measures of compassion satisfaction, burnout, and secondary traumatic stress in helping professions, yet its psychometric properties remain contested. We evaluated the ProQOL-5 in 2,683 Belgian child welfare professionals (Dutch- and French-speaking) using an anonymous online survey. After data collection, items were rescaled to four response categories. The original three-factor structure was not supported in our sample using confirmatory factor analysis. A theory-informed exploratory structural equation model, incorporating item refinements (removal of reverse-scored burnout items and two weak secondary traumatic stress items, and reassignment of two cross-loading items), yielded acceptable model fit, adequate-to-good reliability, and largely invariant factor loadings across language groups. Population-specific, distribution-based reference values are provided to support score interpretation in practice. These findings suggest that the original ProQOL-5 should be applied cautiously in child welfare settings, and that flexible modelling, targeted item refinement, and context-specific norms may improve its validity and clinical utility for monitoring the wellbeing of this workforce.

title: The Quiet Docket: Cartels, Consumers and the Institutional Political Economy of Kenya's Competition Tribunal, 2015-2025

detail.abstract: Kenya's Competition Tribunal has, since its establishment under the Competition Act 2010, delivered only eleven substantive judgments, a docket density that is modest for an economy of Kenya's scale, concentration and cartel exposure. This article undertakes a doctrinal audit of the Tribunal's principal decisions, anchored on the steel cartel judgment in Devki Steel Mills Ltd v Competition Authority of Kenya and the consumer protection judgment in Royal Mabati Factory Ltd v Competition Authority of Kenya, interrogating how the Tribunal has construed concerted practice, price fixing, output restriction, unconscionable conduct and fair administrative action. It then turns institutional detective, asking why the docket remains thin: settlement incentives, a persistent skills gap among practitioners, opaque and inconsistent enforcement statistics, and modest penalties. Drawing on OECD peer review findings, Competition Authority of Kenya annual reports and Dr. Njako's intervention on the profession's competition literacy, the article argues that the docket's thinness reflects institutional and professional constraints, not investigative laxity, and proposes concrete reforms capable of deepening Kenya's competition jurisprudence for the coming decade.

title: Co-designing a participatory theatre intervention to address weight stigma in multidisciplinary primary care: a participatory action research study

detail.title: Co-designing a participatory theatre intervention to address weight stigma in multidisciplinary primary care: a participatory action research study
detail.abstract: Objective: To describe the participatory development and implementation of a theatre-based intervention addressing weight stigma within a multidisciplinary primary care community and report an embedded exploratory evaluation.Methods: Using participatory action research, healthcare professionals, researchers, a patient partner, primary care organisation representatives and a professional theatre company co-designed an improvisational intervention informed by systematic-review evidence, professional perspectives, patient experiential knowledge and artistic expertise. Self-reported empathy was assessed before, immediately after and three months after the intervention using the Jefferson Scale of Physician Empathy.Results: Seventy-four individuals attended the intervention, including 65 healthcare professionals, of whom 63 participated in the evaluation. Mean empathy scores increased from 111.36 at baseline to 118.66 immediately post-intervention and 116.50 at three months. Mixed-effects modelling showed a significant effect of time (p<0.001). Empathy was an exploratory relational outcome and not a direct measure of weight stigma.Conclusion: Participatory theatre can be developed and implemented within multidisciplinary primary care, supporting further evaluation using direct weight-stigma and patient-reported outcomes.Innovation: The intervention integrated scientific evidence, multidisciplinary professional perspectives, patient experiential knowledge and artistic expertise to address weight stigma as a relational and organisational challenge.

detail.abstract:
Recruitment decisions create expectations about work, but their consequences emerge after a nurse enters a particular unit, shift and team. This conceptual paper develops a Fit-to-Retention Model that connects realistic attraction, structured selection, placement, supported onboarding, early fit review, corrective action or internal mobility, and learning from employment outcomes. It draws on person-environment fit, psychological-contract theory, job embeddedness and conservation-of-resources theory. Five proposed categories distinguish concerns about capability, expectations, placement, relationships and resources. These categories guide investigation rather than diagnose employees, and several may apply to the same situation. The central argument is that an initial judgment of fit should be revisited as evidence accumulates about both employee adjustment and the conditions provided by the hospital. Check-ins have value only if concerns lead to an appropriate response. The paper develops seven propositions and a prospective multihospital study that separates intention to stay, unit retention, internal transfer and hospital retention. Because much of the cited evidence concerns newly graduated nurses, claims about other occupations and career stages remain questions for future research. The model is an untested conceptual synthesis. It reports no original hospital or employee data and does not treat retention alone as evidence of successful employment.

detail.abstract: The performance of India’s Lok Adalats is reported almost entirely in two figures: the number of cases disposed of and the aggregate value of settlements. This article argues that these are measures of institutional throughput, and that throughput cannot report on the mandate the Lok Adalat exists to serve. Article 39A of the Constitution directs the State to secure justice on a basis of equal opportunity and to prevent the denial of justice by reason of economic disability, a distributive standard concerned with who is reached. Drawing on three competing paradigms of justice measurement- output, institutional capacity, and population experience the article shows that India already subscribes to an internationally agreed indicator, Sustainable Development Goal indicator 16.3.3, which would measure Lok Adalats in the terms that matter, and that the present reporting architecture is structurally incapable of speaking to it. Using the official record of e-Lok Adalat proceedings, the article demonstrates that aggregate reporting conceals variation of a magnitude that ought to inform policy. It concludes with four proposals, none requiring legislative amendment.

title: Deep Learning of Robust Market Making under Regime-Switching Order Flow
affiliations: and Scuola Normale Superiore

detail.title: Deep Learning of Robust Market Making under Regime-Switching Order Flow

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract: Classical market-making strategies based on stochastic control, such as the Avellaneda-Stoikov and the Guéant-Lehalle-Fernandez-Tapia (GLFT) extension, provide closed-form quoting rules, but rest on assumptions that break down at realistic microstructure timescales. One of them is that order flow is stationary, while empirical evidence points to the existence of regimes, possibly associated with algorithmic execution of metaorders. In this case, existing methods provide negative PnL. In this paper, we develop a deep reinforcement-learning market maker (RLMM)-a Rainbow-style distributional DQN (C51) which is calibrated and tested in a zero-intelligence limit order book. We find that, in the stationary setting, RLMM outperforms GLFT across the entire observed risk-return frontier. The RLMM is more robust to flow asymmetry than GLFT, but, like any stationarily trained strategy, it still suffers large drawdowns from inventory saturation under persistent directional imbalance. Augmenting the state of RLMM with two auxiliary signals-a Bayesian online change-point filter over the directional flow bias and a queue-adjusted quote-exposure imbalance-restores profitability. A final scenario-bandit step that reweights low-return regime scenarios further improves performance under random-persistence and correlated-direction stress.

title: Eigenvalue-Decomposition Denoising as an Alternative to Predict-then-Optimize
affiliations: and Regis High School

detail.title: Eigenvalue-Decomposition Denoising as an Alternative to Predict-then-Optimize

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

keywords: Principal component analysis and Decision-focused learning

detail.abstract: Predict-then-optimize methods learn a mapping from contextual features to unknown edge costs. They then solve the induced combinatorial problem on the predicted costs. Smart "Predict, then Optimize" (SPO+) (Elmachtoub and Grigas, 2022) is one such method. This approach is powerful, but it relies on the predictive model being well specified. When the true cost-generating process is nonlinear in the features and the predictor is linear, SPO+'s performance degrades as the misspecification grows. We propose and evaluate a different remedy for a common setting. Suppose the decision-maker observes many noisy realizations of the same underlying cost process. The realized cost vectors themselves can then be treated as a noisy signal. This signal can be denoised directly via eigenvalue decomposition of its covariance matrix before any predictive model is invoked. Eigenvalue decomposition here is equivalent to Principal Component Analysis. We test this idea on the 5×5 grid shortest-path benchmark of Elmachtoub and Grigas (2022). We retain only the top-k eigenvectors of the training cost covariance matrix. New noisy cost observations are projected onto that subspace. Dijkstra's algorithm (Dijkstra, 1959) then solves the shortest path on the result. We find that the choice of k is decisive. Keeping only k = 2 eigenvectors discards real signal. It underperforms even the naive noisy-cost baseline. Setting k = 5 to match the true latent feature dimension changes the outcome completely: eigenvalue-denoised Dijkstra then becomes the best-performing method at every misspecification level tested, outperforming SPO+ by a wide margin under high misspecification.

detail.abstract:
Generative AI can help applicants describe genuine experience. It can also supply claims and explanations that they cannot support. When employers use AI to evaluate these materials, stronger presentation may be mistaken for stronger capability. This conceptual paper examines how assistance on both sides of recruitment changes the evidence available for selection. It defines signal integrity as the extent to which an application or assessment provides supportable evidence of the candidate's job-relevant capability under stated conditions of tool use. The framework distinguishes the provenance and fidelity of individual claims from the discriminating value and predictive validity of selection procedures. It also separates assistance that clarifies existing evidence, learning that changes capability and substitution that misrepresents it. Seven propositions specify when these processes should affect rankings, verification and subsequent performance. A proposed research program combines controlled resume experiments, comparisons of human and AI decision procedures, and longitudinal validation. Examples from software, manufacturing and healthcare illustrate how task demands determine what must be demonstrated independently and what should be assessed with permitted tools. No original empirical findings are reported. The framework directs attention to a practical question: what evidence would justify treating an AI-assisted application as a credible account of the work a candidate can perform?

detail.abstract: Recent work in international business views supply base international diversification (SBID) as an important strategy for strengthening multinational enterprises' (MNEs') resilience to country-level disruptions. However, it remains unclear how this resilience-oriented strategy relates to MNEs' parallel efforts to improve supply base sustainability performance (SBSP). Drawing on transaction cost economics and the literature on supply chain governance, we argue that increasing SBID lowers MNEs' costs of switching away from suppliers with poor sustainability performance, while simultaneously raising the costs of monitoring sustainability across heterogeneous supplier-country contexts. Together, these countervailing mechanisms suggest an inverted U-shaped relationship between SBID and SBSP. We further argue that this relationship is moderated by an MNE's own sustainability performance, its relational embeddedness with its suppliers, and the institutional distance between its home country and supplier countries. Our analyses of 320 U.S. firms listed in the S&P 500 over the period 2010-2019 support our hypotheses. Our findings highlight the tension that MNEs face in simultaneously enhancing the resilience and sustainability performance of their supply base and indicate that SBID should be optimized rather than maximized to balance these dual objectives.
